The very fact that it grieves you is a sign that the Spirit is at work in you, not that you are beyond reach.

In a sentence. When everything had been arranged like this, the priests went regularly into the outer room to carry out their ministry, but only the high priest entered the inner room, only once a year, and never without blood, which he offered for himself and for the sins the people had committed in ignorance.

On a Tuesday. Imagine for a moment that you were a faithful Israelite. You could stand in the courtyard, but you could never enter the tent. Your priest could enter the first room, but never the second. You would live and die without ever coming nearer to God than a curtain. Now think about what you will do tonight: you will pray, perhaps briefly and tiredly, and you will come straight into the presence of God through Christ, without a bull, a goat or a priest standing between you. Do not let the privilege become ordinary. Before you speak to God tonight, take a moment to remember the curtain, and thank him that you may come in.

For worship. For fourteen centuries God taught his people the distance with a building, and every Yom Kippur the lesson was repeated: one man, one day, with blood, and the sins that mattered most still not reached. He did not do this because he was content with the distance. He did it so that when his Son came, his people would know exactly what he had done. The door that only the high priest could open once a year, Christ has opened for ever, and he did it not with the blood of a bull but with his own, and for the sins the old ceremonies could not touch. The Holy of Holies is no longer a room his people walk past. It is the place where they live.

verseByVerse.quote: By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing (which is symbolic for the present age). According to this arrangement, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper, but deal only with food and drink and various washings, regulations for the body imposed until the time of reformation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing (which is symbolic for the present age). According to this arrangement, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper, but deal only with food and drink and various washings, regulations for the body imposed until the time of reformation.

By this the Holy Spirit indicates. The phrase repays a stop. “Indicates” (dēlountos) means makes clear, shows. The writer is not saying the tabernacle’s design happened to suggest something. He says the Holy Spirit was speaking through the architecture. The Spirit who gave Moses the pattern on the mountain, and who inspired the record of it in Scripture, was teaching through its very structure. The curtains, the restrictions, the single day: these were not merely practical arrangements for a holy God. They were a sermon in cloth and gold, preached silently for centuries.

That the way into the holy places is not yet opened. And the message of the sermon was two words: not yet. “Way” (hodos) is a road. The road into the true presence of God was not open. Every priest who walked into the Holy Place and stopped at the second curtain was preaching it. When Jesus died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51; Mark 15:38). Torn from the top: God did it, not men. And this letter will soon tell us that we now have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain (10:19–20).

As long as the first section is still standing. “First section” (prōtē skēnē, first tent) here probably means the whole first tabernacle arrangement, not only the outer room. As long as that order had standing, as long as it was the way God was to be approached, access was barred. Its very existence said the way was shut.

Which is symbolic for the present age. The word is parabolē, a parable. The tabernacle was an acted parable for the time then present, the old covenant era. And like Jesus’ parables, its meaning was hidden in plain sight, waiting for the one who could explain it.

According to this arrangement, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper. Then the verdict, and it is the heart of the chapter. “Perfect” (teleiōsai) means bring to completion, bring to the goal. “Conscience” (syneidēsis) is the inner moral awareness of guilt, the knowledge we carry about ourselves. There is the limitation, named exactly. Not that the sacrifices did nothing: they did what they were given to do. What they could not do was reach the conscience. A man could bring his goat, watch it die, see the blood applied, walk home ceremonially clean, and still know perfectly well what he had done (10:1–4).

A description you can check from the inside. Anyone can verify that this is true. Religious observance can leave a person outwardly regular and inwardly unrelieved. You can attend, give, sing, serve and still lie awake with the thing you did. And the writer says the old system was designed that way, so that the ache would remain until something could answer it. The sacrifices were not failures; they were signposts, and a signpost that makes you feel you have arrived has stopped doing its job.

But deal only with food and drink and various washings, regulations for the body imposed until the time of reformation. Food laws (Leviticus 11), drink offerings and rules about drink (Numbers 6:3), ritual washings (Leviticus 15; Numbers 19): outward things, addressing the outside of a person. “Regulations for the body” (dikaiōmata sarkos) are ordinances of the flesh, external rules. “Imposed” (epikeimena) means laid on, like a load; Peter called the law a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear (Acts 15:10). And “until the time of reformation” (mechri kairou diorthōseōs) means until the time of setting things straight, of a new order. The word is used of setting a broken bone. The old arrangement had an expiry date written into it from the beginning, and it was never meant to be permanent. The time of setting things right has come in Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that believers under the old covenant had no forgiveness. They were truly forgiven, through faith in God’s promise, looking forward to what the sacrifices pointed to (11:39–40; Romans 3:25; 4:6–8). Abraham was justified by faith; David knew the blessedness of the man whose sin is covered. But the sacrifices themselves could not give the clear and settled conscience that Christ’s finished work now gives. The saints of old were forgiven, and longed for what we have been shown.

Do the food laws and washings apply to Christians today? No. They were regulations for the body, imposed until the time of reformation, and that time has come. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and Peter was told not to call common what God has cleansed (Acts 10:15). The moral law, summarised in the Ten Commandments, still shows us how to love God and our neighbour; but the ceremonial laws, the diet, the washings, the sacrifices, were shadows, and the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Westminster 19.3). A Christian may keep any diet he likes for health or conscience, but no food and no washing brings him nearer to God.

Why do I still feel guilty after I have prayed and gone to church? Because religious activity cannot do what only Christ’s blood does, and sometimes we are leaning on the activity. Ask what you are trusting: the fact that you prayed, or the one you prayed to. A clean conscience comes from looking at the finished sacrifice, not at the quality of your devotion. Sometimes, too, guilt lingers because a specific sin has not actually been confessed, or a wrong done to someone has not been put right; then the remedy is to do that. And sometimes the conscience is simply oversensitive and needs to be taught by Scripture. In each case the answer is the same: bring it to Christ, and believe what God says about his blood.

In a sentence. By this the Holy Spirit was showing that the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been opened while the first tabernacle was still standing; it is an illustration for that time, showing that the gifts and sacrifices offered could not clear the conscience of the worshipper, since they dealt only with food and drink and various ceremonial washings, outward regulations in force until the time when God would set things right.

On a Tuesday. Notice the rituals you use to quiet your conscience. They may not be animals and washings; they may be extra effort at work after a failure at home, a burst of religious activity after a bad week, a resolve to be nicer tomorrow, or simply keeping busy so that you do not have to think. None of them reaches the conscience. Today, when something accuses you, stop performing and go straight to Christ: tell God the thing, and rest on the blood that perfects the conscience. Then do the next duty, not to pay for the sin, but because you are free.

For worship. The Holy Spirit preached for fourteen hundred years in curtains and gold, and the sermon was not yet. He let a whole nation feel the ache of an unrelieved conscience, generation after generation, so that when the answer came they would know it for what it was. And the answer came. God did not leave the bone unset. The time of setting things right arrived in a person, and the curtain that had said not yet was torn from top to bottom by the hand of God. The Spirit who wrote not yet on the tabernacle writes now on the hearts of believers, and what he writes is come in.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and more perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation) he entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and more perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation) he entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption.

But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come. After ten verses of curtains and restrictions, the sentence breaks like a door opening. “Appeared” (paragenomenos) means arrived, came on the scene. “The good things that have come” (tōn genomenōn agathōn) are the blessings of the new covenant, already present: real forgiveness, access to God, a clean conscience. Not things that are coming but things that have come. The old order dealt in anticipation; this one deals in arrival. Some manuscripts read good things to come (mellontōn), as in 10:1, and the difference is small: the good things have arrived in Christ and will be fully enjoyed when he returns. Either way, the man who brings them is already here.

Then through the greater and more perfect tent. “Greater” (meizonos) and “more perfect” (teleioteras). The sanctuary Christ passed through is the heavenly reality the tabernacle copied. It is greater because it is God’s own dwelling, and more perfect because it actually does what the earthly one could only picture: it brings a man into the presence of God.

Not made with hands, that is, not of this creation. “Not made with hands” (ou cheiropoiētou) is the phrase the Bible uses to set human shrines against God’s reality (Acts 7:48; Mark 14:58). And “not of this creation” puts it outside the whole order of made things. The sanctuary he passed through is not a building at all. It is heaven, the presence of God himself (v. 24).

He entered once for all into the holy places. There is the word again, ephapax, once for all, as in 7:27, and set against verse 7 it is the whole argument. The high priest went in once a year, every year, and came out again, and next year he had to go back. This one went in once in all history, at his ascension, and did not need to go again (v. 24). He did not come back out to repeat it. He sat down (1:3; 10:12).

Not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood. Every high priest in history walked behind that curtain carrying blood that was not his. The animal had died in his place, and the man was, in the most literal sense, handling somebody else’s death. This priest brought his own, which means he had already been the victim before he was the officiant. Blood signifies life given up in death (Leviticus 17:11): his life, poured out for us. Not animal blood, which could never take away sins (10:4), but the blood of the sinless Son of God, God and man in one person (Acts 20:28).

Thus securing an eternal redemption. “Redemption” (lytrōsis) is the market-place word for buying a slave out, liberation by the payment of a ransom. “Eternal” (aiōnios) is the letter’s standing contrast with the annual: not a release renewed each autumn, but one that never expires. And the verb (heuramenos, having obtained) is an aorist, a finished achievement; it means to find or obtain, with the sense of achieving something by effort. He did not receive the redemption as a gift. He went and got it, and the cost is in the previous clause.

A redemption actually secured. Notice what the verse says Christ obtained. Not a possible redemption, offered to all and secured for none, waiting to see whether anyone would make it effective. An actual redemption, obtained and secured for those for whom he died. When a ransom is paid, the captive goes free. The death of Christ did not make salvation merely possible; it accomplished it, and it will be applied by the Spirit to every one of those for whom it was paid (John 6:37–39; 10:11, 27–29). That is why the redemption is eternal: nothing in the redeemed can undo what the Redeemer has done.

What it does not mean. “By means of his own blood” does not mean that Christ literally carried a vessel of blood into heaven, as some have imagined. It means he entered by virtue of a death already accomplished, on the strength of his own life laid down, rather than an animal’s. Nor does it mean that his work in heaven completes an unfinished sacrifice. The sacrifice was finished on the cross, as he himself said: it is finished (John 19:30). In heaven he appears for us on the ground of what was done, and intercedes for us (7:25), but he never offers again.

Does eternal redemption mean I can never be lost? Yes, if you belong to Christ. A redemption that could be lost would not be eternal; it would last only as long as the redeemed held on. But the ransom was paid by Christ and accepted by the Father, and the one who redeemed you keeps you (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:33–39). That does not make sin unimportant. The redeemed are given a new heart and will persevere in faith and holiness, though with falls along the way; Hebrews itself warns sharply against drifting, because warnings are one of the means God uses to keep his people. But your security rests on what he secured, not on how firmly you hold him.

In a sentence. But when Christ came as high priest of the good things that are now here, he went through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made by human hands and not part of this created world, and entered the Most Holy Place once for all, not with the blood of goats and calves, but with his own blood, and so obtained a redemption that lasts for ever.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to think your standing with God depends on today’s performance, rehearse the tenses of this verse. He appeared. He entered. He secured. All finished, and none of it waiting on you. Then let that settled fact change how you handle today’s failure: not by lowering your concern about sin, but by facing it as someone already bought out. A redeemed slave does not go back to the market to see whether he is still free. He goes home.

For worship. Every priest before him carried someone else’s death behind the curtain. Christ carried his own. He was the priest and the lamb, the one who offered and the one who was offered, and he did not need an animal to stand in for him, because he was standing in for us. He walked through the true sanctuary, not made with hands, into the presence of the Father, and he did it once, and he did not come out to do it again, because it was done. He did not offer redemption and wait to see who would take it. He paid the ransom in full, with his own blood, and the captives he bought are free for ever. Nothing in heaven, on earth or in the conscience of a believer can undo it.

verseByVerse.quote: For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.

For if the blood of goats and bulls. The argument is from lesser to greater, and it begins by conceding that the old sacrifices genuinely worked. The blood of goats and bulls was shed on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16).

And the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer. The ashes of the red heifer (Numbers 19) were the remedy for corpse-defilement. A spotless red heifer was burned outside the camp, with cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet yarn, and its ashes were kept and mixed with water and sprinkled on anyone who had touched a dead body. Death defiled; and in a world full of death, everyone needed the water sooner or later.

Sanctify for the purification of the flesh. And it worked. The writer grants it without qualification. “Sanctify” (hagiazei) is to make holy, and the rite really did restore ritual purity, so that a man could take part in worship again. But mark what it achieved: purification of the flesh (tēs sarkos katharotēta), outward, bodily cleanness. It made a man ceremonially clean and fit to come back into the camp. It did not touch him.

How much more will the blood of Christ. “How much more” (posō mallon) is the argument from the shadow to the reality. If the shadow worked outwardly, how much more will the substance work inwardly. And three things are said about this offering that make the comparison irresistible.

Who through the eternal Spirit offered himself. First, “through the eternal Spirit” (dia pneumatos aiōniou). Most likely this is the Holy Spirit, who anointed and empowered Christ throughout his ministry (Luke 4:18; Acts 10:38) and in his self-offering. The whole Trinity is in the sentence: the Son offers himself, through the Spirit, to the Father. Whatever else Calvary was, it was not the Father doing something to an unwilling Son, nor the Son persuading a reluctant Father. It was the one God, Father, Son and Spirit, acting together to save. And the Spirit is eternal, which is part of why the sacrifice has eternal value. Second, he offered himself, and the reflexive is the difference between this and every sacrifice before it. No animal ever volunteered. They were led, held and killed. This victim walked to it (John 10:17–18), and the letter has already shown him praying with loud cries and tears about doing so (5:7). He was both priest and sacrifice.

Without blemish to God. Third, “without blemish” (amōmos), the technical requirement for a sacrificial animal (Leviticus 22:20–22), applied here to a moral life. Every lamb was inspected for defects. This one was inspected by enemies who wanted a charge and could not find one; by Pilate, who found no guilt in him; by a dying thief, who said this man has done nothing wrong; and by the Father, who was well pleased (1 Peter 1:19; 2:22).

Purify our conscience from dead works. And there is the answer to verse 9. What the old system could not reach, this reaches: not the flesh but the conscience, the thing that goes on accusing after the ritual is complete. “Purify” (kathariei) is to cleanse. “Dead works” (nekra erga), as in 6:1, are works that lead to death: our sins, and perhaps also the religious works done to earn God’s favour. And the image is precise. Just as touching a corpse defiled a man under the law of the red heifer, so dead works defile the conscience. We have all been handling death. The blood of Christ is the water that cleanses from it.

To serve the living God. The contrast is exact and faintly shocking: dead works, living God. “Serve” (latreuein) is to worship, to serve as a priest. The purpose of cleansing is not merely relief but service. A conscience that has not been cleansed produces religion: activity performed to settle a debt, which never settles it. A cleansed conscience is released into service, which is a different thing altogether, and can only be done by someone who has stopped paying.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a believer will never feel guilt again. When we sin we feel it, and we should; but we bring it to Christ, whose blood goes on cleansing (1 John 1:7–9). Nor does it mean that we serve in order to be cleansed. The order runs the other way: we are cleansed in order to serve.

How do I know my conscience has been cleansed, when I still remember what I did? Cleansing is not forgetting. Paul never forgot that he had persecuted the church (1 Timothy 1:13–15), but he remembered it as a forgiven man, and it made him wonder at grace rather than sink under guilt. A cleansed conscience is one that no longer accuses you before God, because it has accepted God’s verdict on the blood of Christ. The memory may still bring sorrow, and it may make you humble and gentle with others; but when it starts to say that you are condemned, answer it with this verse. God has accepted the offering, and your guilt is gone.

What is the difference between serving to pay and serving because you are free? The work may look the same from outside, and the difference is in the heart. The man who serves to pay is anxious, keeps score, resents interruptions, and is crushed when he fails, because his standing depends on it. The man who serves because he is free works hard too, but gladly; he can rest without guilt, fail without despair, and rejoice when someone else gets the credit. If your service feels like an unpaid debt, you have probably slipped back into dead works. Go back to the blood, and let your service begin again from there.

In a sentence. The blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are ceremonially unclean make them outwardly clean; how much more, then, will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our consciences from deeds that lead to death, so that we may serve the living God!

On a Tuesday. Look at one thing you will do for God today: a task at church, a kindness to a neighbour, a time of prayer. Ask honestly why you are doing it. If the answer is to make up for something, or to keep God on your side, stop for a moment, confess that, and receive afresh what the blood of Christ has already done. Then do the same task again, as a son and not a debtor. It is often the same work. It is never the same experience.

For worship. The ashes of a heifer could make a man clean enough to come back into the camp. The blood of Christ makes a sinner clean enough to come into the presence of the living God. And look how it was offered: by the Son, willingly, through the eternal Spirit, to the Father, without a single blemish found in him by friend or enemy. The whole Godhead bent down to wash the conscience of people who had been handling death all their lives. And having washed us, he does not send us away. He takes us into his service, priests of the living God, working not for our pardon but from it.
verseByVerse.note: The ashes of a red heifer were mixed with water to cleanse anyone defiled by touching a corpse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–28 — A Death That Reaches Backward, and a Return Without Sin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ is the mediator of a new covenant, and his death redeems people even from the sins committed under the first covenant, so that those God calls can receive the promised eternal inheritance. A will takes effect only when the one who made it dies, and in the same way the first covenant was inaugurated with blood: Moses sprinkled the book, the people, the tent and its vessels, for under the law almost everything is cleansed with blood, and without shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. The earthly copies were cleansed with animal sacrifices, but the heavenly realities needed better ones. Christ did not enter a man-made sanctuary but heaven itself, to appear before God for us. He did not offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest entered year after year with blood not his own; he appeared once, at the climax of the ages, to put away sin by sacrificing himself. Just as people die once and then face judgement, Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many, and he will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to bring salvation to those who are eagerly waiting for him.
verseByVerse.theology:
How the Old Testament Saints Were Saved

Christ's death redeems from transgressions committed under the first covenant. There is one way of salvation, looked forward to and looked back on.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: At Sinai the book and the people were sprinkled with the blood of the covenant.

Now: Christ will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those eagerly waiting for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred that redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred that redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.

Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant. “Therefore” (dia touto): because his blood cleanses the conscience (v. 14). The theme named at 8:6 is now grounded in the blood of the previous verse. A “mediator” (mesitēs) stands between two parties to bring them together, and the “new covenant” (diathēkē kainē) is the one God promised through Jeremiah, in which he writes his law on the heart and remembers sins no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34; 8:8–12). Christ is not a go-between who carries messages. He is the one in whose blood the covenant is made.

So that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance. “Those who are called” (hoi keklēmenoi) is a perfect participle: those who have been called and remain called. It is the writer’s quiet word for the people in view. Not those who volunteered, but those whom God has effectually called (3:1; Romans 8:28–30). The initiative is God’s in this letter as everywhere in the New Testament. And “inheritance” (klēronomia) is family language, which has been in the letter since 1:2, where the Son was appointed heir of all things. What is his by right becomes theirs by gift. It is not the land of Canaan, which Israel lost, but eternal life, the new creation, God himself: an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven (1 Peter 1:4).

Since a death has occurred that redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant. “A death” is Christ’s death, and it “redeems” (apolytrōsis): release by ransom. The inheritance comes to the heirs only because a death has taken place. And the clause repays close reading. The death is retrospective in its reach. It deals with sins committed before it happened: the transgressions of people who lived and died under the old arrangement, whose sacrifices could not perfect the conscience. That answers a question every thoughtful reader of the Old Testament eventually asks. If the blood of bulls and goats could not take away sins (10:4), on what basis were Abraham, Moses and David forgiven? The answer here is that they were forgiven on exactly the same basis as we are, and the payment was made afterwards.

Credit against a payment God intended to make. Paul says the same thing when he writes that God in his divine forbearance had passed over former sins, and showed his righteousness at the cross, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25–26). The old sacrifices were, in a sense, credit extended against a payment God intended to make. They pointed forward not merely as pictures but as promises. So there are not two ways of salvation in Scripture, an older one by law and a newer one by grace. There is one, and everyone who has ever been saved has been saved by the same death, some looking forward to it without knowing its name, and some looking back.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Christ died only for Old Testament sins; it means his death covers them too, along with all the sins of all the called, before and after the cross. Nor does “those who are called” mean everyone who hears the gospel invitation. Many hear the outward call and refuse it (Matthew 22:14). The called here are those effectually called by God, whom he draws to Christ and who come.

How do I know if I am one of the called? Not by trying to look into God’s secret decrees, but by looking at Christ. Those whom God calls, he brings to faith in his Son, and the evidence of the call is that you have come to Christ and are trusting him (John 6:37, 44). If you are trusting Christ, however weakly, you were called; nobody comes unless the Father draws him. If you are not sure you are trusting him, the answer is not to wait for a sign but to come to him now, for he has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out. The call of God is heard in the invitation of the gospel.

Were Old Testament believers saved by keeping the law? No. They were saved by grace through faith, exactly as we are (Romans 4:1–8; Galatians 3:6–9). Their sacrifices were God’s appointed way for them to express faith and repentance, and they pointed to the coming sacrifice, but the sacrifices were not the ground of their forgiveness. The ground was the death this verse describes, which God had already determined and which reached back to them. Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness; and the righteousness counted to him was the righteousness of Christ.

In a sentence. That is why Christ is the mediator of a new covenant: so that those God has called may receive the eternal inheritance he promised, now that a death has taken place that sets them free from the sins committed under the first covenant.

On a Tuesday. Read Psalm 32 or Psalm 103 today, and notice that David is rejoicing in a forgiveness he did not fully understand, paid for by a death he never saw. You know the name of the one who paid it. Let that give you both humility and boldness: humility, because David trusted with less light than you have; boldness, because the same death that covered him covers you. And if you are weighed down by an inheritance on earth that has disappointed you, an estate lost, a family broken, a career that never came to much, remember that your real inheritance is kept in heaven and cannot be spent, stolen or contested.

For worship. The death of Christ is not a recent event in the history of salvation. It is the centre of it, and its reach goes backward as well as forward. Abel’s lamb, Abraham’s ram, the blood on the doorposts in Egypt, the goat of every Day of Atonement, all of them were drawing on an account that would be paid in full on a hill outside Jerusalem. God has only ever had one way of saving sinners, and it has always been his Son. And the mediator who made the covenant in his blood is the heir of all things, who did not keep his inheritance to himself but called a people to share it.

verseByVerse.quote: For where a will is involved, the death of the one who made it must be established. For a will takes effect only at death, since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive. Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For where a will is involved, the death of the one who made it must be established. For a will takes effect only at death, since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive. Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.

For where a will is involved. The writer is making a play on a word, and it helps to know what he is doing. The Greek diathēkē means both covenant and testament: a legal arrangement, and specifically a last will. In everyday Greek it usually meant a will. He has been using it in the first sense for two chapters, and here he turns it to the second. An inheritance (v. 15) comes through a will, and a will requires a death.

The death of the one who made it must be established. Before an inheritance is distributed, the death of the testator must be proved. For a will takes effect only at death: “takes effect” (bebaia) means valid, binding, in force. That is simply how inheritance works and always has. A will is a real document the day it is signed, and it does nothing whatever. The named heirs have no claim, the estate does not move, and the whole thing waits on one event.

Since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive. Apply it to the previous verse and the connection appears. Christ is the mediator, and there is a promised eternal inheritance, and an inheritance requires a death. The testator had to die before anybody could receive anything. Only when he died did his will come into force for his heirs.

The cross as the reading of a will. That puts the cross in an unexpected light. It was not only a sacrifice offered and a penalty borne, though it was both. It was also the death that made a will operative, the moment at which an estate long promised became actually available to the heirs. And the will is unlike any other in one respect. In every other case the testator is dead when the will is read, and he has no further say in who gets what. This testator rose on the third day, and he is himself the executor of his own will. He sees to it personally that every heir receives what was left to him.

Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood. “Inaugurated” (enkekainistai) means dedicated, ratified, put into effect. The writer swings back to the other sense of the word, and the Sinai covenant was ratified with blood (v. 19; Exodus 24:3–8). In ancient covenant-making a sacrificial death sealed the agreement. When God made his covenant with Abraham, the animals were cut in two and a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between the pieces (Genesis 15:9–18; Jeremiah 34:18–20). So the two meanings of the word are held together by a single fact: whichever way you read diathēkē, somebody has to die before it operates. And “not even” is an argument from the lesser case. If the shadow required blood, how much more the substance.

Where translations differ. Some translators keep covenant throughout verses 16–17 and read them as being about a covenant ratified by a representative death, since covenants in the Bible were sealed by the death of an animal standing for the covenant-maker. The ESV takes them as a testament, and the logic of verse 17 favours that, because the sentence about a document not being in force while its maker lives fits a will exactly. Both readings land in the same place: the covenant God made with his people could not come into force without the death of Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s covenant is merely a human legal document. The illustration from wills makes one point: a death was necessary. The divine covenant is far greater than any will, and the testator who died is also the one who rose and administers his own will.

If a will can be changed, can God change his mind about me? No. A human will can be altered while the testator lives, but this one came into force by his death, and the testator who rose does not revoke it. The terms are fixed in his blood, and he lives to see that they are carried out (7:25). God’s promises in Christ are yes and amen (2 Corinthians 1:20). The will names its heirs as those who are called and who trust the Son, and if you are trusting him, you are named.

In a sentence. In the case of a will, the death of the person who made it must be proved, because a will comes into force only when someone has died; it never takes effect while the one who made it is still alive, and that is why even the first covenant was not put into effect without blood.

On a Tuesday. If you have ever been named in a will, you know the strange feeling of receiving something because somebody you loved has died. Let that feeling teach you how to receive the gospel. You did not earn your inheritance in Christ; it came to you through his death. So receive it with gratitude rather than entitlement, and with sorrow mixed with joy. And think practically about what you are leaving behind: not only a will for your possessions, but the testimony to Christ you will hand on to your children and friends. Make sure they know where your real inheritance came from.

For worship. The Son is the heir of all things, and he wrote into his will people who had nothing to bring and every reason to be left out: rebels, debtors and strangers to the covenant. To make them his heirs he did what no rich man ever does for a beggar. He died, so that what was his by right could become theirs by gift. And the estate he left is not a portion of his goods but all of them, and himself with them. Those who were named in his blood will never be read out of it, because the one who died to sign it lives to keep it.
verseByVerse.note: The Greek word for “covenant” can also mean a “will,” and the writer uses both senses.

verseByVerse.quote: For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.” And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship. Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.” And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship. Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.

For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people. The scene is Exodus 24, the ratification of the covenant at Sinai, and the writer describes it in some detail because he wants the blood in his readers’ eyes. The terms were read aloud first. Moses read the Book of the Covenant to the people, and they promised to obey (Exodus 24:3–7). Nobody was bound to something they had not heard.

He took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop. Hyssop was a small bushy plant used as a brush. It appears at the Passover, where it painted the blood on the doorposts (Exodus 12:22); in the cleansing of lepers (Leviticus 14:4–7); in David’s prayer, purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean (Psalm 51:7); and at the cross, where a sponge of sour wine was lifted to Jesus on a hyssop branch (John 19:29). The little plant runs through the whole story of cleansing, from Egypt to Golgotha.

And sprinkled both the book itself and all the people. Exodus 24:6–8 mentions the altar and the people. The writer adds the book, and the water, scarlet wool and hyssop, which Exodus 24 does not mention. He draws those details from the other cleansing rites of the law, where blood, water, scarlet yarn and hyssop belong together (Leviticus 14:4–7; Numbers 19:6, 18), perhaps also from Jewish tradition about the ceremony, and gathers them into one picture of covenant cleansing. He adds nothing that contradicts Exodus; he shows what the ceremony at Sinai shared with the rest of the law. And consider the scene as it would have looked: a nation standing in the open, and blood flicked over them and over the scroll of the law. The blood marked both the covenant document and the covenant people as bound together. Even the book of the covenant needed blood before the arrangement could stand.

Saying, This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you. These words are from Exodus 24:8, and they are worth reading twice, because the readers of this letter had heard them again in an upper room, from a man holding a cup: this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many (Mark 14:24; Matthew 26:28), the new covenant in my blood (Luke 22:20). Jesus was quoting Sinai deliberately, and telling his disciples what he was about to do. Every time the church takes the cup at the Lord’s Supper, it hears the voice of Moses at the foot of the mountain, and the voice of Christ on the night he was betrayed, saying the same thing.

And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship. The tabernacle and its furnishings were consecrated with blood and oil (Exodus 40:9–11; Leviticus 8:15, 19). Nothing used in the worship of a holy God by sinful people could be used without being cleansed first.

Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood. The “almost” (schedon) is a careful touch. Some things were purified by water or by fire (Numbers 31:22–24), and there was an exception for the very poor, who could bring flour for a sin offering (Leviticus 5:11–13). But blood was the main means, and the exceptions prove the rule by their rarity.

And without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins. The principle stated flatly. “Shedding of blood” (haimatekchysia) is a word perhaps coined by the writer himself: blood-pouring. “Forgiveness” (aphesis) is release, cancellation. Forgiveness requires a death, life given for life (Leviticus 17:11). Sin deserves death (Romans 6:23), and forgiveness comes only when a substitute dies in the sinner’s place, bearing the penalty he deserved. This is the logic of penal substitution, which the whole sacrificial system taught and which Christ fulfilled.

The sentence modern readers most resist. It should not be softened, and it should be understood. The point is not that God is appeased by suffering, which is the pagan idea of an angry deity bribed with blood. It is that sin is not a debt that can be waived by a stroke of the pen without something being false. A God who simply overlooked evil would not be kind; he would be indifferent to the people it destroyed. A judge who lets the man who abused a child walk free because he is a forgiving sort of person is not merciful but corrupt. Forgiveness is never free. It is free to the one forgiven and costly to the one who forgives, and the cross is what that costs when the wrong is against God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God is bloodthirsty. It means sin is so serious that it can be dealt with only by death, and God in love provided the death himself, in his Son (Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:10). The one who demanded the blood is the one who gave it. Nor does it mean that animal blood could truly forgive; it pointed to the blood that does (10:4).

Why does the Lord’s Supper use wine for blood? Because Jesus deliberately took the covenant words of Sinai and applied them to his own death, and he gave the cup as the sign of it. The wine does not become blood; it is a sign and seal of the blood once shed, and by faith those who drink it truly feed on Christ and the benefits of his death, spiritually and not physically (1 Corinthians 10:16; 11:25–26; Westminster 29.7). It is not a repeated sacrifice, since this chapter insists there is only one. It is a meal of remembrance and communion at which the covenant is renewed in the hearts of God’s people. Come to it as a forgiven sinner, examining yourself, not as someone trying to make yourself worthy.

In a sentence. When Moses had told all the people every command of the law, he took the blood of calves and goats, together with water, scarlet wool and branches of hyssop, and sprinkled the scroll and all the people, saying, This is the blood of the covenant, which God has commanded you to keep; in the same way he sprinkled with blood the tabernacle and everything used in its worship; in fact, under the law almost everything is made clean with blood, and without the pouring out of blood there is no forgiveness.

On a Tuesday. When someone wrongs you, notice how forgiveness actually works. You cannot simply say it did not matter; it did. To forgive is to absorb the cost yourself rather than make the other person pay it: the lost money, the hurt reputation, the pain you carry and refuse to repay. That is a small picture of what God did. So when you find it hard to forgive, look at the cross. And at the next Lord’s Supper, when the cup is passed, hear the words of Sinai in it: this is the blood of the covenant, poured out for the forgiveness of your sins.

For worship. At Sinai the people stood under the blood of calves and goats, and promised to keep a law they would break within weeks. In the upper room Jesus took a cup and said the same words, and then went out and shed his own blood, for people who would break their promises that same night. The blood of the old covenant bound the people to obey; the blood of the new covenant secured forgiveness for those who had not. God did not lower his holiness to forgive us. He paid what holiness required, with his own Son. And the cup we drink, on all the Sundays until he comes, is the sign that it is enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf. Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own, for then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf. Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own, for then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.

Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites. “Copies” (hypodeigmata), as in 8:5, are sketches, outlines, patterns. The earthly tabernacle, being a copy, needed cleansing with animal blood, as the previous verses showed.

But the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. The sentence has puzzled readers: why would heavenly things need purifying? Not because heaven itself is defiled. The likeliest sense is that the heavenly sanctuary required consecration for its use by sinners. Access for defiled people had to be opened by blood, as the tabernacle’s use required its dedication. And the people of God are themselves his true dwelling, the house he lives in (3:6), and they needed cleansing. “Better sacrifices” is plural as a general category, matching the plural of the old rites, but it means Christ’s single sacrifice, offered once (vv. 25–26).

For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself. Earthly shrines are only copies (antitypa, corresponding figures) of the real. Christ entered not a heavenly building but heaven itself, the very presence of God.

Now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf. That last phrase is the one to carry away. “Now”: at this very moment. “Appear” (emphanisthēnai) means to be made manifest, to show oneself before someone’s face. The high priest went behind the curtain representing the tribes, with their names cut into stones on his shoulders and on the breastpiece over his heart (Exodus 28:9–12, 29). This one went into the presence of God carrying us. Christ stands before the face of the Father as our representative, and he is there now (7:25; Romans 8:34; 1 John 2:1).

Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own. For then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. The logic repays following, because it is a reductio. If Christ’s offering worked the way the old ones did, it would need renewing, and since sin has been in the world from the beginning, he would have been dying over and over since Eden. The absurdity proves the point: a sacrifice that has to be repeated is a sacrifice that did not work. One death was enough.

But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages. “Appeared” (pephanerōtai) is a perfect tense: he has been manifested, and the effect remains. This is his first coming. “Once for all” (hapax). And “the end of the ages” (synteleia tōn aiōnōn), the consummation, the completion of the ages, is where the New Testament always locates the cross (1:2): not in the middle of history but at its hinge. Everything before ran toward it; everything since runs from it.

To put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. “Put away” (athetēsis) is a strong word: to abolish, to set aside, to annul. It is the same word used of setting aside the former commandment (7:18), a word for cancelling a law. Sin was not merely covered, as the old rites covered it. It was abolished, its guilt cancelled and its power broken. And it was done “by the sacrifice of himself”: not of an animal, but of himself.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that heaven was dirty. The cleansing language is about consecrating the way of access for sinners. Nor does Christ’s appearing for us mean that the Father is reluctant and must be talked round. It was the Father who sent him (John 3:16), and Christ appears before a Father who loves us as he loves the Son (John 16:26–27; 17:23).

What is Christ doing in heaven now? He is appearing for you. He is not repeating his sacrifice, which is finished; he is presenting himself, the one whose sacrifice was accepted, as the ground on which you are received. He intercedes for his people, praying for them as he prayed for Peter (Luke 22:32; Romans 8:34). He rules all things for the church (Ephesians 1:20–22). And he is preparing a place (John 14:2–3). When you pray, you are not approaching a stranger; you are coming to a Father before whom your Saviour is already standing, with your name on his heart.

Does the Roman Catholic Mass repeat Christ’s sacrifice? Roman Catholic teaching calls the Mass a true and propitiatory sacrifice, the same sacrifice as Calvary offered in an unbloody manner, and denies that it is a new or different one. But this verse rules out any continuing offering of Christ for sin. He does not offer himself repeatedly; he appeared once for all to put away sin. The Lord’s Supper is a remembrance of that one sacrifice and a communion in it, not a re-presentation of the victim to God for propitiation (Westminster 29.2). Hebrews returns to this again and again (7:27; 10:10–14, 18): where there is forgiveness, there is no longer any offering for sin.

In a sentence. So it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified by these sacrifices, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices; for Christ did not enter a sanctuary made by human hands, a mere copy of the true one, but heaven itself, now to appear for us in God’s presence; nor did he enter to offer himself again and again, as the high priest enters the Most Holy Place every year with blood not his own, for then he would have had to suffer many times since the creation of the world; but now he has appeared once for all at the climax of history to do away with sin by sacrificing himself.

On a Tuesday. When you feel your sin has been found out again, or that God must be tired of you, picture where Christ is at this moment: standing in the presence of God, on your behalf. He has not left to see whether you will do better. He is there now. So when you fall today, do not wait to pray until you feel clean enough. Go straight to the Father, through the Son who is already appearing for you, and say what you did. Then get up, because the sin has been put away by a sacrifice that does not need repeating.

For worship. If Christ’s sacrifice had been like the others, he would have been dying since the foundation of the world, over and over, for every generation, and it would never have been finished. But it was not like the others. He came once, at the hinge of the ages, and offered himself, and sin was abolished. Then he went into heaven itself, not a room with a curtain but the very presence of God, and he stands there now, for us. The high priest carried the names of the tribes on stones, for one day, and then laid them aside. Christ carries ours on his heart before the face of the Father, and that day has no evening.

verseByVerse.quote: And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment, so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment, so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.

And just as it is appointed for man to die once. Two facts, stated without argument, and the writer expects no dispute about either. “Appointed” (apokeitai) means laid up, reserved, destined. Death is not an accident of biology but an appointment kept, God’s appointment because of sin (Genesis 3:19; Romans 5:12). And “once” (hapax) is doing work beyond the obvious. It rules out any scheme of repeated lives, and more importantly it establishes the pattern the next verse needs: one death, then the reckoning. Every human being dies once, except those alive at Christ’s return (1 Corinthians 15:51–52), and Enoch and Elijah, whom God took.

And after that comes judgment. Something follows death. “Judgment” (krisis): after death every person faces the judgment of God. There is no second chance after death, no reincarnation, no purgatory, no ceasing to exist. At death the soul goes immediately into conscious existence, the believer to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8), the unbeliever to punishment (Luke 16:22–26). At Christ’s return all will be raised and judged (John 5:28–29; Revelation 20:11–15).

Where Christians differ: is there a second chance after death, or a purgatory? Some teach that those who never heard the gospel will have an opportunity to believe after death. Roman Catholic teaching holds that many believers must pass through purgatory to be purified before heaven. Others teach soul sleep, unconsciousness until the resurrection, or annihilation of the wicked. Verdict: this verse is clear: death, then judgment. Death is followed by judgment, not by a further opportunity, and our eternal destiny is fixed at death (Luke 16:26). Believers enter conscious joy with Christ immediately (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23). There is no purgatory, because by a single offering Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (10:14), and that leaves nothing to be paid afterward. Believers too will stand before God, but for them the verdict was given at the cross; what remains is the review of their lives for reward (2 Corinthians 5:10), not a sentence to be served. Unbelievers face conscious punishment, eternal and real (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11). The time to respond to the gospel is now (3:13; 2 Corinthians 6:2).

So Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many. “So Christ”: and the parallel is the point of the whole sentence. He follows the human pattern exactly. Offered once (hapax prosenechtheis), corresponding to the one death of every person; and then what comes after. But his death was for others. “To bear the sins” (anenenkein hamartias, to carry up sins) is Isaiah’s verb: he bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12). It means to take a weight onto oneself, to carry up as onto an altar. Not to sympathise with sinners but to shoulder what they owed, bearing their penalty in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24).

Does many mean that Christ bore the sins of only some? The word comes from Isaiah 53:12, where it sets the one servant against the great number he saves, and Jesus used it of his own death, a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Many Christians take it to mean simply that his death was for the multitude. Reformed Christians take it to mean that he actually bore the sins of a definite people, all who will be saved, the many sons he brings to glory (2:10). The second is the more likely, since to bear sin is to carry it away, and those whose sins he carried will never have to bear them (compare 2:9). Either way, many is not few, and the invitation is to all: no one who comes to him will find that he was not included.

Will appear a second time. And here the parallel turns, because what follows his death is not judgment for him. He has been judged already, in our place. “Appear” (ophthēsetai) means will be seen: his second coming will be visible. And the picture is from the Day of Atonement. The people waited outside while the high priest was in the Most Holy Place, and when he came out alive, they knew the sacrifice had been accepted, and they rejoiced. So Christ will come out from heaven, to the joy of his people.

Not to deal with sin. Literally “without sin” (chōris hamartias): not to bear sin again. That phrase deserves to be underlined for anyone who is afraid of the second coming. The sin business is finished. He is not returning to reopen the file, to weigh his people again, or to see whether the first visit took. That work was completed at his first coming, and he sat down.

But to save those who are eagerly waiting for him. “Save” (eis sōtērian, for salvation) means the final and full salvation of his people, including the resurrection of their bodies (Romans 8:23; Philippians 3:20–21). “Eagerly waiting” (apekdechomenois) means to wait with eager expectation, like someone watching a road. It is a mark of true believers (Titus 2:13), and the same idea as Paul’s crown for all who have loved his appearing (2 Timothy 4:8). That is the description of a Christian this chapter ends on, after all the blood and curtains and ashes: someone standing at the window, looking down the road, waiting for a man who has already dealt with everything that could have made the waiting frightening.

What it does not mean. “Appear a second time” does not mean there will be a secret coming before his visible return. Scripture speaks of one future return, visible and glorious, at which he gathers his people and judges the world (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). A second appearing, not a second and a third.

Will Christians be judged at the last day? Yes, but not to decide whether they are saved. Every person will stand before God, and the lives of believers will be opened (2 Corinthians 5:10; Romans 14:10–12). But the question of their guilt was settled at the cross, where Christ bore their sins, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). What remains is a Father’s public acknowledgement of his children, and the reward of what was done in his name, even a cup of cold water (Matthew 10:42). That should make us serious about how we live, and not afraid of the day.

What happens to my believing loved ones who have died? They are with Christ, consciously, now. To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), and Paul calls it far better (Philippians 1:23). They are not asleep in the sense of being unconscious, nor in purgatory, nor wandering; they are with him, at rest and in joy, waiting with us for the resurrection of the body. When Christ appears the second time, he will bring them with him (1 Thessalonians 4:14), and their bodies will be raised and made like his. You may grieve, and you should; but you grieve as one who has hope.

In a sentence. Just as everyone is destined to die once and after that to face judgment, so Christ was offered once to carry the sins of many, and he will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to bring salvation to those who are eagerly waiting for him.

On a Tuesday. You have one life and one death, and then the judgment. That is not a reason for panic, but it is a reason for seriousness. Is there anything you are putting off in your relationship with God: a sin you mean to deal with later, a step of obedience you are delaying, a friend you mean one day to tell about Christ? There is no later after death. Do it while it is called today. And ask yourself whether you are eagerly waiting for Christ. If the thought of his return frightens you, look again at the words not to deal with sin. If it barely crosses your mind, ask what has crowded it out, and pray for his coming today.

For worship. Every one of us has an appointment we cannot cancel: death, and then the judgment. Christ kept that appointment for us. He died once, and the judgment that should have followed our death fell on him, as he bore the sins of many. So for his people the order of the verse is changed: after death comes not the judgment but the Judge, and the Judge is the one who was judged in their place. He who came the first time carrying their sins will come the second time without them, because he put them away for ever at the cross, and he will bring nothing with him but salvation.

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

Of these things we cannot now speak in detail.<sup>6</sup>These preparations having thus been made, the priests go regularly into the first section, performing their ritual duties,<sup>7</sup>but into the second only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood, which he offers for himself and for the unintentional sins of the people.<sup>8</sup>By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing<sup>9</sup>(which is symbolic for the present age). 10.title: Once for All: The New and Living Way
10.overview:
Chapter 10 is the summit of the letter’s central argument. Priesthood (chapters 5–7), covenant (8) and sacrifice (9) converge here. The law’s yearly animal sacrifices are set against Christ’s single offering, with Psalm 40 as the key: “I have come to do your will, O God.” By that will, through the offering of his body once for all, “we have been sanctified.”

Then the longest application (vv. 19–39): draw near to God, hold fast the confession, and stir one another up to love and good works. The fourth and severest warning follows (vv. 26–31), balanced at once by encouragement: remember how you once joyfully accepted the loss of your property. You need endurance for a little while more. The coming one will come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — One Sacrifice, and a Priest Who Sat Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer explains why the old sacrifices could never deal with sin. The law was only a shadow of the good things to come, not the reality, so its sacrifices, repeated year after year, could not make worshippers complete; their repetition was itself a yearly reminder of sin, since animal blood cannot remove it. Psalm 40 shows what replaces them: Christ came to do God’s will in the body prepared for him, setting aside the old system. By that will we have been made holy through the once-for-all offering of his body. The old priests stood daily, repeating sacrifices; Christ offered one sacrifice for all time and sat down at God’s right hand, waiting for his enemies to be subdued. The Spirit’s promise of the new covenant in Jeremiah confirms it: God will remember sins no more, and where sins are forgiven no further offering is needed.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Tenses in One Sentence

By a single offering Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified. Where sins are forgiven, there is no longer any offering for sin.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The yearly sacrifices were a reminder of sins, and their repetition confessed that they had not finished the work.

Now: Standing before God does not wait on our progress; our progress flows from a finished offering.

verseByVerse.quote: For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near. Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near. Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?

Meaning first. Hebrews 10 completes the argument about Christ’s sacrifice and turns it into urgent appeal. The old sacrifices, repeated every year, could never take sins away (vv. 1–4). Christ came, as Psalm 40 foretold, to do God’s will in the body prepared for him, and by that will we are sanctified through his offering once for all (vv. 5–10). The priests stand daily; Christ offered one sacrifice and sat down, having perfected for all time those who are being made holy, and where sins are forgiven no further offering remains (vv. 11–18). So, with confidence by his blood, let us draw near, hold fast our hope, and stir one another up, not neglecting to meet together (vv. 19–25). For those who deliberately turn from that sacrifice, no other remains, only judgment (vv. 26–31). Yet remember your former courage, do not throw away your confidence, for the coming one will come, and we are of those who believe and are saved (vv. 32–39). It is the chapter of the priest who sat down.

For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come. The shadow image returns from 8:5. A shadow (skia) shows the outline of something real but is not the thing itself. It tells you something true: a body is there, roughly how tall, roughly what shape. It does not tell you the face, and you cannot shake hands with it. “The good things to come” are the blessings of the new covenant in Christ (9:11): real forgiveness, open access, a cleansed conscience.

Instead of the true form of these realities. The second term sharpens the first. “True form” (eikōn) is the image, the actual likeness, the very substance. The contrast is not between a shadow and nothing, but between a shadow and the thing that casts it. The law had the shadow; Christ is the body that cast it (Colossians 2:17). For fourteen centuries Israel lived with the shadow of the cross falling backward across its history, and the people who saw it most clearly knew that something was coming toward them.

It can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near. “Never” (oudepote): the writer is not describing a system that worked imperfectly, but one that could not, in principle, finish the job. “Continually” (eis to diēnekes) means perpetually; “every year” is the Day of Atonement; and “make perfect” (teleiōsai), as in 7:19 and 9:9, means to bring to the goal, full cleansing and access to God.

Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered? Then a piece of plain reasoning that any worshipper could have done for himself. The repetition is the evidence. A medicine that cures is not taken for ever. If the Day of Atonement had actually dealt with the matter, there would have been no need for another one the following autumn. The fact that the calendar came round again every year was itself a confession that nothing had been concluded.

Since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins. And there is the test the writer applies, and it is an experiential one. “Having once been cleansed” (hapax kekatharismenous) means cleansed once for all. “Consciousness of sins” (syneidēsis hamartiōn) is a conscience of sins, the sense of guilt. A sacrifice that had truly worked would leave a person without a nagging sense of guilt before God: not because he had become forgetful or hardened, and not because he would never again be aware of sinning, but because the thing had been genuinely settled. He would no longer carry the burden of unremoved guilt.

The same accusation, year after year. Put that plainly to any religious system, including the ones people build for themselves inside Christianity. If a person is still trying to quiet the same accusation this year that he was trying to quiet last year, the method is not working, and the repetition is the proof. Penance that has to be done again, a vow renewed every January, a frantic burst of devotion after every fall: these are the Day of Atonement come round again. The writer is preparing to tell his readers about a sacrifice that does not need to be repeated, because it worked.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the old sacrifices were useless, or that God did not command them. They were God’s appointed shadows, pointing to Christ, and believers who offered them in faith were truly forgiven. But they could not achieve what only Christ’s sacrifice could.

Should a Christian ever feel guilty? Yes, when he sins; that is the conscience working as God made it, and the Spirit uses it to bring us back (2 Corinthians 7:10). What this verse rules out is the guilt that stays after a sin has been confessed and forgiven, as if the matter were still open before God. That guilt is not humility; it is unbelief about the sacrifice. The answer to it is not to do something more, but to believe what God says: the sin is cleansed, once for all. Feel sorrow for sin, confess it, turn from it, and then let it go, because God has.

In a sentence. The law is only a shadow of the good things that were coming, not the realities themselves, and so it can never, by the same sacrifices repeated endlessly year after year, make perfect those who come near to worship; otherwise the sacrifices would have stopped, because the worshippers, cleansed once for all, would no longer have felt guilty for their sins.

On a Tuesday. Is there a sin you keep confessing, though you have already confessed it and turned from it? Notice the pattern: the same accusation, the same apology, the same uneasy relief that never lasts. Today, confess it one last time if you must, and then say aloud that Christ has cleansed it once for all. When it comes back tomorrow, do not confess it again as though it were still on the books. Thank God instead that it has been dealt with.

For worship. The shadow fell across Israel for fourteen centuries, and every year it was the same shape: a priest, a goat, a curtain, and a nation that went home and came back the next autumn. And then the one who cast the shadow stepped into the light. He is not an outline or a likeness; he is the reality, and his sacrifice did what no animal could do, because it finished what it began. The calendar of the Day of Atonement has stopped. There is no next year for the sins of God’s people, because the Son of God dealt with them once, and the conscience that was cleansed by his blood has nothing left to fear.

verseByVerse.quote: But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.

But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. This is one of the most penetrating observations in the letter, and it inverts what you would expect. The Day of Atonement is usually thought of as the day sins were dealt with. The writer says its actual effect was to bring them to mind. “Reminder” (anamnēsis) is remembrance, recollection. Picture the ceremony. The high priest lays both hands on the head of the live goat and confesses over it all the iniquities of the people, and the goat is led away into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:21). The whole nation stands and hears its sins recited. That is not an annual clearing of the books. It is an annual reading of them aloud.

The effect was cumulative. A devout Israelite grew old watching the same goat led out into the desert, knowing the priest would be doing it again next autumn. Each Day of Atonement said: your sins are still there. Contrast the new covenant, in which God says he will remember sins no more (8:12; 10:17).

The other remembrance. And there is a striking echo. Jesus used the same word, anamnēsis, of the Lord’s Supper: do this in remembrance of me (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24–25). The old ritual remembered sins; the new remembers the Saviour who removed them. Israel gathered once a year to hear its sins read out. The church gathers week by week to remember the one who took them away.

For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. Then the reason, with a bluntness that must have startled the first hearers. “Impossible” (adynaton) is the same absolute word as 6:4 and 6:18. Not inadequate, not partial: it cannot be done, and it never could. “Take away” (aphairein) means remove, lift off. Consider what a sentence that is to write to people who were being drawn back to the temple, and what it says about the whole sacrificial system God himself commanded. The writer is not accusing anyone of doing it wrongly. He is saying the mechanism was never capable of the result.

Why an animal cannot do it. And the reason is not hard to see once stated. Sin is a personal and moral matter between a creature and his Maker, and an animal is neither a person nor a moral agent. It has done nothing and consented to nothing. A creature that cannot understand the transaction cannot conduct it. It is not of the same nature as the sinner, it cannot willingly offer itself, and it is not of infinite worth. Only the sacrifice of a sinless man, who is also God, could take away sin: a man, to stand in the place of men; sinless, to have no debt of his own; God, to give the offering infinite value.

So what were the sacrifices for? Everything the letter has said supplies the answer. They were the shadow, teaching a nation for fourteen centuries that sin costs life, that God provides the victim, and that somebody innocent dies in the place of somebody guilty. They were a language being taught, so that when the reality came there would be words to describe it. When John the Baptist pointed at Jesus and said, Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29), every Jew in earshot knew exactly what he meant, because God had spent centuries teaching them the word lamb.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Old Testament believers were not truly forgiven. They were, but not by the animals. They were forgiven by God’s grace through faith, on the credit of the sacrifice Christ would offer: his death redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant (9:15; Romans 3:25). The sacrifices were the means God gave for their faith to lay hold of his promise, not the ground of their pardon.

How should I remember my sins at the Lord’s Supper? Remember them truly, but remember them as forgiven. Paul tells us to examine ourselves before we eat (1 Corinthians 11:28), and that means honest confession of what is wrong and a turning from it. But the Supper is not the Day of Atonement, where sins are read out and left hanging. It is a remembrance of Christ, who bore them. So look at your sins only long enough to see them laid on him, and then look at him. Come to the table not because you are worthy, but because you need him and he has invited you.

In a sentence. Instead, those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins, because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take sins away.

On a Tuesday. Think about what you remember most when you think about your life before God: your sins, or your Saviour? Many Christians live as though every day were a Day of Atonement, reciting their failures and never hearing the answer. Today, whenever a past sin comes to mind, let it be the start of a remembrance and not the end of one. Name it, and then say: and Christ took that away.

For worship. For fourteen hundred years the goat went out into the wilderness, and the people watched it go, and knew it would have to go again. Then the Lamb of God came, and he did not go out into the wilderness carrying sins that would come back. He went out of the city carrying them to a cross, and they did not come back. God, who could have left his people remembering their sins for ever, chose instead to give them a meal at which they remember his Son. He has not asked us to forget what we were. He has given us something better to remember.

verseByVerse.quote: Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure. Then I said, ’Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.’”
verseByVerse.commentary:
