Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure. Then I said, ‘Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.’”

Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said. The writer puts Psalm 40 on the lips of the incarnate Son, at the moment of his coming, and it is a striking piece of interpretation. “Came into the world” (eiserchomenos eis ton kosmon) is his incarnation. David wrote the words, but they find their full meaning in the Son, and the writer hears the psalm as the Son’s own words to the Father about why he came. Imagine it: the eternal Son, entering the womb of Mary, speaking to his Father about the purpose of his coming.

Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired. The Old Testament says this repeatedly, and it is easy to misread. “Sacrifices” (thysia) are animal sacrifices and “offerings” (prosphora) grain offerings. God commanded them; he cannot be renouncing his own institution. The prophets say the same thing in the same idiom: to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22); I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6; Psalm 51:16–17; Micah 6:6–8). The meaning is comparative: not these for their own sake, but something they were pointing toward. What God desired was obedience from the heart.

But a body have you prepared for me. Here is a detail worth knowing. The Hebrew of Psalm 40:6 reads, literally, ears you have dug for me, an odd phrase, probably meaning ears opened to hear and obey. The Greek translation the writer uses reads a body you have prepared for me. The two are not at odds. An ear is the organ of obedience, and the Greek translators took the part for the whole: God prepared a whole person for obedience. Under the Spirit’s guidance the writer uses the Greek because it points precisely to the incarnation, and it lands with peculiar force in a letter about the incarnation. God did not want a body brought to the altar. He prepared one, and it walked there. The Father prepared a human body for the Son, in which he could obey perfectly and offer himself as the sacrifice (v. 10).

In burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure. “Burnt offerings” (holokautōmata, offerings wholly burnt) and “sin offerings” (peri hamartias) were the main categories of Levitical sacrifice. God took no pleasure in them as ends in themselves.

Then I said, Behold, I have come to do your will, O God. That is the sentence the writer will build on, and notice what it contains and what it does not. No bargaining, no conditions, no mention of the cost. Just arrival and willingness (idou hēkō, behold, I have come). His whole life was devoted to doing the Father’s will: my food is to do the will of him who sent me (John 4:34; 6:38). And it ended in a garden where the same will was spoken through sweat like drops of blood: not as I will, but as you will (Matthew 26:39, 42).

As it is written of me in the scroll of the book. The “scroll of the book” (kephalis bibliou) is the roll of Scripture, which testifies of Christ (Luke 24:27, 44; John 5:39). The Son is described as coming to fulfil something already written about him. Whatever else this implies, it means the incarnation was not a rescue plan improvised after things went wrong. It was in the book.

A will saying yes. And the whole quotation answers a question the chapter has raised. If bulls and goats cannot take away sins, what can? The answer is not a better animal. It is a will: a human will, in a prepared body, saying yes. What God wanted from the beginning was a human being who would give himself wholly to him, and in the whole history of the race there had never been one. So God prepared one.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that God never wanted the Old Testament sacrifices at all; he commanded them. It means he did not desire them as ends in themselves or as substitutes for obedience. He desired what they pointed to: the perfect obedience and self-offering of his Son.

Did Jesus know from the beginning that he had come to die? Yes. The psalm puts these words in his mouth as he came into the world, and the Gospels show him speaking of his death long before it came (Mark 8:31; 10:45; John 10:17–18). As a true man he grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52), and his human understanding of his mission deepened through Scripture and prayer. But the Son did not stumble onto the cross. He came to do the Father’s will, and the cross was at the centre of that will from the start. That is why his death was an offering and not an accident.

In a sentence. That is why, when Christ came into the world, he said to God: You did not want sacrifices and offerings, but you prepared a body for me; you were not pleased with burnt offerings and sin offerings; then I said, Here I am, I have come to do your will, my God, as it is written about me in the scroll.

On a Tuesday. Notice how much of your religion is offerings rather than obedience: the hymn you sing on Sunday while nursing a grudge, the money given while refusing to forgive, the Bible reading done while the plain command you read is set aside. God does not want the offering instead of you. He wants you. Before you do any religious duty today, say to God the words of this psalm, and mean them about one specific thing: here I am, I have come to do your will.

For worship. When the Son of God entered the world, the first thing Scripture records him saying is not a complaint about what it would cost, but a sentence of pure willingness: behold, I have come to do your will. The Father had prepared a body, and the Son stepped into it gladly, knowing where it would be taken. He did not come to bring God another sacrifice. He came to be one. And everything God had ever wanted from the human race, a heart that loved him and a will that obeyed him, he found at last in this man, and found it for us.
verseByVerse.note: “A body have you prepared for me” follows the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew of Ps 40:6 reads “you have given me an open ear.”

verseByVerse.quote: When he said above, “You have neither desired nor taken pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and sin offerings” (these are offered according to the law), then he added, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He does away with the first in order to establish the second. And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he said above, “You have neither desired nor taken pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and sin offerings” (these are offered according to the law), then he added, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He does away with the first in order to establish the second. And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

When he said above. The writer now takes his own quotation apart, and the method repays watching, because it is how the New Testament reads the Old. He divides the psalm into two statements and puts them in order. First a negative: God did not desire sacrifices and offerings. Then a positive: behold, I have come to do your will.

You have neither desired nor taken pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and sin offerings. All four kinds of sacrifice are listed together, and the whole sacrificial system is gathered into one phrase. Then comes a short parenthesis, and it is remarkable: these are offered according to the law. The psalm’s rejection of sacrifices applies to the very offerings the law required. God, through David, in the middle of the old covenant, signalled that the law’s sacrifices were not his final desire.

Then he added, Behold, I have come to do your will. He does away with the first in order to establish the second. The conclusion is drawn from the sequence itself. The two statements stand side by side in the psalm, and the order is not accidental: the second is offered as the replacement for the first. You do not announce what you have come to do unless something else is being set aside. “Does away with” (anairei) is a strong verb: to take up and remove, to abolish. And “establish” (stēsē) is its opposite: to make stand. The first is the sacrificial system; the second is Christ’s obedience to God’s will. One thing is taken down so that another can be set up in its place, and both actions are the Son’s.

And by that will we have been sanctified. Then the summit of the chapter. “By that will” (en hō thelēmati): the will of God, his saving purpose, which the Son came to do. What sanctifies us is not our willing but his. And “we have been sanctified” (hēgiasmenoi) should stop any reader who has spent years anxious about his own progress. It is the Greek perfect: completed, with the result standing. Not we are being sanctified, not we hope to be. It has happened. Here sanctification means being set apart, consecrated to God, made fit for his presence, a definitive, once-for-all act (as in 1 Corinthians 6:11), not the ongoing process of growth in holiness.

Through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. The “offering” (prosphora) is of the “body” (sōma) prepared for him (v. 5), and it was made “once for all” (ephapax), the word the whole letter has been driving toward. By his death on the cross he made his people holy, once and for all time. The body God prepared in the womb of Mary was given on the cross, and the will that said I have come said it finished.

Two kinds of holiness, in the right order. The letter is not confusing definitive sanctification with the daily business of becoming holy: verse 14 will speak of those who are being sanctified in the same breath. Both are true, and the order matters enormously. A Christian is set apart definitively by what Christ did, and is then progressively made to match it. The second is a lifetime’s work. The first is finished.

What it does not mean. “Sanctified” here does not mean believers are already morally perfect. That process continues (12:14; 2 Corinthians 3:18). It means we have been definitively set apart for God through Christ’s sacrifice, made his, and fit to come into his presence.

If I am already sanctified, why do I still struggle with sin? Because you have been set apart for God, but you have not yet been made completely like him. Think of a bride on her wedding day: she is fully and truly married, though she will spend a lifetime learning what that means. Your struggle is not evidence that you are not his; often it is evidence that you are, since the unconverted do not fight sin as an enemy (Galatians 5:17). The struggle is the outworking of what was done once. Fight on from the position Christ has given you, not toward it.

In a sentence. First he said, You did not want sacrifices, offerings, burnt offerings and sin offerings, and you were not pleased with them, even though the law required them; then he said, Here I am, I have come to do your will; he sets aside the first to establish the second; and by that will, carried out by Christ, we have been made holy through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

On a Tuesday. Start today from what is already true. You have been sanctified, set apart for God, by the offering of Christ’s body. So when you face temptation, do not say I must become holy or God will reject me; say I belong to God, so this is not who I am. And let that fact touch the ordinary things: your body, which belongs to him, your time, your words. A thing set apart for God is not used for anything else.

For worship. The whole old order was taken down by the Son, and he did it not by destroying it but by fulfilling it: he did the will that the sacrifices could only point to. And by that will, his will, done in his body on the cross, we were made holy once for all. Our sanctification did not begin in our resolutions. It began in the counsel of the Father, was accomplished in the obedience of the Son, and is applied by the Spirit. We are holy to the Lord because Jesus was willing.

verseByVerse.quote: And every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God, waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet. For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God, waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet. For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.

And every priest stands daily at his service. One word, and the writer has been preparing it since 1:3. “Stands” (hestēken). There were no chairs in the tabernacle. Not one: the furniture is listed in detail in Exodus and no seat appears, because a priest whose work was finished was a contradiction in terms. They stood, every day, for fourteen centuries.

Offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. “Repeatedly” (pollakis, many times); “the same”: endless repetition of identical sacrifices. “Take away” (perielein) means strip off, remove entirely. The verdict of verse 4 restated, now with the emphasis on the endlessness. Same sacrifices, same priest, same standing, same result.

But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God. One sacrifice (mian), effective for ever. There is the contrast, and it is made entirely with a posture. Everything the letter wants to say about the finality of the cross is carried by a man sitting down in a building that had no chairs. Sitting signals completion. The contrast is total: they stand, he sits; they offer repeatedly, he offered once; theirs never take away sins, his does for ever. And he sits at the right hand of God, the place of honour and of rule, which no Levitical priest ever approached.

Waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet. Psalm 110:1 once more (1:13). He is seated and he is waiting, which tells you where we are in the story. The work of atonement is over; the subduing of enemies is not, and the letter’s readers were feeling the difference. “Waiting” (ekdechomenos) is not idle. He reigns while the Father subdues his enemies, through the advance of the gospel now and finally at his return (1 Corinthians 15:24–28).

For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified. Then verse 14, and it is one of the sentences to write on the inside of the skull. Two tenses in one sentence, and holding them together is the whole Christian life. “Perfected” (teteleiōken) is a perfect tense: done, complete, and it remains complete, and “for all time” removes any question of expiry. “Being sanctified” (tous hagiazomenous) is present and continuous: unfinished, still in progress this morning. The same people are described both ways at once. In God’s sight, on the basis of one offering, they are already finished: complete, accepted, cleansed before him. In their own experience they are halfway through and struggling. Our standing is perfect; our condition is improving; and the one guarantees the other. Get them the wrong way round and the Christian life becomes unbearable: a person who thinks his standing depends on his progress will never rest.

Where Christians differ: can a believer lose what Christ’s sacrifice achieved? Some teach that a believer’s perfected standing can be forfeited, through serious sin or through ceasing to believe. Verdict: this verse says Christ has perfected his people for all time by a single offering. What is perfect for all time cannot be undone. Christ’s death did not merely make salvation possible; it actually and permanently perfected those for whom it was made, guaranteeing their sanctification and final glory (Romans 8:30). This is the ground of both definite atonement and the perseverance of the saints.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are sinless now. They are perfected in standing and being sanctified in experience. Nor does the security of the perfected make the warnings of this chapter empty; God uses them to keep those whom Christ has perfected (v. 39).

How can I be perfect and still be such a mess? Because the perfection is in Christ’s offering, not in your performance. God looks at you through the single sacrifice and sees you complete, as a man is counted fully paid once his debt is cleared, even if his house is still untidy. At the same time the Spirit is at work in you, so that the mess is being cleaned up, slowly and really. The two belong together: you are being sanctified because you have been perfected, not in order to be. When you see your mess, do not doubt your standing; thank God for it, and ask him to go on making you what he has declared you to be.

In a sentence. Every priest stands day after day performing his religious duties, offering again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins; but when this priest had offered one sacrifice for sins for all time, he sat down at the right hand of God, and since then he waits for his enemies to be made his footstool, for by one sacrifice he has made perfect for ever those who are being made holy.

On a Tuesday. Picture where Christ is as you go about your day: seated. Not pacing, not anxious, not still working to make up for your failures. Then let that change how you work. Much Christian activity is done standing, as if the work of acceptance were never finished. Do your duties today seated, so to speak: from rest, not toward it. When you fail, remember that the one who perfected you is sitting at the right hand of God, and his work does not wobble when yours does.

For worship. The seat Christ took is not a priest’s stool at the end of a long shift. It is the throne at the right hand of the Majesty on high, and he took it with the work of atonement complete. He sits there not because he is idle, but because nothing remains to be done for the sins of his people, and he waits with the calm of a king for every enemy to be laid at his feet. His rest is our standing. By one offering he has perfected for all time everyone he died for, and while he is seated, their acceptance cannot be shaken.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after saying, “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds,” then he adds, “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.” Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after saying, “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds,” then he adds, “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.” Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.

And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us. Present tense again, as at 3:7. “Bears witness” (martyrei): testifies now. The Jeremiah passage quoted at length in chapter 8 is brought back in shortened form, and it is introduced as testimony being given now, in the room. What the prophet wrote, the Spirit says, to us, today.

This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord. Note that the writer quotes only two clauses of Jeremiah 31:33–34, and which two. He leaves out the promise that all shall know the Lord, and the covenant formula about being their God. He takes the law written on hearts, and the sins remembered no more. That is not carelessness. He is quoting for a purpose, and the purpose arrives in verse 18.

I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds. The first promise, from Jeremiah 31:33 (quoted in 8:10). The new covenant does not abolish God’s law; it writes it inside. What was once on stone, outside a man and accusing him, is now in the heart, changing him.

Then he adds, I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more. The promise from 8:12 (Jeremiah 31:34), the climax of the new covenant: complete, permanent forgiveness. “Lawless deeds” (anomiai) are iniquities, breaches of law. And the writer now does something with it that he did not do in chapter 8. He draws an inference.

Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin. “Forgiveness” (aphesis) is release, cancellation; “no longer any offering” (ouketi prosphora). The logic is inescapable once stated. If God has undertaken never to bring up a person’s sins again, then there is nothing left for a sacrifice to do. An offering exists to deal with an outstanding matter. Where the matter is closed, the offering is not merely unnecessary; it is unintelligible. This is the conclusion of the whole argument from 7:1: since sins are fully forgiven, no further sacrifice is needed or possible.

Why going back made no sense. And that is the writer’s decisive argument against the thing his readers were contemplating. Going back to the temple would not be a harmless supplement or a matter of ancestral loyalty. It would be to keep offering for sins that God has said he will not remember, which is to imply that the promise is not true. To go back to the old sacrifices, or to offer any other sacrifice for sin, is to deny that Christ’s sacrifice was enough.

No offering for sin in the church. The verse also settles a question that has divided Christians. If there is no longer any offering for sin, then whatever the church does when it gathers, it is not offering a sacrifice for sin. The New Testament knows sacrifices of praise and of doing good (13:15–16), and calls a Christian’s body a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1). It knows no repeatable offering for sin, and this verse is why. The Lord’s Supper is a remembrance of the one sacrifice and a communion in it, not a further offering of it (Westminster 29.2). With that the great doctrinal argument of the letter is complete. From verse 19 the writer turns, with a therefore, to what his readers must do about it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers no longer offer anything to God. They offer spiritual sacrifices: praise, good works, generosity, and themselves (13:15–16; Romans 12:1; 1 Peter 2:5). But these are thank offerings, not offerings for sin.

How can an all-knowing God forget my sins? He does not suffer a lapse of memory; the God who knows all things knows what you did. To remember sins no more is covenant language: he will never again bring them up against you, never act toward you on the basis of them, never hold them over you. It is like a judge who has acquitted a man and will not try him again for the same charge. So when your own heart or the accuser brings up a forgiven sin, you may answer that God himself has promised not to. If he will not hold it against you, you need not hold it against yourself.

In a sentence. The Holy Spirit also testifies to us about this, saying first, This is the covenant I will make with them after that time, says the Lord: I will put my laws in their hearts and write them on their minds; and then adding, Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more; and where these have been forgiven, there is no longer any need for a sacrifice for sin.

On a Tuesday. Is there something you are still offering God to cover a sin he has forgiven: extra effort, self-punishment, a refusal to enjoy good gifts until you feel you have paid? Stop offering it. There is no longer any offering for sin. Instead offer him what he asks for: praise, thanks and a life given to him (13:15). And the next time you are tempted to say you cannot forgive yourself, remember that God has said he will remember it no more, and your verdict does not outrank his.

For worship. The Spirit of God still speaks the promise of Jeremiah, in the present tense, to every believer who hears it: I will remember their sins no more. The God who sees everything has chosen, for Christ’s sake, never to bring them up again. He has written his law on our hearts so that we love what he loves, and he has closed the file on everything we have done against it. No priest needs to stand any longer, and no offering needs to be brought, because the Son of God has made the last one. All that remains for us to offer is praise, and he deserves all of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–39 — Let Us Draw Near, Hold Fast, and Consider One Another
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because Jesus’ blood has opened a new and living way into God’s presence, and he is our great priest, the writer urges three things: come near to God with sincere, cleansed hearts and full assurance; hold firmly to the hope we confess, because God is faithful; and think how to stir one another to love and good works, not abandoning meeting together. Then comes a solemn warning: for anyone who deliberately rejects Christ after knowing the truth, there is no other sacrifice, only judgement, for falling into the hands of the living God is terrifying. But the readers should recall how bravely they once endured persecution and even the seizure of their property, knowing they had a better and lasting possession. They must not throw away their confidence. They need endurance, because the coming one will not delay, and they are not people who shrink back but people who believe and are saved.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Curtain Is His Flesh

The way into the holy places has been opened through the curtain, his flesh. So draw near, hold fast because he who promised is faithful, and stir one another up.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: These believers had once joyfully accepted the plundering of their property.

Now: The warning of verses 26–31 is aimed at deliberate repudiation of Christ, not at a struggling believer; and it ends in assurance: we are not of those who shrink back.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh, and since we have a great priest over the house of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh, and since we have a great priest over the house of God,

Therefore, brothers. And the letter turns. “Therefore” (oun) marks the great move from teaching to application. Everything from 4:14 to 10:18, the priest, the covenant, the sanctuary and the sacrifice, now becomes the ground of three exhortations. And he calls them brothers: the warnings that follow are spoken inside a family.

Since we have confidence to enter the holy places. The word is parrēsia, as at 4:16: boldness, freedom, the free citizen’s right to speak openly in the assembly. And the place named is the one the whole letter has been circling: the room behind the curtain, which one man entered once a year and everybody else never. “To enter” (eis tēn eisodon) means for the entrance. What only the high priest could do once a year, every believer may now do at any time.

By the blood of Jesus. That is the ground, and it is the only one offered. Not by sincerity, not by improvement, not by a life that has earned an audience. By his blood, his sacrifice. And note the name: Jesus, the human name, the name of the man who bled.

By the new and living way that he opened for us. “New” (prosphatos) means fresh, recent; the word originally meant freshly slain. The way into God’s presence was cut by a fresh death. And “living” (zōsa) is the arresting adjective: not a dead ritual path, and not a road at all, but a way that is alive, because it is a person. I am the way, Jesus said (John 14:6). “Opened” (enekainisen) means inaugurated, dedicated, from the same root as 9:18. He opened the road and walked it first.

Through the curtain, that is, through his flesh. The identification is startling, and it repays sitting with. The curtain (katapetasma) was the barrier, the thing that kept people out. And the writer says the curtain is his flesh. Which means the way in was opened by the tearing of it. When his body was broken on the cross, the temple veil was torn from top to bottom (Mark 15:38), and the Gospels record it as an act done from above rather than below. His body was rent, and the barrier with it. The way into God’s presence is through the torn body of Christ.

A beautiful barrier. There is a further note in it that the readers would have felt. The curtain was beautiful: blue and purple and scarlet, of fine twined linen, worked with cherubim (Exodus 26:31). The barrier between God and man was not ugly. It was magnificent, and it had to be destroyed. So it was with the flesh of Christ: the most beautiful human life ever lived, and it had to be torn so that we could come in.

And since we have a great priest over the house of God. The second ground: not only an open way but a man standing at the end of it who belongs to us. “Great priest” (hierea megan) is a Hebrew way of saying high priest. “Over the house” recalls 3:6, where Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son, and we are that house. We have both a way and a priest: a road to walk and someone waiting at the end of it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we approach God casually. We come with confidence because of Christ, but still with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire (12:28–29). Boldness is not swagger. It is the freedom of a child who knows he will be received.

What does confidence before God actually feel like? It is not a feeling of being good enough; it is the settled knowledge that you will be welcomed, because of Jesus’ blood. You may come to prayer feeling dull, ashamed or unsure of what to say, and still come with confidence, because your confidence is not in your state but in the way Christ opened. A child who has broken something still runs to his father, not because he is proud of himself, but because he knows his father. That is the confidence of this verse.

In a sentence. So, brothers and sisters, since we have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place through the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his body, and since we have a great priest in charge of God’s household,

On a Tuesday. Notice what you think qualifies you to pray. If you wait until you feel spiritual, or until you have done enough, you will pray little and fearfully. Today, at a moment when you feel least worthy, after a sharp word or a failure, pray anyway, and begin by saying: I come by the blood of Jesus. Then speak to God plainly, as one who has been let in.

For worship. For centuries one man passed the curtain once a year, and came out again. Now a whole family walks through it every day, because the Son of God let his own flesh be torn to make the way. He did not show us the road and leave us to find it. He is the road, freshly slain and for ever alive, so that every step towards God is a step taken in him. And he stands at the end of it as our great priest over the house of God, the door held open, waiting for his brothers and sisters to come in.

verseByVerse.quote: let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.

Let us draw near. The first of three exhortations (vv. 22, 23, 24): draw near, hold fast, consider one another; faith, hope and love, in that order. “Draw near” (proserchōmetha), as in 4:16, is the priestly word for what only priests could do, now commanded of everybody: approach God in worship and prayer. Four qualifications follow, and they divide into two pairs: two about the person coming, two about what has been done to him.

With a true heart. A genuine one (alēthinos), without pretence, not hypocritical or divided (Isaiah 29:13). This rules out the approach that keeps something back, and it also rules out coming in somebody else’s borrowed words. God is not interested in a performance at the throne.

In full assurance of faith. The same phrase as 6:11 (plērophoria), meaning carried to complete conviction, full confidence. Not certainty about oneself, which nobody has, but certainty about the ground just described: the blood, the way, the priest. Not doubting whether we are welcome, but confident because of Christ’s finished work.

With our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience. Then the second pair, and both verbs are passive: things done to us rather than by us. And both are perfect tenses: done, and remaining done. “Sprinkled” (rerantismenoi): the image is the sprinkling of blood that consecrated priests at their ordination (Exodus 29:21; Leviticus 8:30), and the people at the covenant’s ratification (9:19). Our hearts have been sprinkled with Christ’s blood. And the target is the conscience again, the thing 9:9 said the old sacrifices could not reach. An “evil conscience” is a conscience burdened with guilt. What accuses a man on the inside has been dealt with, and that is why he can come with a true heart rather than a defended one.

And our bodies washed with pure water. Priests were also washed at their ordination (Exodus 29:4; 30:19–21), and God promised through Ezekiel: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean (Ezekiel 36:25). “Washed” (lelousmenoi) means bathed. Most interpreters see here a reference to Christian baptism, the outward sign of the inward cleansing named in the same breath (Acts 22:16; 1 Corinthians 6:11; Titus 3:5; 1 Peter 3:21). Some read the washing as purely figurative, a picture of moral cleansing. The more likely reading is that the writer does mean baptism, and the pairing is deliberate: inward cleansing and outward sign, the whole person made fit.

No requirement of worthiness. Put the four together and notice what is not among them. There is no requirement of worthiness, no interval of preparation, no measure of progress. Every qualification is either an attitude of honesty or something Christ has already done, which is exactly the point, because a throne you must qualify for is not a throne of grace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that baptism cleanses the conscience by itself. Even if baptism is in view, the water does not do the cleansing. The heart is sprinkled clean by Christ’s blood, received by faith; baptism is the public sign and seal of that cleansing, given to those who have drawn near in faith. That is one reason this app, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, holds to the baptism of believers, while honouring paedobaptist brothers who read the covenant signs differently and who love the same Saviour.

What if I do not feel full assurance? Then come anyway, and come honestly. Full assurance of faith is assurance about Christ, not a constant feeling about yourself. Feelings of doubt are common in true believers, and Scripture is full of them (Psalm 42; Mark 9:24). The way to grow in assurance is not to stay away until you feel sure, but to draw near and look at the ground: the blood, the way, the priest. Assurance grows as faith looks at Christ, and it often comes while you are praying rather than before. Bring your doubts with you to the throne of grace; they are safer there than anywhere else.

In a sentence. Let us come near to God with a sincere heart and with the full confidence that faith gives, since our hearts have been sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and our bodies have been washed with pure water.

On a Tuesday. Before you pray today, take a moment to remember two things that have been done to you. Your heart has been sprinkled with the blood of Christ, so your guilty conscience has no right to keep you away. And if you have been baptised, remember your baptism: the day you were washed in water as a sign that you belong to Christ. Then come, and do not pretend. Tell God what is actually in your heart.

For worship. Every priest of Israel was washed and sprinkled before he could approach God, and he could go no further than the curtain. Now every believer has been sprinkled with better blood and washed with the water of the new covenant, and has been called to go all the way in. The Lord Jesus has done everything that qualifies us to come. He has made worshippers out of rebels and priests out of the people who were once kept outside, and the throne they approach is a throne of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.

Let us hold fast the confession of our hope. The second exhortation, and it is the one aimed most directly at these readers’ situation. “Hold fast” (katechōmen) means grip, retain, do not let go, as in 3:6, 14 and 4:14. “The confession” (homologia) is the word from 3:1 and 4:14: what they had said publicly, probably at baptism, and were under pressure to unsay. In a hostile city a confession is not a private opinion; it is the thing that got their property confiscated. And “of our hope” is our confident expectation of glory.

Without wavering. A single word (aklinē), meaning not leaning, not tilting: something that stays upright under pressure rather than swaying between two positions.

For he who promised is faithful. Then the reason, and it is one short clause carrying the whole weight. Read it carefully, because the logic is not the one we would supply. He does not say hold on because you are strong, or because you have held on so far, or because giving up would be shameful. The ground of our holding is his faithfulness (pistos). He will keep every promise (6:13–18; 11:11; 1 Corinthians 1:9; 1 Thessalonians 5:24). Our grip may be weak, but his is not.

Perseverance and determination. That is the difference between Christian perseverance and mere determination. A man gritting his teeth is relying on his grip, and grips fail. A man holding fast because the promiser is faithful is relying on something outside himself, and the holding on is a response to reliability rather than a substitute for it. Notice too what is held: the confession of our hope. Not of our feelings, which come and go, and not of our achievements. Hope is by definition about something not yet in hand, which is why holding it requires anything at all.

The good confession before Pilate. The confession they were tempted to unsay has a history older than their baptism. Paul tells Timothy to hold to his confession in the presence of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession (1 Timothy 6:12–13), using the same word. Standing alone, bound, before the power of Rome, Jesus did not waver: he said he was a king and that he had come to bear witness to the truth (John 18:37), and it cost him his life. This letter calls him the apostle and high priest of our confession (3:1). Every Christian who holds fast under pressure is holding to what Jesus held to first, and is held by the one who did not let go.

The answer to drift. And this is the answer to the drift of 2:1. A congregation slipping away is not usually losing an argument; it is losing its grip in the dark. The writer does not give them a new argument. He points at the character of the one who made the promise, and tells them to hang on to that.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we hold on by our own power. We hold fast because God is faithful and holds us. But we are truly called to hold fast, and those whom God holds do hold on.

How do I hold fast when my faith feels weak? By looking away from your faith to the one who promised. Weak faith holding a strong Saviour is safe; strong faith in a weak saviour is not. In practice, holding fast means keeping on with the ordinary means: reading and hearing God’s word, praying even when it feels empty, gathering with God’s people, coming to the Lord’s Supper, and saying again what you believe. You will not always feel strong. You are not asked to. You are asked to keep your grip on a promise made by someone who has never broken one.

In a sentence. Let us keep a firm grip on the hope we profess, without wavering, because the one who made the promise can be trusted.

On a Tuesday. Is pressure making you want to soften or hide your hope? Perhaps at work, with family, or among friends who mock faith. Hold it straight. Look for one place today where you would normally go quiet about Christ, and say plainly, gently, what you hope in. And when you feel your grip loosening, recite a promise of God aloud, and remember that he who promised is faithful.

For worship. Every promise God has made he has kept: a son for Abraham, a land for Israel, a Messiah for the prophets who longed to see him. And the greatest of his promises he kept at the greatest cost, giving his own Son to die, so that all the promises of God find their yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). The God who did not spare his Son will not go back on his word to those for whom the Son was given. We do not hold fast because we are strong. We hold fast because he is true, and his hand is around ours, and neither our weakness nor the world’s pressure can loosen his grip.

verseByVerse.quote: And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.

And let us consider how to stir up one another. The third exhortation, and it turns outward. The first two were about our approach to God; this one is about each other. “Consider” (katanoōmen) is the verb from 3:1, where it was applied to Jesus: to fix the mind on, to study attentively. Here it is applied to other Christians. Working out how to help a particular person forward requires the same kind of attention as contemplating Christ, and the writer uses the same word for both.

Provoke one another. “Stir up” is a startling choice. The noun is paroxysmos, from which we get paroxysm; it means a sharp provoking, an irritation. It is the word Luke uses of the bitter quarrel between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:39). So the instruction is to provoke one another, and the only thing that redeems it is the object.

To love and good works. Provoke, yes, but to love and good works: love that shows itself in practical deeds. There is a kind of friction between Christians that is entirely legitimate: the friend who will not let you settle, whose example makes your comfort uncomfortable, whose generosity shames your caution, and who asks the question you were hoping nobody would ask.

Not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some. And here is the first concrete symptom the letter has named. The drift of 2:1 and the dullness of 5:11 have a visible expression: people had stopped coming. “Neglecting” (enkataleipontes) means forsaking, abandoning, deserting. “Meet together” (episynagōgē) is assembling, gathering. And note that it is called a habit (ethos, custom). Not a decision, not a repudiation: a pattern that had established itself, which is exactly how drifting works. Absence from the gathered church is often the first step in falling away.

The reasons would have been good ones. Meeting was dangerous; assembling with Christians marked you out in a city that had already plundered their property. Others may have been drifting, or quietly returning to the synagogue. The writer names it anyway, because the previous verses have just made gathering the mechanism of everything else: you cannot stir up one another, or be stirred, from a distance. The Christian life is not meant to be lived alone.

The Son who sings in the assembly. When believers gather, they do not meet alone. This letter has already put on the lips of Jesus the words of Psalm 22: I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise (2:12). The risen Son is not ashamed to call them brothers, and he stands among them leading the praise of his Father. And the word for meeting together is the one Paul uses of the last great gathering, our being gathered together to him at his coming (2 Thessalonians 2:1). That is why the verse ties the meeting to the Day. Every gathering of his people is a small and early form of the one he will call when he comes.

But encouraging one another. “Encouraging” (parakalountes) means exhorting, urging, coming alongside, as in 3:13, where the writer told them to exhort one another every day, as long as it is called today. Encouragement in the New Testament is not flattery. It is putting courage into someone.

And all the more as you see the Day drawing near. “The Day” is the day of Christ’s return and judgment (1 Corinthians 3:13; 1 Thessalonians 5:2, 4), and every passing day brings it closer (engizousan, drawing near). It may also include the approaching destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, a foretaste of the final judgment that some of the first readers would live to see. The instinct under pressure is to withdraw and go quiet. The letter says the opposite: the nearer the Day and the harder the times, the more of this, not less.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that church attendance alone makes a person a Christian. But a professing Christian who habitually neglects gathering with God’s people is in spiritual danger. Nor does it condemn those who cannot attend through illness or other genuine hindrance.

Does watching a service online fulfil this command? The word is about gathering, being together in one place, and the stirring up it describes needs people who are present to each other. For the sick, the housebound and those cut off by persecution, a livestream is a real mercy, and no one should be made to feel guilty for what they cannot help. But for those who can come, watching is not meeting, and a settled habit of staying away is exactly the drift this verse warns against.

What if my church is difficult, or I have been hurt there? Then take the hurt seriously, and do not take it out on Christ’s body by leaving it altogether. Some churches are unsafe, and if you or your children have been abused or controlled, you must get away and get help; God never asks anyone to stay under abuse. But most of the time the difficulty is ordinary: awkward people, dull sermons, a slight that still stings. Talk to someone you trust, go to the person who hurt you if you can (Matthew 18:15), and if you must move, move to another faithful church, not to no church. Every church is full of sinners; that is who it is for.

In a sentence. And let us think about how we can spur one another on toward love and good deeds, not giving up meeting together, as some are in the habit of doing, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.

On a Tuesday. Think of one specific person in your church and one specific way to spur them on to love and good works this week: a message telling them what you saw God doing in them, an invitation to serve alongside you, a question about how they are really doing. Then look at your own attendance honestly. If Sunday worship has become optional, decide now that it will be the fixed point of your week, and that other things will fit around it.

For worship. The Son of God did not save a scattered crowd of individuals. He loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), and he bought every member of his household at the same price. So the awkward brother in the next row and the weary sister by the door are people he died for, and he has given them to us to provoke to love, to warn, to encourage and to carry. Each one he paid for, he will bring in. Not one of the family he purchased will be missing when he calls them home.

verseByVerse.quote: For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.

For if we go on sinning deliberately. The fourth warning, and it must be read with the same care as chapter 6, and with attention to the words the writer actually chose. Note the “we”: the preacher includes himself, as he does in every warning. “Deliberately” (hekousiōs, willingly, wilfully) stands first in the Greek sentence, in the emphatic position. And the phrase is a technical one. The law distinguished sins committed unintentionally, for which sacrifice was provided (Leviticus 4), from sin done with a high hand, for which there was no offering at all and the sinner was cut off (Numbers 15:27–31). The writer is using that category, and his readers would have recognised it instantly. “Go on sinning” (hamartanontōn) is a present participle: continuing, persisting. Not a fall but a settled course.

After receiving the knowledge of the truth. With full information (epignōsis, full knowledge). This is not the sin of the ignorant or the deceived. They knew the gospel; they had heard it, understood it, and been among those who confessed it. Rejecting known truth is more serious than rejecting what one has never understood.

The sin in view. Put those together and the sin in view is specific: the informed, deliberate, persistent repudiation of Christ by someone who knows exactly what he is walking away from. In context it is apostasy, the opposite of holding fast (v. 23), and verse 29 will describe it in the plainest terms: trampling the Son of God underfoot. It is not occasional sins of weakness, which all believers commit (1 John 1:8–10).

There no longer remains a sacrifice for sins. And the logic is the same as verse 18, running the other way. There is one sacrifice, offered once. The old sacrifices are obsolete, and Christ’s is the only one. A person who rejects it has not exhausted a supply; he has refused the only one there is, and there is no second provision behind it. To turn from Christ is to turn from the only remedy.

But a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries. Only a terrifying anticipation of judgment awaits. “Fury of fire” (pyros zēlos) is literally a zeal of fire, a fiery jealousy, and the language is Isaiah’s (Isaiah 26:11): God’s holy zeal against those who oppose him. And the word for adversaries (hypenantioi, opponents) makes the point: this is what awaits enemies, not stumbling sons. Apostates join the enemies of God (Philippians 3:18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer who falls into serious sin is lost for ever. David committed adultery and murder, and was restored (Psalm 51). Peter denied Christ, and was restored. The warning is against a deliberate, persistent rejection of Christ. And “consume” does not mean annihilation; Scripture describes the punishment of the wicked as conscious and eternal (Matthew 25:46; Mark 9:48; Revelation 14:11). Fire that consumes describes the destructive, ruinous character of judgment, not the end of the person who suffers it.

Am I lost if I have sinned deliberately since becoming a Christian? No, not if you still want Christ. Every believer sins knowingly at times; that is what makes David and Peter such comfort. The sin of this verse is not a deliberate act of sin but a deliberate abandonment of the Saviour: turning your back on his sacrifice and treating it with contempt. The very fact that you are troubled, and want to be forgiven, shows that you have not done that, because the apostate does not grieve over his rejection of Christ; he despises it. Come back to the sacrifice that still remains for you, confess your sin, and believe the promise of 1 John 1:9.

Why does the warning say “we” if true believers cannot fall away? Because the writer speaks to the whole church as it appears, which includes true believers and some who only profess, and he cannot see hearts. And because warnings are one of the means God uses to keep his true people. A true believer hears the warning and is driven closer to Christ; that is how perseverance works. The guardrail on a mountain road does not imply that cars regularly go over; it is the reason they do not. God has promised to keep his own (v. 39; John 10:28), and he keeps them partly by warnings like this one.

In a sentence. If we deliberately keep on sinning after we have received the knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins is left, only a terrifying expectation of judgment and of raging fire that will consume God’s enemies.

On a Tuesday. Let this warning do its work in you without crushing you. Ask whether there is any area where you have quietly decided to go on in a known sin, telling yourself that grace will cover it. That is the road that leads, if it is followed, to the place this verse describes. Turn off it today: confess the sin, cut off what feeds it, and tell someone who can help you. And if you are a tender conscience who reads this and fears you are already lost, remember that this passage describes someone who has trampled on the sacrifice, not someone who longs for it, and run to the sacrifice that remains for every sinner who comes.

For worship. There is only one sacrifice for sins, and God has given it: his own Son, offered once. The severity of this warning is the measure of the sacrifice’s worth. If there were many ways back to God, rejecting one would not matter much. But there is only one, and it cost the blood of the Son of God, and that is why turning from it is so terrible. And that same sacrifice still stands today, sufficient for every sinner who comes to it, however deliberately he has sinned. The door that is shut to the one who tramples it is wide open to the one who knocks.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” And again, “The Lord will judge his people.” It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” And again, “The Lord will judge his people.” It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses. The argument runs again from lesser to greater, as at 2:2–3. That is Deuteronomy 17:2–7, and the offence in view there is idolatry, going and serving other gods. “Set aside” (athetēsas) means rejected, nullified. Deliberate rejection of the covenant brought the death penalty, and the safeguard was the testimony of witnesses.

How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved. The writer puts it as a question and invites his readers to do the arithmetic themselves. If rejecting the shadow was so serious, how much more rejecting the substance?

By the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God. Three descriptions follow, and they escalate. “Trampled underfoot” (katapatēsas) is to stamp on, to treat with contempt, walk on. Instead of honouring the Son whom God exalted to his right hand, seated above the angels with his enemies under his feet (1:13), the apostate treats him as dirt beneath his own.

And has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified. “Profaned” (koinon hēgēsamenos) means considered common, unholy, ordinary: to reckon something holy as ordinary, treating Christ’s blood as if it were the blood of a common criminal. “By which he was sanctified” (en hō hēgiasthē) is the hardest phrase in the passage, and it has been much debated, since it appears to describe the apostate as having been sanctified by the blood.

A hard phrase. Some take the apostate to have been truly renewed and then to have lost it; a few refer the words to Christ, consecrated as high priest by his own blood (John 17:19). The reading that fits the context and the rest of Scripture best is that he was outwardly set apart as part of the covenant community, sharing its privileges without inward regeneration, as all Israel was sprinkled with covenant blood at Sinai (9:19–20) though many of them were unbelievers. He is like the field in 6:7–8 that drank the same rain as the fruitful one and bore thorns.

And has outraged the Spirit of grace. “Outraged” (enybrisas) means insulted, treated with arrogant contempt, with insolence. “The Spirit of grace” is the Holy Spirit, who brings God’s grace and had worked among them (6:4). There is an echo here of the unforgivable sin of blasphemy against the Spirit (Mark 3:28–29). To insult the one whose whole work is grace is to cut oneself off from grace.

For we know him who said, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, and again, The Lord will judge his people. Two quotations from Deuteronomy 32, the Song of Moses. The first (32:35; also Romans 12:19) says that God himself will judge. The second (32:36) is the sharper. Not the nations: his people. Belonging to the covenant community is not a shelter from God’s judgment; it is the reason judgment begins there (1 Peter 4:17).

It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. “Fearful” (phoberon) is terrifying. To fall into his hands is to fall under his direct judgment, with no mediator. And note the phrase, because it cuts both ways. To fall away is to fall away from the living God (3:12), and there is nowhere to fall except into his hands. David once chose to fall into the hands of the LORD, for his mercy is great (2 Samuel 24:14). The same hands are the only refuge and the only danger, and which they are depends entirely on how a man comes. For those who come through Christ, they are a Father’s hands. For those who have rejected his mercy in Christ, God’s hands mean only judgment.

Where Christians differ: does this verse show that the sanctified can be lost? Christians answer in three main ways. Arminians hold that a real believer can turn away and be lost, and they point to the strong words here: he was sanctified by the blood. Some take the warning as hypothetical, describing what would happen if a believer fell away, though God will not let it happen. Others hold that the writer describes someone who belonged to the covenant community, knew the truth and shared its privileges, but never truly trusted Christ, and at last walked away (6:4–8). Verdict: sanctified in Hebrews can refer to the outward consecration of covenant membership, as when the whole people of Israel was sprinkled with covenant blood. The apostate had been outwardly identified with the new covenant community, baptised and sharing its life, and so in an outward sense set apart by the covenant blood, without inward renewal. Those whom Christ has perfected for all time by his single offering (v. 14) cannot be lost. Verse 39 makes the distinction: there are those who shrink back and are destroyed, and those who have faith and are saved. The letter rests its readers’ perseverance on Christ, who is able to save to the uttermost (7:25). God keeps his own, and warnings like this one are among the means he uses to do it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is cruel or arbitrary. His judgment is just: the punishment fits the magnitude of the offence, which is the rejection of his greatest gift.

How can I tell the difference between a true believer and someone only outwardly sanctified? Often, in this life, you cannot tell with certainty about someone else, and you are not asked to. Both may be baptised, attend, and know the truth. The difference shows over time: true faith goes on trusting Christ, loves him, and comes back to him after falling, while a merely outward profession eventually treats him as common and walks away. For yourself, the question is not whether you have been baptised or how long you have attended, but whether you are trusting Christ now and want him. If you do, you are not the person of this verse. Look to him, not to your record.

Can someone who has walked away from Christ ever come back? Yes, if they come back. Many who drifted, even for years, have returned, and their return showed that they were his all along, like the prodigal son, who was a son in the far country. Only God knows who has finally hardened himself, and the warning describes the end of that road, not every person who has wandered on it. So pray for those you love who have walked away, and keep the door open. If you are the one who walked away and you want to return, the fact that you want to is God drawing you. Come.

In a sentence. Anyone who rejected the law of Moses died without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses; how much more severely, do you think, will someone be punished who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, treated as unholy the covenant blood by which he was set apart, and insulted the Spirit of grace? For we know the one who said, It is mine to avenge; I will repay, and again, The Lord will judge his people; it is a terrifying thing to fall into the hands of the living God.

On a Tuesday. Treat the blood of Christ as holy today. Notice where it becomes common in your thinking: a careless joke about the cross, the Lord’s Supper taken absent-mindedly, an assumption that grace means God does not mind. Repent of that. And then let the fear of God do its proper work: not to drive you from him, but to drive you into his hands as a child. The safest place in the universe is the hands that are most to be feared, when you have fallen into them through Christ.

For worship. The Son of God is not a common thing, and his blood is not common blood. He is the one the Father has seated at his right hand, and the blood of the covenant is the price of the redemption of his people. The Spirit of grace is the one who opened our eyes to see it. And the living God, whose hands are terrible to his enemies, opened those same hands to receive us, because the hands of his Son were nailed to a cross in our place. Those who are in Christ will never fall into his hands as enemies. They rest in them as children, and no one can snatch them out of the Father’s hand (John 10:29).

verseByVerse.quote: But recall the former days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings, sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction, and sometimes being partners with those so treated. For you had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But recall the former days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings, sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction, and sometimes being partners with those so treated. For you had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.

But recall the former days. And the tone changes completely. Having brought them to the edge, the writer turns and reminds them who they are, exactly as he did in 6:9–12 after the harshest passage in the letter. “Recall” (anamimnēskesthe) means remember, keep remembering. This paragraph tells us what had actually happened to these people.

When, after you were enlightened. “Enlightened” (phōtisthentes), as in 6:4: when they first came to faith, when the light of the gospel broke on them. And note the timing: the suffering came after the light, not before. Becoming Christians is what brought it on them.

You endured a hard struggle with sufferings. “Endured” (hypemeinate) is the verb of steady endurance, and the word for struggle (athlēsis) is the athletic contest word, from which we get athlete: a great contest, fought in public. It was possibly the persecution under the emperor Claudius, who expelled Jews from Rome around AD 49, partly because of disturbances over one Chrestus (probably Christ), according to the Roman historian Suetonius (Acts 18:2).

Sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction. The verb (theatrizomenoi) is a theatre word: made a spectacle of, put on a stage. Mocked and abused in public, in a culture where honour and shame were the currency of a life. Paul used the same picture of the apostles: we have become a spectacle to the world (1 Corinthians 4:9).

The reproach was his before it was theirs. The word for reproach (oneidismos) is one this letter keeps for Christ. Moses considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt (11:26), and the readers are told at the end to go to Jesus outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured, since he suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood (13:12–13). So the mockery they met in the streets was not a strange new trouble. It was the shame he carried first, when he was mocked, spat on and crucified in public, now falling on those who bore his name. To be shamed for Christ is to be found standing where he stood.

And sometimes being partners with those so treated. “Partners” (koinōnoi) are sharers. Which took its own kind of courage. It is one thing to be dragged out yourself; it is another to walk over and stand beside somebody who has been, sharing their shame, when you could have stayed indoors.

For you had compassion on those in prison. “Had compassion” (synepathēsate) is to suffer with, the same word used of Christ in 4:15, who is able to sympathise with our weaknesses. Prisoners in the Roman world depended on friends and family for food and care. Visiting a prisoner in that world meant identifying yourself publicly with his crime (13:3; Matthew 25:36). These people went.

And you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property. Read that twice. Not endured. Not tolerated. Joyfully accepted (meta charas), while their houses were being emptied, presumably by neighbours, with no legal recourse whatever. “Plundering” (harpagē) is seizure, robbery: their goods were confiscated or looted. It is what Jesus said would happen: blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you; rejoice and be glad (Matthew 5:11–12), and what the apostles did, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41).

Since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one. And there is how they did it. Not by stoicism, or by pretending the loss was small. By knowing they owned something the mob could not reach and could not carry. “Better possession” (kreittona hyparxin) is better property; “abiding” (menousan) is lasting, permanent, the letter’s word for what lasts, set against everything that wears out like a garment (1:11). Their real treasure was in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal (Matthew 6:19–21; 1 Peter 1:4). Some manuscripts add in heaven.

Be what you already were. These people had once made that calculation under real pressure and come out singing, which is precisely why the writer reminds them. He is not asking them to become something new. He is asking them to be what they already were. Memory is one of God’s gifts for perseverance: the grace that carried you once is evidence that it will carry you again.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Christians should be careless about possessions or seek their loss. It means that when faithfulness costs us our goods, we can let them go with joy, because our true wealth is secure.

How can anyone be joyful when they are being robbed? Not by being glad about the loss itself, which is still a real wrong, but by being more glad about something else. The joy came from what they knew: they had a better and lasting possession. A man who has just inherited a fortune can lose his wallet with a smile. That is the joy here. It is not natural cheerfulness, and it does not deny grief; it is the fruit of a heart that has put its treasure in heaven. Such joy grows by setting your mind on what you have in Christ long before the loss comes.

Should Christians resist injustice, or just accept it joyfully? Both have their place. Paul appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen when that served the gospel (Acts 16:37; 22:25; 25:11), and Christians may rightly use lawful means to protect themselves, their families and the weak. But when the only way to keep your goods is to deny Christ, or when there is no remedy, you let them go, and you can do it with joy. The question is not whether you may seek justice, but whether your heart is free to lose everything and still have Christ.

In a sentence. Remember those earlier days after you had first received the light, when you stood your ground through a great struggle with suffering, sometimes publicly exposed to insults and persecution, at other times standing side by side with those so treated; you felt for those in prison and joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property, because you knew that you had better and lasting possessions.

On a Tuesday. Visit, write to, or pray for a believer in prison for their faith this week. Remember them as if you were with them. Then remember your own former days: the early zeal, the costs you once gladly paid, the boldness you had when you first believed. Ask what changed. And look at your possessions with this verse in mind. Is there anything you own that you could not lose with joy? That is the thing to hold more loosely, and to give some of it away.

For worship. The God who gave these believers their light also gave them their joy, in a burning city, with their houses emptied. He did it by showing them what they had in heaven, a possession that no mob can carry and no emperor can confiscate. That possession is Christ himself, and the inheritance kept for us in him. He was stripped of his own clothes at the cross, and soldiers gambled for them, so that we might be given riches that last. Those who own him have already been given more than the world can take away.
verseByVerse.note: Possibly the persecution under the emperor Claudius, who expelled Jews from Rome about AD 49.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward. For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward. For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.

Therefore do not throw away your confidence. The verb is deliberate and slightly shocking. Not do not lose it, as though it might slip out of a pocket. To throw away (apobalēte) is an act: you do it on purpose, the way a soldier throws away a shield to run faster. And “confidence” (parrēsia) is the same word as verse 19, 3:6 and 4:16: the boldness to speak, the freedom to come. What they are in danger of discarding is not a mood but their access, the bold faith they once had. The word was also used of the frankness that could get a man into trouble in a public assembly. There is a version of quietness that looks like humility and is actually the shield going over the wall.

Which has a great reward. The writer is not embarrassed by the motive. He has told them their possession is better and abiding (v. 34), and here he says the boldness itself is worth keeping because of what it brings. “Reward” (misthapodosia) is recompense, payment. Reward language runs through this letter (11:6, 26), and it is never treated as a lower motive. God rewards persevering faith, and he wants us to want the reward.

For you have need of endurance. A plain sentence, and notice what it concedes. Not need of better arguments, or clearer teaching, or a fresh experience. Endurance (hypomonē): remaining under a weight without buckling, steadfastness, patient perseverance under pressure (12:1–3; James 1:3–4). That is the writer’s diagnosis after ten chapters of theology, and it is a humbling one for anyone who assumes that people leave the faith because they have run out of reasons. These readers had the reasons. What they were short of was staying power.

So that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised. And note the order. Doing comes first and receiving after: not because the promise is earned, but because it lies at the end of a road that must actually be walked. “Done the will of God” means persevering in faith and obedience, as Christ did God’s will (v. 7). “Receive what is promised” (komisēsthe tēn epangelian) is to carry off the promise, to obtain it: the eternal inheritance (9:15). Endurance is not waiting; it is continuing to obey while nothing visible changes.

The will he did first. The phrase done the will of God has already appeared in this chapter, on the lips of the Son: behold, I have come to do your will, O God (v. 7), and by that will we have been sanctified (v. 10). The will these weary believers must keep doing is the will Christ has already done for them, to the cross and through it. They are not asked to win by their endurance what he won by his. They are asked to walk the road that his obedience has made safe, behind the one who endured the cross and is now seated at the right hand of the throne (12:2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the reward is earned by works. The reward is the gracious inheritance promised to those who persevere in faith. Endurance is how faith shows itself over time.

Is it wrong to serve God for a reward? No, provided the reward is God himself and what he gives, not a lever for getting something else from him. Moses looked to the reward (11:26), and Jesus endured the cross for the joy set before him (12:2). God made us to want joy, and he is the greatest joy. What would be wrong is serving him only for earthly payment, or thinking the reward is wages we have earned. It is a Father’s gift to his children, out of all proportion to anything they did, and it is meant to strengthen us to keep going.

What if I am worn out and do not think I can keep going? Then you are exactly the person this verse was written for. These readers were tired too. Endurance is not the absence of weariness; it is continuing under it, one day at a time, and it is given by God as you look to Christ (12:2–3). Do the next faithful thing, not the whole of the rest of your life. Get rest if you need rest, ask for help, and tell God honestly that you are weak. He gives power to the faint (Isaiah 40:29–31), and he has promised that the one who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

In a sentence. So do not throw away your confidence; it will be richly rewarded; you need to keep going, so that when you have done what God wants, you will receive what he has promised.

On a Tuesday. What tempts you to give up: a long illness, a hard marriage, a prayer unanswered, a church that disappoints, a temptation that keeps returning? Name it. Then ask God for endurance for today only, and take the next faithful step: the next prayer, the next act of kindness, the next Sunday. And notice where you are tempted to go quiet about Christ to avoid trouble; that is the shield going over the wall. Pick it up again.

For worship. The God who asks for endurance is the God of endurance and encouragement (Romans 15:5), who bore with a stiff-necked people for forty years in the wilderness and did not let them go. He does not hold out a reward and leave his children to struggle towards it unaided. He gives the strength he asks for, and the reward he promises is beyond all they have lost: a share in the inheritance of his Son, who received the name above every name and a people for his own. What the Son received, he shares with his brothers, and the faithfulness that kept him to the end keeps them.

verseByVerse.quote: For, “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay; but my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For, “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay; but my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”

For, Yet a little while. The writer quotes Habakkuk, the prophet of waiting, whose book opens with the complaint: O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? (Habakkuk 1:2). The answer he received was that the vision awaits its appointed time; if it seems slow, wait for it (Habakkuk 2:3). The words blend Isaiah 26:20 and Habakkuk 2:3–4, following the Greek translation, and the Greek for a little while (mikron hoson hoson) doubles itself, a little while, how little, how little, to press the shortness of the wait.

And the coming one will come and will not delay. Where Habakkuk’s Hebrew speaks of the vision coming, the Greek text the writer follows speaks of a person: “the coming one” (ho erchomenos), a title for the Messiah (Matthew 11:3). The writer applies it to Christ’s return. The promise of God’s deliverance has a face. “Will not delay” (ou chronisei): it may seem slow, but it will come at the right time (2 Peter 3:8–9).

But my righteous one shall live by faith. It is the sentence that changed Luther’s life, and Paul builds two letters on it (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11). Hebrews uses it differently, and the difference is instructive. Paul takes it to answer the question how a man is justified: by faith, not works. Hebrews takes it to answer how a man keeps going: by faith, not sight. The emphasis here falls on live. The righteous man does not merely begin by faith; he lives by it, day after day, now and eternally. Faith is not a one-time act but a way of life, and the whole of chapter 11 is about to illustrate what that looks like over a lifetime.
