And if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him. The verb (hyposteilētai) means to draw back, to withdraw, to cower. It was used of furling a sail and of a soldier shrinking from danger. Paul uses it of himself at Miletus: I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:27). And the contrast is exact. Faith goes forward when it cannot see; shrinking back is what faith looks like when it fails. The wilderness generation shrank back at the border of a good land, and it is the same failure of nerve. “My soul has no pleasure in him” (ouk eudokei) is a restrained way of saying something severe, and its restraint is characteristic of Scripture at its most serious. It is not rage. It is the withdrawal of delight, which from God is worse.

Textual note. The writer reverses the order of Habakkuk’s two clauses in the Greek translation, so that my righteous one becomes the subject of if he shrinks back. This makes clear that the warning is addressed to those who profess to be God’s people.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the coming of Christ was expected within a few years only, and that the writer was mistaken. A little while is God’s perspective; from his view, the whole age between the comings is brief, and a thousand years are as one day (2 Peter 3:8). Every generation lives in the last hour, and every believer’s waiting is short compared with the eternity that follows.

Why does it feel as if Christ is taking so long? Because we measure time by our lifetimes, and God measures it by his purpose. Peter answers the question directly: the Lord is not slow as some count slowness, but patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9). Every day of delay is a day in which more of his people are being gathered in. Meanwhile the righteous live by faith: they go on trusting and obeying in the gap, as Habakkuk did. And for each of us, the waiting ends at death, when we go to be with him, which can never be more than a little while away.

In a sentence. For, In just a very little while, the one who is coming will come and will not be late; but my righteous one will live by faith, and if he draws back, I will take no pleasure in him.

On a Tuesday. Live this day by faith rather than sight. Name one thing you are waiting for God to do, and one thing you can do today in faith while you wait: a duty to fulfil, a temptation to refuse, a hope to speak of. And watch for the moments when you are tempted to shrink back, to lower the sail because the wind is against you. Faith keeps the sail up. The coming one will come, and he will not be late.

For worship. The vision has a face. What Habakkuk waited for in the watchtower, and what every faithful Israelite longed for, was not an event but a person, and he is coming. He came once, in the fullness of time, not a day late. He will come again, not a day late. And in between he keeps his righteous ones alive by faith, through every long night and every how long, O LORD. God delights in those who trust him in the dark, and he will not keep them waiting one moment longer than his love requires.

verseByVerse.quote: But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.

But we are not of those who shrink back. The chapter that contains the letter’s most frightening warning ends with the writer putting himself and his readers firmly on the right side of it, and the placing is deliberate. “We” (hēmeis de ouk esmen): he includes himself, as he has done again and again since 2:1. And “are not of those” is a statement of category, not of achievement. He is not saying we have performed better. He is saying we belong to a different kind. “Shrink back” (hypostolē, drawing back, retreat) picks up verse 38.

And are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls. “Destroyed” (eis apōleian) means unto destruction, perdition, the word Paul uses in Philippians 3:19 (their end is destruction). The end of those who shrink back is eternal ruin (Philippians 1:28; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). Set against destruction is “preserve their souls” (eis peripoiēsin psychēs): literally the gaining, keeping or possessing of the soul, an idiom for coming through alive. Those with true faith keep going and are saved. There are only two categories: those who shrink back and perish, and those who believe and are saved.

How the warnings work. The writer describes the danger in the strongest terms available, and then tells his readers he does not believe it applies to them, exactly as he did at 6:9 after the harshest passage in the letter. Warning and assurance are not alternatives. The warning is one of the means by which the assurance turns out to be true.

Defined by faith. And the two categories are defined by one thing only, which the writer names last: faith. Not endurance, though he has just demanded it; not good works, though he has commended theirs. Faith is what distinguishes those who arrive from those who turn back. That is why Hebrews 11 follows. Having said that the difference between destruction and preservation is faith, the writer defines it, and then spends forty verses producing a crowd of people who had it, so that a struggling congregation could see what the word looks like when it is worn by real men and women over a lifetime. And the crowd ends not with one of them but with Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith (12:1–2). Faith preserves the soul because of where it looks: away from itself, to the one who ran the race first and finished it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the writer is uncertain about his readers. He expresses confidence that they belong to those who believe, which is why he warns them: the warning is one of the means God uses to keep his own.

How can I be sure I am one of those who have faith? Look first at Christ, and then at the evidence. Are you trusting him, and him alone, for your acceptance with God? That is faith, however weak it feels. Then notice the signs that faith is alive: you still come back to him after you fall, you want to be holy even when you are not, you love his people, and you cannot let him go. These are not the grounds of your salvation, but they are its fruit. If you find them in yourself, take this verse as spoken to you: you are not of those who shrink back.

In a sentence. But we are not the kind of people who draw back and are lost; we are those who believe and are saved.

On a Tuesday. Say this verse aloud today, as a confession of who you are in Christ: I am not of those who shrink back. Then live it in one concrete place where you have been tempted to retreat: a conversation you have been avoiding, a stand you have been putting off, a habit of prayer you let lapse. And think of one person you know who seems to be drawing back. Pray for them by name, and send them a word of encouragement this week.

For worship. Faith is the whole difference between those who are lost and those who are saved, and faith is God’s gift. He gives it, he sustains it through every night of shrinking fear, and he brings it home. The God who has just shown us the fire is the God who stoops to say of trembling believers, you are not of those. He can say it because the one in whom we believe is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, and will lose none of those the Father has given him (John 6:39). Our souls are preserved because they are held, and the hands that hold them were pierced for them.

10.text: <sup>1</sup>For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near.<sup>2</sup>Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?<sup>3</sup>But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year.<sup>4</sup>For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.<sup>5</sup>Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me;<sup>6</sup>in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure.<sup>7</sup>Then I said, ’Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.’”<sup>8</sup>When he said above, “You have neither desired nor taken pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and sin offerings” (these are offered according to the law),<sup>9</sup>then he added, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He does away with the first in order to establish the second.<sup>10</sup>And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.<sup>11</sup>And every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins.<sup>12</sup>But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God,<sup>13</sup>waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet.<sup>14</sup>For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.<sup>15</sup>And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after saying,<sup>16</sup>“This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds,”<sup>17</sup>then he adds, “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.”<sup>18</sup>Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.<sup>19</sup>Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus,<sup>20</sup>by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh,<sup>21</sup>and since we have a great priest over the house of God,<sup>22</sup>let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.<sup>23</sup>Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.<sup>24</sup>And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works,<sup>25</sup>not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.<sup>26</sup>For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins,<sup>27</sup>but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.<sup>28</sup>Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses.<sup>29</sup>How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace?<sup>30</sup>For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” And again, “The Lord will judge his people.”<sup>31</sup>It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.<sup>32</sup>But recall the former days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings,<sup>33</sup>sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction, and sometimes being partners with those so treated.<sup>34</sup>For you had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.<sup>35</sup>Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward.<sup>36</sup>For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.<sup>37</sup>For, “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay;<sup>38</sup>but my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”<sup>39</sup>But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.

11.title: By Faith: The Great Cloud of Witnesses
11.overview:
Ten chapters have argued that Jesus is better. Chapter 11 shows what it looks like to live on that: a gallery of people who took God at his word about things they could not see, and acted on it. Faith here is never an opinion held; it is always something done that makes no sense without a promise from God.

The gallery is honest. Its members are often inconsistent (Sarah laughed, Jacob deceived, Samson was a disgrace), and its outcomes are opposite: some shut lions’ mouths, some were sawn in two. All are commended, and none received what was promised. The chapter ends by saying why: God was keeping something better, so that they and we would be made perfect together. The readers were tempted to go back to the age these saints longed to see the end of.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — By Faith: Title Deeds and Tents
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer defines faith as a firm grip on what is hoped for and conviction about what cannot be seen, and shows it at work in the people of old. By faith we understand that God made the universe by his word. Abel, Enoch and Noah trusted God and were approved; without faith no one can please him. Abraham left home not knowing where he was going, lived in tents in the promised land as a foreigner, and looked for a city built by God; Sarah, past age, received power to conceive. They all died without receiving what was promised, seeing it from far off and admitting they were strangers seeking a better, heavenly homeland, and God is not ashamed to be called their God. Abraham offered Isaac, reasoning that God could raise the dead; Isaac, Jacob and Joseph spoke in faith about a future they would not see.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith as a Title Deed

Faith gives the things hoped for a footing in the present, because it rests on the reliability of the one who promised. Everyone in this gallery is commended for something they did that made no sense apart from God's word.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob lived in tents in the land of promise and died without receiving it.

Now: God is not ashamed to be called the God of people who are visibly waiting for a better country.

verseByVerse.quote: Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen. For by it the people of old received their commendation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen. For by it the people of old received their commendation.

Meaning first. Hebrews 11 is the great chapter on faith, answering the call of 10:38–39 to live by faith and not shrink back. It opens by describing faith as confident assurance about what we hope for and conviction about what we cannot see (vv. 1–3). Then it walks through the Old Testament, showing faith at work in a long line of people. Abel offered a better sacrifice; Enoch pleased God and was taken; and without faith it is impossible to please God (vv. 4–6). Noah built the ark; Abraham left home not knowing where he was going, lived as a stranger in the promised land, and looked for God’s city; Sarah received power to conceive (vv. 7–12). All of them died without receiving the promises in full, confessing that they were strangers seeking a heavenly country, and God is not ashamed to be called their God (vv. 13–16). Abraham offered Isaac, believing God could raise the dead; Isaac, Jacob and Joseph blessed their children and looked ahead to the future (vv. 17–22). Moses’ parents hid him; Moses chose suffering with God’s people over the treasures of Egypt, considering reproach for Christ greater wealth; he kept the Passover; Israel crossed the Red Sea; Jericho fell; Rahab was spared (vv. 23–31). And many more, judges, kings and prophets, conquered by faith, while others were tortured, mocked, imprisoned, stoned and killed, people of whom the world was not worthy (vv. 32–38). Yet none of them received the fulfilment in their lifetime, because God had planned something better, so that they would be made perfect together with us (vv. 39–40). The chapter shows that faith trusts God’s word about the unseen and the future, and acts on it, whatever the cost. It is a gallery of the dead, and every one of them is still speaking.

Now faith is. It is not quite a definition. The writer is not saying what faith is in the abstract; he is saying what faith does. “Faith” (pistis) is trust, confidence, reliance, and this is not a full account of saving faith, but a description of how it works, particularly in relation to the future and the unseen. That is exactly the difficulty these readers were in. They could see the temple, the neighbours, the empty houses. What they could not see was the thing they had been promised.

The assurance of things hoped for. “Assurance” is hypostasis, literally that which stands under, a substructure, a foundation. The same word was used at 1:3 of the very being of God, and at 3:14 of confidence. In the papyri it appears in property documents for a title deed, the paper that establishes a claim to something you do not yet hold. That is a remarkable thing to say about faith. It does not merely wish for the things hoped for; it gives them a footing in the present. It treats God’s promises as already real. A man with a title deed to a house he has never seen owns it, and behaves accordingly. Faith is the title deed to what God has promised: the city, the inheritance, the resurrection, the return of Christ.

The conviction of things not seen. “Conviction” is elenchos, a word from the law courts: proof, evidence, the demonstration that settles a case. Faith functions as evidence of what cannot be seen: God himself, heaven, Christ at the right hand of God, and the events still to come (2 Corinthians 4:18; 5:7). We look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen, Paul says, for the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.

Not a leap in the dark. Both words guard against a misunderstanding that has done real damage. Faith in Hebrews is not a leap in the dark, and it is not believing without grounds. It is the settled confidence that treats God’s word as the evidence it is, because the ground of faith is not the strength of the believing but the reliability of the promiser (10:23). Faith is only as good as what it rests on, and this faith rests on God.

For by it the people of old received their commendation. “The people of old” (hoi presbyteroi) are the elders, the ancients: the Old Testament believers. “Received their commendation” (emartyrēthēsan) means they were witnessed to, well spoken of, and the word recurs through the chapter (vv. 4, 5, 39). God himself is the one bearing witness, in Scripture, that they pleased him. The whole gallery that follows exists to show that this is what he approves.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is wishful thinking or a leap in the dark. Faith rests on God’s word and character, which are utterly reliable (6:18; 10:23). Nor does faith create reality; it trusts the reality God has promised. A person does not make heaven exist by believing in it, any more than a title deed builds the house.

How is faith different from positive thinking? Positive thinking trusts that things will turn out well because you expect them to; faith trusts that God will do what he has said because he has said it. Positive thinking is about outcomes you choose; faith is about promises God has made, and it can be just as confident when the outcome looks bad, because it is not resting on the outcome. Abraham, as this chapter will show, expected his son to die and still trusted God. Positive thinking would have been useless on Mount Moriah. Faith was not.

In a sentence. Faith is confidence that what we hope for is real, and certainty about what we cannot see, and it was for their faith that the people of long ago received God’s approval.

On a Tuesday. Pick one promise of God you find hard to believe today: that he will never leave you, that he works all things for good to those who love him, that your sins are forgiven, that Christ will return. Write it down. Then ask what you would do differently today if you held it like a title deed, as something already yours. Do that one thing. Faith grows by being acted on.

For worship. Everything faith holds is held because God is true. The title deed is good because the one who signed it cannot lie, and the evidence is sound because the witness is God himself. He has not asked us to hope in a vacuum. He has given us his word, sworn with an oath, sealed in the blood of his Son, and he bears witness to all who take him at it. The unseen city is real because he is building it, and the unseen Christ is real because he is seated at the right hand of the Majesty on high, and the faith that looks at him is the gift of the God who made him visible to us.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible.

By faith we understand. The first example is not a person, and the choice is deliberate. Before Abel, before Noah, before Abraham, the writer begins with the whole congregation and something every one of them believes. “By faith” (pistei) is the phrase that will open each example in the chapter, repeated again and again like a drumbeat. And note the pairing: faith and understand (nooumen, perceive with the mind, comprehend). They are not opposites here. Faith is presented as the faculty by which something is genuinely known, not a substitute for understanding but the means of it.

That the universe was created by the word of God. “Universe” (tous aiōnas) is the ages, the worlds, all of space and time, as in 1:2. “Created” (katērtisthai) means framed, fitted together, put in order. And “by the word of God” (rhēmati theou) is by God’s spoken word. Which is exactly how Genesis tells it: God said, and it was (Genesis 1:3; Psalm 33:6, 9). Nothing was worked with, shaped, or wrestled into form. He spoke.

How long did God take? The verse teaches that God made the world out of nothing, by speaking. It does not say how long he took. That question belongs to Genesis itself. Many read the days as six ordinary days, pointing to the fourth commandment: in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them (Exodus 20:11). Other Christians who hold to the full authority of Scripture read the days differently, and Reformed Christians have differed on this without dividing. In any reading the point of this verse stands: the world exists because God spoke.

So that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible. The visible world does not have a visible origin. Trace it back as far as you like and you do not arrive at earlier stuff; you arrive at a word. God created from nothing, ex nihilo, by his word alone; he calls into existence the things that do not exist (Romans 4:17; Colossians 1:16). This was a radical claim against Greek philosophy, which generally held that matter was eternal and that a god at best shaped it.

Why start with creation? Because the chapter is about acting on the strength of what cannot be seen, and creation is the first and largest instance. Nobody watched it happen. There were no witnesses, and there is no possibility of any. Every person who believes the world was made does so on the strength of testimony rather than observation. So the writer establishes at the outset that this is not a strange way to hold anything. His readers already order their whole understanding of reality around an event none of them saw, and he is about to ask them to keep ordering their lives around a promise they cannot see either. The first lesson of faith is that the God who made everything from nothing can be trusted to keep every promise.

The invisible is the more solid. There is a further thread here that runs through the chapter. If the visible came out of the invisible, then the invisible is the more solid of the two. That is the conviction Moses will act on when he endures as seeing him who is invisible (v. 27), and the one these readers needed when their visible property was being carried out of their houses.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith rejects evidence or reason. Creation itself bears witness to its Creator: the heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1; Romans 1:20). But the fact that the world was made by God’s word out of nothing is known with certainty only by trusting God’s revelation.

Does science contradict this verse? No honest science contradicts it, because science studies the visible world, and this verse is about where the visible world came from. Science can describe how things work and trace them back a long way, but it cannot see behind the beginning, and it cannot tell you why there is something rather than nothing. Christians should welcome the study of creation, which was largely founded by believers who wanted to think God’s thoughts after him. Where particular theories conflict with what God has plainly said, the theories are human and changeable, and God’s word stands.

In a sentence. It is by faith that we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what can be seen was not made from anything visible.

On a Tuesday. Go outside today and look at something made: the sky, a tree, your own hand. Remember that it was not there, and then God spoke, and it was. Then take the worry you are carrying and set it next to that fact. The God who made something out of nothing is not short of resources for your situation. Tell him so, in a sentence, before you go back inside.

For worship. Before there was anything, there was God, and he spoke. Light came at his word, and the sea took its bounds, and the stars were set in their places by the breath of his mouth. Nothing resisted him and nothing helped him. And the same word that framed the worlds became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:1–3, 14), and the one through whom all things were made upholds them now by the word of his power (1:3). The God who made the universe out of nothing is the God who makes new creatures out of sinners, and he does it the same way: he speaks.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain, through which he was commended as righteous, God commending him by accepting his gifts. And through his faith, though he died, he still speaks. By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him. Now before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain, through which he was commended as righteous, God commending him by accepting his gifts. And through his faith, though he died, he still speaks. By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him. Now before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God.

By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain. Genesis does not say why Abel’s offering was accepted and his brother’s refused; it records the fact and moves on (Genesis 4:3–5). The writer supplies the reason: faith. “More acceptable” (pleiona) means greater, better, fuller. Not the material of the offering, then, and not the technique. It was not merely that Abel’s was an animal and Cain’s was grain, for both kinds were later commanded in the law. Abel offered by faith, from a heart right with God, and he brought the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions, the best (Genesis 4:4). Cain’s heart was wrong, as his murder of Abel showed (1 John 3:12).

The same act is not the same act. Two men brought what they had, and God saw what was underneath it. That is a sobering thing to know about worship, and it is the earliest instance in Scripture of the principle this letter keeps applying: the same act performed by two people is not the same act. Two people may sing the same hymn, put the same amount in the offering, kneel in the same pew, and God sees one offering and not the other.

Through which he was commended as righteous. “Commended” (emartyrēthē) means testified to, and “righteous” (dikaios) is what Jesus called him: righteous Abel (Matthew 23:35). His righteousness came by faith.

God commending him by accepting his gifts. God himself bore witness to Abel’s faith by accepting his offering. The first man in Scripture to be called righteous was declared so by God, on the ground of faith.

And through his faith, though he died, he still speaks. A beautiful sentence, and it works two ways. In Genesis it is Abel’s blood that cries out from the ground (Genesis 4:10); here it is his faith that goes on speaking. He is the first man in the Bible to die and the first to be murdered, and he is still saying something to a congregation thousands of years later. Notice this about the whole chapter. Everyone in it is dead, and every one of them is still talking. And this letter will later say that the blood of Christ speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (12:24). Abel’s blood cried for justice; Christ’s blood cries for mercy.

By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death. The shortest biography in Genesis: Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him (Genesis 5:24). In a chapter of Genesis that records the years and the death of every generation, and the refrain he died, he died, he died, one man has no death recorded. “Taken up” (metetethē) means transferred, translated, removed. God took him directly to himself, as he later took Elijah (2 Kings 2:11).

And he was not found, because God had taken him. The words follow the Greek translation of Genesis 5:24. People looked for him, and he was not there. He had gone on ahead.

Now before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God. The Greek Old Testament renders walked with God as pleased God (euarestēkenai tō theō), which is where the writer gets the phrase, and it supplies the hinge into verse 6. To walk with God is to please him, and to please him requires faith.

Opposite outcomes, both commended. Set the two men side by side, and the chapter has already made an important point. Abel died young and violently; Enoch did not die at all. Faith produced opposite outcomes in the first two examples, and both are commended. Anyone reading this chapter as a list of what faith gets you has been warned in the first two entries of the gallery.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Abel earned acceptance by the quality of his offering. His faith made the offering acceptable. Nor does Enoch’s being taken mean we should expect the same; it was a unique sign of God’s pleasure and of life beyond death, in a world that had just learned to die.

What does it mean to walk with God? It means living each day in his company, as two people walk together on a road, going the same way, talking as they go. In practice it is ordinary: speaking to him through the day, listening to his word, keeping in step with what he wants, turning back quickly when you wander off. Enoch did it for three hundred years while raising sons and daughters (Genesis 5:22), so it is not a life withdrawn from the world. The question is not whether you have had dramatic experiences, but whether you are going his way and keeping him company.

In a sentence. By faith Abel offered God a better sacrifice than Cain did, and because of his faith he was declared righteous when God approved his gifts, and by faith he still speaks, even though he is dead; by faith Enoch was taken from this life, so that he did not experience death; he could not be found, because God had taken him away, for before he was taken he was commended as one who pleased God.

On a Tuesday. Look at one act of worship you will offer this week, your prayers, your giving, your singing, and ask what God sees underneath it. Is it offered in trust, as to a God you believe receives it? Or is it habit, or a performance, or a payment? Then find one ordinary moment today to walk with God: on the way to work, doing the washing up, waiting for a child. Speak to him there. Enoch’s walk was made of days like yours.

For worship. From the very first pages of the Bible, God has been looking for faith, and finding it. He saw it in a shepherd’s offering and called him righteous. He saw it in a man who walked with him for three centuries, and he took him home without death. The first murder could not silence Abel’s faith, and the first death could not touch Enoch. And the better blood that speaks now is the blood of the Son of God, whose voice cries mercy over every believer, and who will one day take all who walk with him to where Enoch went.

verseByVerse.quote: And without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.

And without faith it is impossible to please him. The word is impossible (adynaton) again, the letter’s absolute, used of restoring apostates (6:4), of God lying (6:18), and of bulls and goats taking away sins (10:4). Not difficult, but impossible. It is not that faithless obedience is inferior. It cannot please him at all. That should be allowed to land, because it cuts against a very natural assumption. A person may live decently, give generously and behave better than most of the congregation, and none of it registers as pleasing God if it is not done in faith. Paul says the same thing from the other side: whatever does not proceed from faith is sin (Romans 14:23). Faith is not one virtue among many; it is the root of all that pleases God.

Why it has to be so. The reason is not arbitrary. To do good without trusting God is to treat him as somebody to be managed rather than believed, and no relationship can be pleased by a partner who does not take the other at his word. A husband who brings his wife flowers every week but does not believe a word she says has not pleased her.

For whoever would draw near to God. “Draw near” (proserchomenon) is the key verb of the letter for approaching God in worship (4:16; 7:25; 10:22). Then the two things anyone drawing near must believe, and they are strikingly modest.

Must believe that he exists. “Exists” (estin) is simply is. Not a developed doctrine of God: that he is there, the living God, not an idea or a force. This is the most basic element of faith. But even demons believe that, and shudder (James 2:19); saving faith goes further.

And that he rewards those who seek him. “Rewards” (misthapodotēs) means one who pays wages, a rewarder. That he is worth approaching: that the seeking is not into an empty room. God is not indifferent, distant or stingy; he responds to those who seek him and gives them himself and his blessings (Jeremiah 29:13; Matthew 7:7–8). “Seek” (ekzētousin) means search diligently, seek out. True faith trusts both God’s existence and his goodness.

The harder of the two. Notice that the second is the harder. A great many people believe God exists and behave as though seeking him were pointless. The practical atheism of the half-believing is not a denial of God’s existence but a settled expectation that nothing will come of approaching him. Hebrews says faith is precisely the confidence that something will.

Reward without apology. And the reward language should not be apologised for. It runs through the chapter: Moses was looking to the reward (v. 26), the patriarchs to a city (v. 10). Seeking God for what he gives is only mercenary if what he gives is something other than himself. It is not. Fear not, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great (Genesis 15:1).

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith earns God’s favour, or that we seek him for what he gives rather than for himself. The great reward is God himself. Nor does it mean that seeking originates in us; no one seeks God on his own (Romans 3:11), and God draws us to seek him (John 6:44).

What about those who have never heard? This verse does not say that a vague belief in God is enough. The faith that pleases God draws near to him through Christ (7:25), and the God who rewards those who seek him is the God who sends them the message, as he sent Peter to Cornelius (Acts 10). Some Christians hold that God may save those who respond sincerely to what they know of him, or that he will give them a chance after death. But Scripture offers no such promise, and this letter closes the door on a second chance (9:27). Creation leaves everyone without excuse (Romans 1:20), but salvation comes by hearing the gospel (Romans 10:14). The answer is not to speculate about them but to go to them.

Can my good deeds before I believed please God? Not in the sense this verse means. They may be good for others, and God in his kindness restrains evil and uses even the deeds of unbelievers. But they are not done in faith, from love for God, for his glory, and so they cannot make a person acceptable to him (Westminster 16.7). That is humbling, and it is freeing. You do not have to bring a record to God. You come with empty hands, trusting Christ, and from then on even your small and imperfect works are pleasing to him, because they are offered through his Son (13:21; 1 Peter 2:5).

In a sentence. Without faith it is impossible to please God, because anyone who comes to him must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who earnestly seek him.

On a Tuesday. Notice where you are seeking God as though nothing will come of it: the prayer you have stopped praying, the Bible you open without expecting anything, the worship you attend while your mind is elsewhere. Go back to one of them today, and before you start, tell God that you believe he is there and that he rewards those who seek him. Then seek him as if that were true. It is.

For worship. God is not hiding to make himself hard to find. He is the rewarder of those who seek him, and the reward is himself. He is there, and he is good, and he delights to be found. And he has done more than wait for us: he has come looking for us in his Son, and he has drawn us to seek him by his Spirit. Every heart that has ever turned toward him has found that he was already turned toward it. No one has ever sought the living God in vain.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household. By this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household. By this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.

By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen. Everything in this verse turns on the phrase about the unseen. “Warned” (chrēmatistheis) means divinely instructed. “Events as yet unseen” were a worldwide flood, which had never happened (Genesis 6:13–17). Noah was told about something for which there was no evidence whatever, and quite possibly about a kind of rain he had never watched fall. Faith trusts God’s warnings about the future even when nothing in present experience supports them (v. 1).

In reverent fear. One word (eulabētheis) meaning godly caution, moved with holy fear, taking care. It is the same disposition credited to Christ at 5:7. Noah took God seriously, which is the whole of his commendation.

Constructed an ark for the saving of his household. “Constructed” (kateskeuasen) means prepared, built. And here is where faith becomes visible. It was not a private conviction; it was a very large wooden object in a field, taking years, perhaps decades, in full view of neighbours who had every reason to think him mad. And it was “for the saving of his household”: the obedience of one man carried seven other people through (Genesis 7:1; 1 Peter 3:20). It is the same pattern as Rahab in verse 31, and it should be noticed by anyone whose family is watching them believe.

Faith that does something. That is what this chapter means by faith throughout, and it should be stated plainly, because the word has softened in modern use. Not one person in this gallery is commended for holding an opinion. Every single one is commended for something they did that made no sense apart from a word from God.

By this he condemned the world. “Condemned” (katekrinen) means judged against. Not by preaching at it, though Peter calls him a herald of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5). By building. A man taking God at his word in public passes a verdict on everyone who has heard the same word and done nothing, not by criticising them but simply by acting as though it were true. His actions said judgment was coming; their scoffing showed they did not believe.

And became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith. “Heir” (klēronomos); “the righteousness that comes by faith” (tēs kata pistin dikaiosynēs). The phrase is Paul’s (Romans 4; Philippians 3:9), and it is placed here on a man who lived before Abraham, before the law, before circumcision. Noah was declared righteous by God (Genesis 6:9; 7:1) on the basis of faith. Noah found favour in the eyes of the LORD (Genesis 6:8): grace came first. The righteousness that comes by faith is not a New Testament invention. It is how it has always worked.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Noah was saved by building the ark. He was saved by faith in God’s word, which showed itself in building the ark. Faith and obedience are inseparable but distinct: the obedience was the shape his faith took, not the ground of his acceptance.

What if my family thinks my faith is foolish? Noah’s neighbours certainly did, and God did not ask him to win the argument; he asked him to keep building. Live faithfully, kindly and consistently, without preaching at people who are not listening, and without hiding what you believe. Your steady obedience is itself a testimony, and God often uses it over years. Pray for your family by name. And remember that Noah’s faith was for the saving of his household; God has often been pleased to bring families to himself through one member who believed first.

In a sentence. By faith Noah, when he was warned by God about things not yet seen, reverently built an ark to save his family, and through his faith he condemned the world and became heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.

On a Tuesday. Is God calling you to obey him in something that looks foolish to others: giving generously when money is tight, keeping the Lord’s Day when everyone else works, refusing to cut a corner at work, staying faithful in a hard marriage? Do it by faith, as Noah did. And think about your household. What are you building that will carry them through: family prayer, an open Bible at the table, a home where Christ is spoken of naturally? Lay one plank of it this week.

For worship. God warned the world for a hundred and twenty years, and he warned it through a man with a hammer. He did not have to warn anyone. He did it because he is slow to anger and does not wish that any should perish. And when the flood came, he shut the door himself (Genesis 7:16), and the ark rode on the very waters of judgment. Christ is our ark. The judgment that drowned the world broke over him, and everyone who is in him is carried through it, safe, to a new creation. Noah built a boat by faith; God built a Saviour by grace.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going. By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise. For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going. By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise. For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God.

By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called. Abraham receives more attention than anyone else in the chapter (vv. 8–19), and his first act is obedience. “Obeyed” (hypēkousen) means listened and obeyed. And “called” (kaloumenos) is a present participle: while he was being called. He obeyed immediately (Genesis 12:1–4). The obedience began before the call had finished ringing.

To go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. The place was Canaan, promised to him and his descendants (Genesis 12:7; 15:18–21).

And he went out, not knowing where he was going. That last clause is one of the great descriptions of faith in Scripture, and the order of events is the point. He obeyed first and found out afterwards. God said go, and did not say where until he had gone. Consider what it cost in that world. A man of seventy-five leaving his father’s household (Genesis 12:1–4), having already left the city of Ur, for an unnamed destination, with no map, no contract, and no possibility of verifying anything he had been told. Security in that culture was land and kin, and he left both. Faith trusts God’s leading without needing to see the whole route.

By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land. Here is the sharper irony, and the writer means it to be felt. He arrived, and he was still a stranger. “Went to live” (parōkēsen) means lived as a resident alien, sojourned. The land was promised to him, and he never owned a field in it. The only ground he ever bought was a cave to bury his wife in (Genesis 23).

Living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise. He lived in a tent for a hundred years in the country God had given him (Genesis 12:8; 26:25; 33:18–19). Three generations under canvas. The son and the grandson inherited the promise and the tent together, and none of the three saw it kept.

For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations. And there is the explanation, in the contrast between a tent and a city with foundations. A tent is the least permanent structure a man can live in: pegs and cloth, moved every season. Foundations are the opposite: the part of a building that does not move. “Looking forward” (exedecheto) means waiting eagerly, expecting. The city is the heavenly Jerusalem (12:22; 13:14), which John saw with twelve foundations (Revelation 21:2, 10–14). Abraham looked beyond Canaan to a heavenly inheritance. He could live in the temporary because he was expecting the permanent. That is the logic of the whole chapter, and it is the answer to the readers’ situation: people whose houses had been emptied, told about a man who never had a house and did not mind, because he was waiting for something with foundations.

Whose designer and builder is God. The words are an architect’s and a craftsman’s. “Designer” (technitēs) is craftsman, architect; “builder” (dēmiourgos) is maker, constructor. God himself designed and built it. Abraham never saw the city; he did know who was building it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Abraham had no interest in the land; it was truly promised. But he understood the land as a pointer to something greater, as the New Testament makes clear: the promise to Abraham and his offspring was that he would be heir of the world (Romans 4:13).

How do I know if God is calling me to go somewhere? God does not usually speak to us as he spoke to Abraham, in a direct word naming a journey. He guides us now through his written word, through wisdom, prayer, the counsel of mature Christians, and the circumstances he opens and closes. So the question is less what has God secretly decided, and more what does faithfulness require: what would serve Christ, love my family, and use my gifts well. Then act, even without seeing the whole road. Abraham’s faith was not knowing where; it was knowing who.

In a sentence. By faith Abraham obeyed when God called him to leave for a place he would later receive as his inheritance, setting out without knowing where he was going; by faith he made his home in the promised land like a foreigner in a strange country, living in tents, as did Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise, for he was waiting for the city with lasting foundations, whose architect and builder is God.

On a Tuesday. Hold your earthly home and plans loosely. You are travelling to a better city. Let that shape one decision this week: how much you spend on the house compared with how much you give, whether a career move serves Christ or only yourself, how you speak about the place you live. And if you are unsettled, moving, between homes, or without one, take heart from Abraham. Living in a tent is not a sign that God has forgotten you. It is the way his people have always lived.

For worship. God called a man out of a city of idols and told him to walk. He gave him a promise and a tent, and let him live in the land for a century without owning it, and Abraham was content, because God had shown him something better. The God of Abraham is a builder. He has drawn the plans of a city with foundations that will never shift, and he has laid its cornerstone in Christ, and he is building it still, out of living stones gathered from every nation. We have not seen it yet. But we know the architect, and we know that what he begins, he finishes.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age, since she considered him faithful who had promised. Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead, were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as many as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age, since she considered him faithful who had promised. Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead, were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as many as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore.

By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive. The commendation is generous, and any reader of Genesis will feel the generosity. “Sarah herself” (autē Sarra): even Sarah. She laughed when she overheard the promise, and then denied laughing (Genesis 18:12–15). She had earlier arranged a substitute in Hagar rather than wait. Her faith was not straightforward. And Hebrews says: by faith. This is one of the clearest instances in Scripture of God commending what he sees underneath a mixed performance. He is not describing her as she behaved on her worst afternoon. He is describing what was actually there, and it was genuine. Her faith was not perfect, but it was real, and it grew.

Who received the power. The phrase “power to conceive” (dynamin eis katabolēn spermatos) is literally power for the laying down of seed, and the expression usually refers to the father’s part. So some take this verse as applying to Abraham, with Sarah as a secondary subject: by faith Abraham, together with Sarah, received power to become a father. Either way, both shared in the miracle by faith.

Even when she was past the age. Sarah was ninety and had always been barren (Genesis 11:30; 17:17).

Since she considered him faithful who had promised. There is the thing itself, and it is the same phrase as 10:23: he who promised is faithful (pistos). Faith in this chapter is repeatedly a judgment about the character of the promiser rather than a feeling about the promise. Not trusting her own ability, but God’s reliability.

Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead. The phrase is blunt, and Paul uses it too (Romans 4:19). “As good as dead” (nenekrōmenou) means deadened. A hundred-year-old body and a ninety-year-old womb, and the writer does not soften either. That is important to the argument, because faith here is not optimism about the possible. Abraham and Sarah were not hoping for a favourable outcome within the range of nature. The situation was, humanly, closed, and the New Testament is careful to say so rather than pretend the odds were merely long.

Were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as many as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore. The two images are God’s own from the Genesis promises (Genesis 15:5; 22:17; 32:12), and they were given to a childless man on a particular night, when he was taken outside and told to look up. From one man as good as dead, a nation. And through Christ, Abraham’s spiritual children from every nation: if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:7, 29). The readers of this letter were the proof. They were the sand, sitting in a room somewhere, hearing about the night their ancestor was told to count the stars.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Sarah never doubted. She laughed. Faith is not the absence of struggle but trusting God despite it.

Is my faith real if it is mixed with doubt and failure? Very often, yes. Sarah’s was, and Hebrews commends it. The question is not whether your faith is pure, but whether it is resting on God. A trembling hand holding a rope is as safe as a steady one, because the rope does the holding. Bring your doubts to God honestly, as the father did who said, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24), and keep looking at God’s faithfulness rather than at your own feelings. Faith grows by being fed on God’s promises and tested in hard places, and God is patient with it.

In a sentence. By faith even Sarah, who was past childbearing age, was enabled to have a child, because she considered God faithful to his promise, and so from this one man, who was as good as dead, came descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky and as countless as the sand on the seashore.

On a Tuesday. What seems dead or impossible in your life: a marriage that has gone cold, a child far from God, a long infertility, a sin you cannot seem to break? Do not pretend it is not dead, as the writer does not pretend about Abraham. Bring it to God as it is, and tell him that you consider him faithful who has promised. Then look up, as Abraham did, at something he has made, and remember whose promise you are trusting.

For worship. God chose to build his people out of a couple who could not have children, so that no one could ever say the nation came from human strength. He let the situation become hopeless first, and then he kept his word. And he has been doing the same ever since: bringing life out of barrenness, sons and daughters out of dead hearts, a multitude no one can number out of one man as good as dead. The God who turned Sarah’s laughter of disbelief into the laughter of joy, and gave her a son named Laughter (Genesis 21:6), is the God who raised his own Son from the grave, and he is faithful who has promised.

verseByVerse.quote: These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return. But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return. But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city.

These all died in faith. The writer pauses the roll-call to say what all of them had in common, and it is not what a modern reader expects from a chapter about faith. “Died in faith” (kata pistin apethanon) means died according to faith. They lived by faith and died still trusting. Faith carried them to the end.

Not having received the things promised. Read that against any account of faith that measures it by results. Every one of them died without getting it. They did not see the full fulfilment: the land, the nation, the Messiah, the heavenly city. Abraham never owned the land, never saw the nation, never met the offspring in whom all the families of the earth would be blessed. He got Isaac and a burial cave. They died without receiving what was promised, but they did not die without salvation. They were saved as we are, by faith in God’s promise of the Christ who was to come, and his death covers their sins too (9:15).

But having seen them and greeted them from afar. “Greeted” (aspasamenoi) means welcomed, saluted. The image is of travellers sighting a country from the deck of a ship and waving at a shore they will not reach on this voyage. They saw it. They were glad. They did not land. Jesus said that Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad (John 8:56).

And having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. “Strangers” (xenoi) are foreigners; “exiles” (parepidēmoi) are temporary residents, sojourners. That is Abraham’s own description of himself when he came to buy the burial cave: I am a sojourner and foreigner among you (Genesis 23:4). Jacob spoke to Pharaoh of the days of his sojourning (Genesis 47:9). Believers are pilgrims in this world (1 Peter 1:1; 2:11).

For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. The writer listens to how they talked and draws a conclusion from it. A man who calls himself a stranger has told you he belongs somewhere else. “Homeland” (patris) is fatherland, native country. Pilgrims are going somewhere.

If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return. Then verse 15 closes the obvious escape. Ur was still there. The road ran both ways, and nobody was stopping them. They could have gone back to Mesopotamia. They did not, because their hearts were set on something else. Their homesickness was not for anywhere they had left.

But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. “Desire” (oregontai) is to stretch out for, to long for. “Better” (kreittonos), the letter’s word again. “Heavenly” (epouraniou). They longed for heaven, God’s country, the new creation: our citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20).

Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God. And that is one of the most moving sentences in Scripture. “Not ashamed” (ouk epaischynetai): as Jesus is not ashamed to call us brothers (2:11). God calls himself the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob (Exodus 3:6), three men who lived in tents and died holding nothing, and the writer says he is not embarrassed by the association. Jesus used the same title to prove the resurrection: he is not God of the dead, but of the living (Matthew 22:32). People who are visibly waiting for another country do not embarrass him. It is the ones who have settled here who make the title awkward.

For he has prepared for them a city. “Prepared” (hētoimasen): God has already made it ready (John 14:2–3; Revelation 21:2). The reason he is not ashamed is that their hope is not a fantasy. He has actually built the thing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should despise this world or withdraw from it. It means our deepest loyalty and hope are elsewhere, which frees us to serve here without clinging. The pilgrim can work hard, love his neighbours and seek the good of the city where he lives (Jeremiah 29:7), precisely because he does not need it to be heaven.

Is it wrong to enjoy life here and want things to go well? No. God gives us richly all things to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17), and a pilgrim may delight in a good meal, a happy marriage, a beautiful place and work well done. What this passage warns against is settling: treating this world as home, so that we would not really mind if Christ never came. The test is what you long for most, and what you could lose without losing everything. Enjoy the inns on the road with thanks; just do not mistake them for the destination.

Does God feel ashamed of me when I fail? Not if you belong to him. This verse says God is not ashamed to be called the God of people like Jacob, who was a schemer and a liar for much of his life. What made the difference was not their performance but their faith, which looked to his promise and away from this world. Christ, too, is not ashamed to call his people brothers (2:11). The shame of your sin was borne by him at the cross, where he despised the shame (12:2). You may feel ashamed of yourself; God, in Christ, is not ashamed of you.

In a sentence. All these people were still living by faith when they died; they did not receive the things promised, but saw them and welcomed them from a distance, admitting that they were foreigners and strangers on earth; people who say such things show that they are looking for a country of their own, for if they had been thinking of the country they had left, they could have gone back; instead they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one, and so God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.

On a Tuesday. Listen to how you speak this week. Do you talk like a stranger and exile, or like someone who has settled? Notice what you complain about losing, and what you dream about gaining. Then do one thing that only makes sense if you are going home: give something away you would like to keep, spend an hour with someone who cannot repay you, or tell a friend about the city you are looking for.

For worship. The God of heaven has chosen to be known by the names of three nomads. He is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and he is not ashamed of them, because they believed him. They lived in tents and died in hope, and he has prepared a city for them, and for all who share their faith. And the same God has given us a better name to call him by: the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who came from that city to bring us there. We are strangers here because we have a home. He has built it, and he is not ashamed to be our God.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son, of whom it was said, “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.” He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son, of whom it was said, “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.” He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.

By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac. Genesis 22, the hardest chapter in the Old Testament, and the writer takes it as the summit of Abraham’s faith rather than as a problem to be explained. “Tested” (peirazomenos) means tried, proved. God tested Abraham (Genesis 22:1), not to tempt him to sin, but to prove and strengthen his faith. “Offered up” (prosenēnochen) is a perfect tense: as good as offered. In intention and obedience the sacrifice was complete, though God stopped his hand.

And he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son. “Only son” (monogenēs) means unique, one and only. Abraham had Ishmael too, but Isaac was the unique son of promise: take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love (Genesis 22:2). The writer sets out the contradiction deliberately, because it is the point.

Of whom it was said, Through Isaac shall your offspring be named. From Genesis 21:12. The promised line ran through Isaac. Everything God had promised depended on this boy. He was the promise, in a body. And God told Abraham to kill him. If Isaac died childless, the promise would fail.

Trusting God against God. So the test was not merely whether Abraham loved God more than his son, terrible as that is. It was whether he would obey a command that appeared to destroy the promise it came from. He was being asked to trust God against God.

He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead. “Considered” (logisamenos) is a reckoning word: he worked it out. This was not blind obedience or a suspension of thought. Abraham reasoned: the promise runs through Isaac; God does not lie; God has commanded Isaac’s death; therefore if Isaac dies, God will raise him. It is arithmetic, and it is the only arithmetic that fits both facts. Faith reasons from God’s promises. And it is remarkable, because no one had ever been raised from the dead. There was no precedent in the world for what Abraham concluded God would do. He inferred the resurrection from the character of God alone. Genesis records the conclusion in his own words, when he tells the servants to wait: I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you (Genesis 22:5). He said we.

From which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back. The word is parabolē, in a parable, as a figure. Isaac was as good as dead and came back down the mountain alive, a picture of resurrection. And the whole episode is a picture: a father, an only son, wood carried up a hill by the son, and a substitute provided by God at the last moment. Abraham named the place The LORD will provide, and two thousand years later, on a hill in the same region, he did. The greater Father did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32; John 3:16), and received him back from the dead, not figuratively but in reality.

How could God command a father to sacrifice his son? He never intended it to be carried out. It was a test (Genesis 22:1), and God stopped Abraham’s hand: do not lay your hand on the boy (Genesis 22:12). The same God forbade child sacrifice in the plainest terms (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31; Jeremiah 7:31). The story is unique, and it points beyond itself: God spared Abraham’s son and did not spare his own. It gives no one warrant to harm anyone in God’s name.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God approves of human sacrifice. He stopped it and provided a ram instead, and the law forbade child sacrifice. The test revealed faith and pointed to God’s own provision of his Son.

What should I do when God seems to contradict his own promises? Do what Abraham did: reason from who God is. When circumstances seem to say that God has forgotten you, or that his word cannot be true, hold on to the fixed points: God does not lie, God is good, and God can raise the dead. Then obey what you know, even when you cannot see how it will work out. Abraham did not know about the ram when he climbed the mountain. He knew God. Many believers have found that the provision came only at the last moment, and only on the mountain.

In a sentence. By faith Abraham, when God tested him, offered Isaac as a sacrifice; he who had received the promises was ready to offer his one and only son, even though God had said to him, It is through Isaac that your offspring will be counted; Abraham reasoned that God could even raise the dead, and in a manner of speaking he did receive Isaac back from death.

On a Tuesday. Is there something you love that you are holding back from God: a child, a career, a relationship, a dream? Offer it to him today, not by destroying it, but by putting it into his hands and saying that it is his. Then trust him with it. And if you are facing a test that seems to contradict God’s promises, write down this sentence and keep it where you will see it: God is able even to raise the dead.

For worship. On Mount Moriah a father raised a knife over his only son, and a voice from heaven stopped him, and a ram caught in a thicket died instead. Two thousand years later, on a hill not far away, another Father gave up his only Son, and there was no voice to stop it, and no ram, because the Son was the ram. God did not spare his own Son. He asked of Abraham what he did not in the end require, and he gave himself what he did not spare. And on the third day he received his Son back from the dead, not in a figure but in fact. The LORD has provided.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau. By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, bowing in worship over the head of his staff. By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau. By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, bowing in worship over the head of his staff. By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones.

Three dying men. Three men in three verses, and what unites them is easily missed: all three acts of faith are performed by dying men about a future they will not see.

By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau. “Future” (peri mellontōn) means concerning things to come. Isaac blessed his sons with blessings about the future (Genesis 27:27–40). Remember how that scene actually went. Isaac was blind, deceived by his wife and his younger son, and he intended the blessing for Esau. He was, in the plainest terms, taken in. Yet when he discovered the deception, he trembled very violently, and then said of Jacob: yes, and he shall be blessed (Genesis 27:33). That is the moment Hebrews commends. Isaac recognised that God’s purpose had gone through his own mistake, and he did not try to undo it. His blessings expressed faith that God’s promises would be fulfilled in their descendants.

By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph. Another old blind man, and another crossing of hands. Jacob blessed Ephraim and Manasseh, and deliberately gave the greater blessing to the younger, over Joseph’s objection (Genesis 48:14–19). God’s choice, not human order. The man who had stolen a blessing by deceit gives one away, at the end, by the same principle he had once tried to force.

Bowing in worship over the head of his staff. The detail is tender. An old man too weak to stand unsupported, leaning on a staff, as he had once crossed the Jordan with nothing but a staff (Genesis 32:10), worshipping. The staff was the symbol of his pilgrim life. Dying, he worshipped.

Staff or bed? The word follows the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 47:31. The Hebrew, with different vowels, reads bed. The Hebrew consonants for bed (mittah) and staff (matteh) are the same, and the vowels were added much later; the Greek translators read them as staff. Both readings picture a dying old man bowing in worship, and neither changes the point.

By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites. This is the most striking of the three. “Made mention” (emnēmoneusen) means remembered, spoke of. Joseph was the second man in Egypt, with a palace, a title and a family established in the best land of the country. Nothing in his circumstances suggested that his descendants would ever leave, and the exodus was centuries away. Yet he spoke of God bringing Israel out: God will surely visit you (Genesis 50:24). Joseph, though powerful in Egypt, knew Egypt was not home.

And gave directions concerning his bones. He made Israel swear to carry his bones to Canaan (Genesis 50:25). He would not be embalmed into an Egyptian tomb, however grand. His faith took the form of a funeral instruction: a set of bones in a box, sitting in Egypt for centuries as a standing statement that this was not home. And they kept the promise. Moses took the bones (Exodus 13:19), the box travelled forty years in the wilderness, and they were buried at Shechem after the conquest (Joshua 24:32), over four hundred years later.

What it does not mean. It does not mean these men were perfect. Isaac favoured Esau, Jacob was a deceiver, and the family was full of rivalry. Faith, not perfection, is what is commended.

How should a Christian face death? As these men did: still trusting, still worshipping, and still thinking about the future of God’s people. Death is an enemy, and it is right to grieve and even to fear the dying. But for a believer it is not the end of the story; it is the doorway to being with Christ, and the body will be raised. Practically, that means putting your affairs in order, speaking blessings and the gospel to your family, forgiving and asking forgiveness, and telling those you leave behind where your hope is. A deathbed can be one of the most powerful pulpits there is.

In a sentence. By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau with regard to their future; by faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons, and worshipped as he leaned on the top of his staff; by faith Joseph, when his end was near, spoke about the exodus of the Israelites from Egypt and gave instructions about burying his bones.

On a Tuesday. Think about what you will pass on: not only money or possessions, but blessing and faith. Is there a child, grandchild or younger believer you could bless this week, in words, telling them what you see God doing in them and what you hope for them in Christ? And if you have not yet made a will, or written down for your family what you believe and how you want to be buried, consider doing it. Joseph’s bones preached for four hundred years.

For worship. God kept his promises across centuries, through blind fathers, scheming sons and a coffin in Egypt. He wove his purpose through Isaac’s mistake and Jacob’s crossed hands, and he carried Joseph’s bones out of Egypt exactly as Joseph said he would. Not one word of his failed. And he is the God who has promised that the bodies of his people, buried in every land, will be raised at the last day. Our graves, like Joseph’s coffin, are a statement that this is not home. The exodus is coming.
verseByVerse.note: “Staff” follows the Greek Old Testament of Gen 47:31; the Hebrew text as later pointed reads “bed”; the consonants are the same.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–40 — The Turn: Some Were Tortured
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The examples continue. Moses’ parents hid him, unafraid of the king. Moses himself refused the privileges of Egypt’s court, choosing to suffer with God’s people, counting reproach for Christ greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures. He left Egypt, kept the Passover, and led Israel through the sea. Jericho’s walls fell and Rahab was spared. Then the writer piles up names, Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets, who by faith won victories and escaped death. But faith did not always mean rescue. Others were tortured, mocked, flogged, imprisoned, stoned, sawn in two, killed by the sword, and wandered destitute in deserts and caves; the world was not worthy of them. None of them received the promise in full, because God had planned something better that includes us, so that they would not be made complete without us.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Chapter Turns Over Mid-Verse

In verse 35 faith that raised the dead becomes faith that was tortured to death — the same faith, opposite outcomes, both commended. Of such people the world was not worthy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David and Samuel were far from consistent, and they are in the roll.

Now: All these died waiting for what the church now has; apart from us they are not made perfect.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict. By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking to the reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict. By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking to the reward.

By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents. The first act of faith in the Moses section is not his. It belongs to a mother and father, Amram and Jochebed (Exodus 6:20), defying a royal edict with a baby in a basket. Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew baby boy to be thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1:22), and they hid Moses at great risk (Exodus 2:1–3).

Because they saw that the child was beautiful. “Beautiful” (asteios) means fine, well formed, pleasing; it is used of Moses in Exodus 2:2 and Acts 7:20, where Stephen says he was beautiful in God’s sight. Every parent thinks their baby is beautiful. Perhaps they sensed that God had a special purpose for this one.

And they were not afraid of the king’s edict. “Edict” (diatagma) is decree. Faith overcame fear of the most powerful ruler on earth. Exodus tells us the midwives feared God rather than Pharaoh (Exodus 1:17), which is the same calculation. This is civil disobedience when the state commands sin: we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. “Grown up” (megas genomenos), having become great, was at about forty (Acts 7:23). “Refused” (ērnēsato) means denied, renounced. Weigh what was refused. Whatever his exact standing, he was raised in the royal household of the greatest power on earth, with its education, wealth and prospects. Stephen says he was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (Acts 7:22). He walked away from it to identify with his people (Exodus 2:11–12).
