Choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God. The verb (helomenos) is a choosing word: he weighed two options and took one. “Mistreated with” (synkakoucheisthai) is to suffer hardship together with. He chose solidarity with despised slaves over the palace.

Than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. And the two adjectives do all the work. The pleasures were real: the writer does not pretend Egypt was miserable. But they were fleeting (proskairos), temporary, lasting a season. Set against them was mistreatment, which was also real, and permanent company with the people of God. That is the calculation this chapter keeps making, and it is not asceticism. It is arithmetic about duration. For Moses, staying in the palace would have been sin, because it meant denying God’s people and God’s call.

He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt. A startling phrase, since Moses lived some fourteen centuries earlier. How could he suffer reproach for Christ? It most likely means the reproach borne by God’s anointed people, and so by the Anointed One with whom they are identified, the same disgrace in a different century (Psalm 89:50–51). Moses identified with the people through whom the Messiah would come, and looked ahead to him by faith: he wrote of me, Jesus said (John 5:46). “Greater wealth” is a deliberately commercial word, set against the literal treasures of the richest kingdom in the world. Moses did not weigh spiritual benefit against material loss. He weighed one wealth against another and concluded that reproach was the better asset. And the readers were facing reproach for Christ themselves (10:33; 13:13).

For he was looking to the reward. “Looking” (apeblepen) means looked away to, fixed his eyes on; “reward” (misthapodosia), as in 10:35. The reason he could count that way, and it is verse 6 again. He was not being noble. He was looking at a figure the Egyptians could not see, and he weighed the eternal against the temporary and chose wisely (2 Corinthians 4:17–18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean wealth or high position is sinful in itself. Joseph and Daniel served faithfully in pagan courts. For Moses, remaining meant disobeying God’s call. The question is always: what does faithfulness require of me here?

Is it right to disobey the government? Christians are to submit to governing authorities and honour them, because God has appointed them (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17). But when the state commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, we must obey God rather than men, as Moses’ parents, the midwives, Daniel and the apostles did. Such disobedience should be open, peaceful and limited to the point of conflict, and we should be willing to bear the consequences, as they were. It is not a licence to rebel whenever we dislike a law.

Why are the pleasures of sin called pleasures? Because they are. Sin rarely tempts us with misery; it offers something sweet, and the Bible is honest about it. The problem is not that sin is never enjoyable, but that its enjoyment is short and its cost is long, and it takes what belongs to God. The way to resist is not to pretend sin is dull, but to set against it a greater pleasure: at your right hand are pleasures forevermore (Psalm 16:11). Moses gave up the palace because he had seen something better.

In a sentence. By faith Moses’ parents hid him for three months after he was born, because they saw he was no ordinary child, and they were not afraid of the king’s order; by faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be known as the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing to be ill-treated along with the people of God rather than to enjoy the short-lived pleasures of sin, and regarding disgrace for the sake of Christ as of greater value than the treasures of Egypt, because he was looking ahead to his reward.

On a Tuesday. What fleeting pleasure or advantage might you have to give up to be faithful to Christ this week: a promotion that requires dishonesty, a friendship that pulls you from God, a habit you enjoy that you know is sin? Do the arithmetic Moses did, and write it down if it helps: what it offers, how long it lasts, what it costs. Then look to the reward. And notice where you are embarrassed to be identified with God’s people, the unimpressive church, the awkward believer. Stand with them.

For worship. Moses left a palace for a brickyard, and he counted it riches, because he had seen the reward. But Christ left more than Moses ever did. He left the glory of heaven and the throne of the universe, and he chose to be mistreated with the people of God, and bore their reproach to the end. The reproach that Moses carried in advance, Christ carried in full, outside the city gate. He was rich, and for our sake he became poor, so that we by his poverty might become rich. The treasures of Egypt are dust. The reproach of Christ is wealth that lasts for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king, for he endured as seeing him who is invisible. By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood, so that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king, for he endured as seeing him who is invisible. By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood, so that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them.

By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king. There is a difficulty here worth naming, since Exodus says that Moses fled to Midian because he was afraid (Exodus 2:14–15). The likeliest reading is that this refers to the exodus itself rather than the flight (Exodus 12:31–42), when he led Israel out in defiance of Pharaoh: the writer follows the order of events, and the Passover comes in the next verse. Others take it as the flight to Midian, interpreted as a decision of faith rather than mere panic, describing the settled disposition of a life rather than one bad afternoon. Either way, Hebrews is not rewriting the history; it is characterising a man.

For he endured as seeing him who is invisible. It is the finest sentence in the chapter, and the paradox is deliberate. Seeing the invisible (ton aoraton hōs horōn): the writer puts two words together that cannot go together, in order to say what faith actually does. God is invisible (1 Timothy 1:17), yet Moses lived as though he saw him. And it connects back to verse 3. If the visible world was made out of what cannot be seen, then the invisible is the more solid of the two, and a man who reckons with it is not being fanciful but realistic. Moses stood in front of the most visible power on earth, unimpressed, because he was looking at somebody else in the room. He feared God more than Pharaoh, so he did not fear Pharaoh. “Endured” (ekarterēsen) means persevered, held out, was steadfast, the same idea as 10:36: remaining under weight. That is what the seeing produced: not a mystical experience, but forty years of staying put.

By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood. “Kept” (pepoiēken) means instituted, and it is a perfect tense: he established it for all time. The Passover (Exodus 12) was a new ritual, never done before. Consider what that instruction required. A lamb killed, and its blood painted on the doorposts of every Israelite house, and every firstborn son in the country would live or die that night on the strength of it. Nothing about blood on a doorframe would strike anyone as protective. Moses had only the word of God that it would work, and he obeyed God’s instructions exactly.

So that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them. “Destroyer” (ho olothreuōn) is the one who destroys: the angel of death, or the Lord himself acting in judgment (Exodus 12:23). And the Israelites were not exempt by nationality. The angel passed over houses with blood on them, and only those, which is the letter’s whole argument in a single night’s history: not who you are descended from, but whether the blood has been applied. Where the blood was, judgment passed over. And the Passover lamb pointed to Christ, our Passover lamb, who has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7; John 1:29), whose blood protects us from judgment.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Moses never felt fear. It means fear did not govern his decisions; faith in God did.

How can I see someone who is invisible? Not with the eyes, but by trusting what God has shown of himself in his word and in his Son. Jesus is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15); whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). So you see the invisible God by looking at Christ in the Scriptures, until his reality becomes more weighty to you than what you can see around you. Practically, that means time in the Gospels, prayer that speaks to him as present, and remembering through the day that he is there. The more real he is to you, the smaller everything else becomes.

In a sentence. By faith he left Egypt, not afraid of the king’s anger, and kept going because he saw the one who is invisible; by faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch the firstborn of Israel.

On a Tuesday. Who is your Pharaoh: a boss, a family member, a group of friends, a culture whose disapproval you dread? Notice how large they loom in your decisions. Then picture the invisible God in the room, as Moses did, and ask what you would do if you feared him more than them. And when you take the Lord’s Supper next, remember the Passover: you are safe tonight not because of who you are, but because the blood has been applied.

For worship. On the night of the Passover, the only thing that stood between the firstborn of Israel and death was the blood of a lamb on the wood of a doorframe. And on the day of the cross, the only thing that stands between us and the judgment of God is the blood of the Lamb of God on the wood of a cross. God provided the lamb in Egypt, and he provided his Son at Calvary. Where the blood is, judgment passes over. The invisible God whom Moses saw by faith has made himself visible in Christ, our Passover, and the Destroyer cannot touch those who are sheltered by his blood.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land, but the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned. By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days. By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land, but the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned. By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days. By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.

Who faith belongs to. Three acts of faith, and the writer has chosen them to make a point about who faith belongs to.

By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land. “The people” is Israel collectively, hemmed in between the sea and Pharaoh’s army, going forward at God’s command (Exodus 14:13–22). Their faith was weak: they had complained bitterly only hours before that Moses had brought them out to die in the wilderness (Exodus 14:10–12). Yet they obeyed, and walked between walls of water on the seabed.

But the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned. “Attempted” (peiran labontes) means having made trial. The same water, the same seabed, the same walls of water on either hand, and two entirely different outcomes. The Egyptians did precisely what Israel did, and it killed them (Exodus 14:23–28). So the crossing was not a technique. What made the difference was not the action but what stood behind it, exactly as with Abel’s sacrifice in verse 4. What saved Israel was not the act of walking but God, received by faith. This is the chapter’s consistent claim, and it carries into any consideration of religious practice: the same act performed by two people is not the same act.

By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days. Joshua 6: no siege engines or battering rams, only marching, trumpets and a shout, as God commanded. Here faith takes the form of doing something visibly absurd for a week. An army walking in silence round a fortified city, once a day, watched from the battlements by men who presumably found it very funny by the fourth morning. Nothing happened on days one through six. That is a detail worth holding on to. Faith frequently looks foolish for a period before it looks like anything at all, and the seventh day is the only one anybody remembers.

By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient. The writer keeps the description. He does not call her the innkeeper or pass over her history, and the placing is deliberate: immediately after Moses and the exodus stands a Canaanite woman of that trade, in the same list, commended on the same terms. A Gentile, a Canaanite, a prostitute, alongside Abraham and Moses. “Disobedient” (apeithēsasin) describes the people of Jericho, who knew of God’s works, had heard of the Red Sea and were melting with fear, but did not believe (Joshua 2:9–11).

Because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies. “Friendly welcome” is literally with peace (met’ eirēnēs). She hid the spies and confessed faith in Israel’s God. She had heard what happened at the Red Sea and drew a conclusion the rest of her city refused: the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath (Joshua 2:11). She had less evidence than anyone in Israel and believed more than most of them. James also commends her faith shown in action (James 2:25).

Where Christians differ: did God approve Rahab’s lie? Rahab lied to the king’s men to protect the spies (Joshua 2:4–6). Some hold that deceiving those bent on murder is not the false witness the ninth commandment forbids, and point to the Hebrew midwives, with whom God dealt well (Exodus 1:19–20). Others, with Augustine and Calvin, hold that the lie was a sin, forgiven like the rest of her past, and that God honoured her faith in spite of it. Verdict: Scripture commends Rahab’s faith and her protection of God’s people, not her lie. Hebrews and James praise her welcome and her action, not her deception. God used her despite her imperfect understanding, as he uses all his people. Believers today should seek to protect the innocent without sinning, while recognising the extraordinary pressures some face.

A Canaanite prostitute in the family. Two things follow. She is one of only two women named in this chapter, and the only Canaanite, and she ended in the genealogy of Christ: Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab (Matthew 1:5). She became part of Israel, the great-great-grandmother of David, and an ancestor of the Messiah. If the readers of this letter were wondering whether the family of faith was narrowing, the answer is that it always had a Canaanite prostitute in it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Rahab’s past did not matter. It means grace reaches the most unlikely people, and faith transforms them. She did not stay what she was.

Can God really use someone with my past? Look at the names in this verse. A people who had grumbled their way to the shore of the Red Sea; a Canaanite prostitute who lied to protect strangers. God did not choose them because they were respectable, and he does not wait for us to be. Whatever you have done, if you trust Christ, your past is forgiven, and God delights to show his grace by using people the world would have written off. That does not mean the consequences of sin always vanish, or that you should not make amends where you can. But your history is not the end of your story; Rahab’s certainly was not.

In a sentence. By faith the people passed through the Red Sea as though it were dry land, but when the Egyptians tried to do the same they were drowned; by faith the walls of Jericho fell after the army had marched around them for seven days; by faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies, was not killed along with those who were disobedient.

On a Tuesday. Is there something God has told you to keep doing that seems to be achieving nothing: praying for a person who shows no interest, teaching a children’s class that seems not to listen, loving a neighbour who is cold? You may be on the fourth day of seven. Keep walking. And look round your church for the Rahab: the person whose past makes others uncomfortable. Welcome them the way she welcomed the spies, with peace.

For worship. The same sea that saved Israel drowned Egypt, and the same city that fell around Rahab spared her house, because the scarlet cord was in her window. God does not save by technique or by birth, but by faith in him, and he reaches over every wall to find it. He went into Jericho for a prostitute, and he wrote her into the line of his Son. The family tree of Jesus is full of people like Rahab, and that is no accident: he came to call not the righteous but sinners, and he is not ashamed of them.

verseByVerse.quote: And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets— who through faith conquered kingdoms, enforced justice, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets— who through faith conquered kingdoms, enforced justice, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight.

And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of. The preacher looks at his material and gives up on the attempt to cover it, a common device in ancient speeches, and the remark is a piece of skill, because the impression of an inexhaustible supply is stronger than another twenty examples would be. The author speeds up.

Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah. Then names, and they are not the ones we would have chosen. Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah are from Judges (Judges 4–16). Gideon defeated the Midianites with three hundred men (Judges 7), but demanded two signs with a fleece first, and later made an ephod that became an idol (Judges 8:27). Barak, urged by Deborah, defeated Sisera (Judges 4), but would not go to battle unless she came with him. Samson’s life was a catalogue of appetite and folly, yet at the end he called on God and destroyed the Philistine temple (Judges 16:28–30). Jephthah defeated the Ammonites (Judges 11), and made a rash vow with terrible consequences.

Of David and Samuel and the prophets. David, the king after God’s own heart, who also committed adultery and murder. Samuel, the last judge and first great prophet, whose sons took bribes. The prophets: Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel and others.

What the roll is measuring. Not one of them is a model of consistency, and the writer must have known it; his readers knew those stories far better than we do. He puts them in the roll of faith anyway, which tells you what the roll is measuring. Not achievement, and certainly not character. The bare fact of having taken God at his word, in the middle of lives that were often a mess. Faith, not perfection.

Who through faith conquered kingdoms. Then the achievements, rattled off at speed. Joshua, the judges, David (2 Samuel 8).

Enforced justice. Literally worked righteousness (eirgasanto dikaiosynēn): judges and kings like Samuel and David who ruled justly (1 Samuel 12:3–5; 2 Samuel 8:15).

Obtained promises. They received specific promises and fulfilments from God: not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made had failed (Joshua 21:45).

Does obtained promises contradict verse 39? No. These men received particular promises in their lifetimes: victories, deliverances, sons. What none of them received was what was promised in the full sense, the coming of Christ and the city God has prepared. God kept his smaller promises along the way, and every one of them was a pledge of the great one.

Stopped the mouths of lions. Daniel in the lions’ den (Daniel 6:22); Samson and David also killed lions (Judges 14:6; 1 Samuel 17:34–37).

Quenched the power of fire. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the furnace (Daniel 3:23–27), where a fourth figure walked with them in the flames.

Escaped the edge of the sword. David from Saul (1 Samuel 19–27); Elijah from Jezebel (1 Kings 19); Jeremiah from those who sought his life (Jeremiah 26:24).

Were made strong out of weakness. That one deserves its own moment, because it is the pattern of nearly every name on the list. Not strong men who stayed strong. Weak men who were made strong, which is a passive verb and locates the strength somewhere other than in them. Gideon, the least in his father’s house (Judges 6:15); Samson, blind and shackled at the end (Judges 16:28); Hezekiah, raised from his sickbed (Isaiah 38). My power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9).

Became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight. Jonathan and his armour-bearer (1 Samuel 14), David, Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20). The list ends at its most triumphant, and the very next words in the chapter are women received back their dead, and then the whole thing turns over.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith always brings visible victory. The next verses describe those who suffered and died in faith. Nor does including Samson and Jephthah mean their sins were acceptable; Scripture records them honestly as warnings. Jephthah’s rash vow, however it was fulfilled, is not held up as a model.

Why does God put such flawed people in the hall of faith? Because the chapter is about faith, and faith is trust in God, not confidence in oneself. If the list were made of flawless people, none of us could hope to be on it. God includes Samson and Jephthah to show that he works through the faith of sinners, and to give hope to everyone who knows his own failures. But the honesty of Scripture cuts both ways: their sins brought real harm, to themselves and others. God’s grace in using them is not permission to imitate their folly. It is an invitation to trust the same God.

In a sentence. What more should I say? I do not have time to tell about Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah, about David and Samuel and the prophets, who through faith conquered kingdoms, ruled with justice and gained what was promised; who shut the mouths of lions, put out the fury of flames and escaped the edge of the sword; whose weakness was turned to strength; and who became powerful in battle and routed foreign armies.

On a Tuesday. Feeling too weak or flawed to be used by God? Look at this list. God uses weak people who trust him. Name your weakness to God today, specifically, whether it is fear, lack of ability, a past failure or a body that does not work as it used to. Then take one step in the thing he has given you to do, asking him to make you strong out of weakness. It is his strength you need, not yours.

For worship. Time would fail to tell of all that God has done through people who trusted him: lions shut up, fire made harmless, armies scattered, weak men made strong. And the strength was always his. He chose the fearful and the flawed and the foolish, so that no one could boast in his presence. And all of them were pointing to one greater than themselves: the true Judge and King and Prophet, who conquered the kingdom of darkness, worked perfect righteousness, and was crucified in weakness and raised in power. Every victory in this list is a small picture of his.
verseByVerse.note: Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah are from Judges; the lions’ mouths recall Daniel, and the fire recalls his three friends.

verseByVerse.quote: Women received back their dead by resurrection. Some were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life. Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword. They went about in skins of sheep and goats, destitute, afflicted, mistreated— of whom the world was not worthy—wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Women received back their dead by resurrection. Some were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life. Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword. They went about in skins of sheep and goats, destitute, afflicted, mistreated— of whom the world was not worthy—wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.

Women received back their dead by resurrection. Faith at its most spectacular: a dead child handed back alive. The widow of Zarephath, whose son Elijah raised (1 Kings 17:17–24), and the Shunammite woman, whose son Elisha raised (2 Kings 4:18–37).

Some were tortured, refusing to accept release. The turn comes mid-verse, and it is the most important structural feature of the chapter. With that clause the chapter changes direction entirely. Faith does not always bring deliverance. The word for tortured (etympanisthēsan) refers to being beaten to death on a rack or frame, an instrument shaped like a drum. “Refusing to accept release” means they were offered a way out, by renouncing their faith, and would not take it. This probably refers to the martyrs under the Syrian king Antiochus IV Epiphanes around 167 BC, in the Maccabean period, recorded in 2 Maccabees 6–7, which the readers probably knew: the old scribe Eleazar, and a mother and her seven sons, who were tortured to death rather than eat pork and deny the law of God.

So that they might rise again to a better life. The Greek is literally a better resurrection (kreittonos anastaseōs), the same word as the first clause. Some got their dead back by resurrection; some died for it. The identical faith produced both. And theirs was better than being restored to mortal life like the sons of the widows, who would one day die again. They looked to the final resurrection to eternal life.

Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. Jeremiah was beaten, put in the stocks, imprisoned and lowered into a muddy cistern (Jeremiah 20:2; 37:15; 38:6); Micaiah was imprisoned and fed on bread and water (1 Kings 22:27).

They were stoned. Zechariah the son of Jehoiada was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 24:20–22; Matthew 23:35).

They were sawn in two. Jewish tradition says the prophet Isaiah was sawn in two under King Manasseh, a tradition recorded in a later writing called the Ascension of Isaiah.

They were killed with the sword. Prophets killed by Jezebel and Ahab (1 Kings 19:10); Uriah the prophet, struck down by King Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 26:23).

They went about in skins of sheep and goats. This is the prophet’s uniform, Elijah’s garment of hair (2 Kings 1:8), and it is a picture of the men God sent to Israel living like vagrants in the country they were sent to. Fugitives with nothing else to wear.

Destitute, afflicted, mistreated. “Destitute” (hysteroumenoi) is lacking, in need; “afflicted” (thlibomenoi) is oppressed; “mistreated” (kakouchoumenoi) is ill-treated, the same word as verse 25 of Moses. They chose the same lot he chose.

Of whom the world was not worthy. Then, in the middle of the squalor, the writer interrupts himself. It is the great reversal of the chapter and one of the finest asides in Scripture. The world looked at these people in their goatskins, sleeping in caves, and reckoned them worthless, not fit to live. God’s verdict is that the world was not good enough for them. The judgment ran the other way.

Wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth. Elijah in the wilderness (1 Kings 19); the prophets Obadiah hid by fifties in a cave and fed with bread and water (1 Kings 18:4, 13); the faithful of the Maccabean period hiding in caves (1 Maccabees 2:29–38; 2 Maccabees 6:11).

The paragraph they most needed. And this is the paragraph the letter’s readers most needed. A congregation whose property had been plundered could look at the first half of the list and wonder why their faith had produced no such deliverance. The second half says: it produced these people too, and God is not ashamed of them either.

Where Christians differ: does this make the Maccabean books Scripture? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches include 1 and 2 Maccabees in their Old Testament. Verdict: the author refers to events of the Maccabean period, as he refers to the tradition about Isaiah, as true history, without quoting those books as Scripture. Referring to historical events recorded in a book does not make that book inspired. The Old Testament canon received by Jesus and the apostles is the Hebrew Scriptures (Luke 24:44), which do not include the Apocrypha. The canon is closed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that suffering is a sign of God’s disfavour, or that those who suffered had less faith than those who were delivered. Both groups lived by faith; God simply chose different outcomes for them.

Why does God deliver some believers and not others? Scripture does not give us God’s reasons in each case, and this chapter refuses to rank the delivered above the martyrs. James was killed with the sword and Peter was freed from prison in the same chapter of Acts (Acts 12:1–11). What we are told is that God is wise and good in both, that he is with his people in the fire whether he takes them out of it or through it, and that every one of them will rise. If you prayed for healing and it did not come, it was not because your faith was too small. Some of God’s strongest saints are in the second half of this list.

In a sentence. Women received their loved ones back, raised from the dead, while others were tortured, refusing to be released, so that they might gain a better resurrection; some faced jeers and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment; they were stoned, sawn in two and killed by the sword; they went around in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, persecuted and ill-treated, wandering in deserts and mountains, living in caves and holes in the ground, people of whom the world was not worthy.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for persecuted believers around the world, of whom the world is not worthy; find out the name of one country or one prisoner, and pray specifically. If your faith costs you something this week, a friendship, a promotion, a reputation, do not assume God has failed you. You are in the second half of the list, and it is good company. Ask God for courage, and for the better resurrection to be more real to you than the comfort you are losing.

For worship. The world has always measured God’s people by the wrong scale. It saw goatskins and caves and saws, and called them worthless. God saw them and said the world was not worthy of them. And he was right, because he had seen another like them: the Man of Sorrows, despised and rejected, mocked and flogged, who had nowhere to lay his head, and who refused release because he had come to die. The world was not worthy of him either. He rose to the better resurrection first, and every one of these, from the widow’s son to the last martyr, will follow him out of the grave.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition says the prophet Isaiah was sawn in two under King Manasseh.

verseByVerse.quote: And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect.

And all these, though commended through their faith. The chapter ends where verse 13 stood: with everybody still waiting. “Commended” (martyrēthentes), as in verse 2, forms a frame for the chapter. The conquerors and the sawn in two, the ones who shut lions’ mouths and the ones the lions ate: all commended, all approved by God.

Did not receive what was promised. And none of them satisfied. “What was promised” (tēn epangelian) is the great promise: the coming of the Messiah, the new covenant, and its fulfilment in the eternal inheritance. They received many smaller promises (v. 33), but not the ultimate one.

Since God had provided something better for us. And there is the reason, and it is astonishing. They did not receive it because God had something better in view, and the something better involves us. “Provided” (problepsamenou) means foreseen, planned in advance. “Something better” (kreitton ti) is everything the letter has been arguing: the better covenant, the better sacrifice, the better priest, the coming of Christ, the full revelation and accomplishment of salvation. They lived on promises; we live after the fulfilment. They saw the shadow and greeted it from afar; we have the substance.

That apart from us they should not be made perfect. Read that slowly. Abraham cannot be completed without the congregation that first heard this letter read. Moses waits on us. The whole company of the Old Testament faithful is not brought to its end separately and earlier, but together with people who were not born for centuries. “Made perfect” (teleiōthōsin) is the letter’s word: brought to completion. Their final perfection, resurrection and glory awaited Christ’s work and will be completed together with us at his return. God’s plan is to bring all his people, from both testaments, to glory together as one family (12:23; Revelation 7:9).

Where were the Old Testament saints in the meantime? Some traditions teach that they waited in a holding place below until Christ descended to set them free. Scripture gives little ground for that. Jesus told the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43), and this letter speaks of the spirits of the righteous made perfect, already in God’s presence (12:23). Believers who died before Christ were with God in conscious blessing. What they wait for, with us, is the resurrection of the body, the perfection that will come to the whole church together.

A congregation that did not know what it had. Which places the readers of this letter in a position they had entirely failed to appreciate. They were drifting back toward the era these giants had lived in and longed to escape, and the whole gallery of them had died waiting for what this discouraged little congregation actually possessed. And the final note is one of solidarity across the centuries. There is one people of God, not two. Everyone in this chapter and everyone reading it arrives at the same moment, by the same faith, through the same sacrifice. And the writer is about to say what that means for people who are tired: they are not running alone, and the stands are full.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Old Testament believers were not saved. They were saved by faith in the promise, on the basis of Christ’s future work (9:15). It means they did not live to see that work accomplished, and their final glory awaits the completion of God’s plan.

If they had such faith with so little, what does that say about me? It should humble you and encourage you. Humble, because Abraham trusted God with a promise and a tent, and you have the whole Bible, the cross, the empty tomb and the Spirit. Encourage, because the same God who sustained their faith with less will sustain yours with more. You are not asked to be a hero. You are asked to trust the God they trusted, now that he has kept the promise they died waiting for. Read their stories, and let them shame your complaints and strengthen your hope.

In a sentence. All these people were commended for their faith, yet none of them received what had been promised, because God had planned something better for us, so that only together with us would they be made perfect.

On a Tuesday. Thank God specifically today for one thing you have that Abraham, Moses or David longed to see: the name of Jesus, the finished cross, the open way into God’s presence, the Spirit in your heart, the whole New Testament. Then think of yourself as part of one long family. Pick one person from this chapter and read their story this week, not as ancient history, but as the story of your own family, whose ending you will share.

For worship. God has been gathering one family across all the ages, and he will not bring any of them to the finish line alone. Abraham and Moses and the martyrs in the caves are waiting for the day when the whole family is complete, and on that day they will be made perfect together with us, and we with them. The something better God planned for us is his Son, the substance of every shadow they saw. They died greeting him from afar. We know his name. And one day the great cloud of the faithful and the last believer to come to Christ will rise together, and stand together, and see together the one they all believed in.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.<sup>2</sup>For by it the people of old received their commendation.<sup>3</sup>By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible.<sup>4</sup>By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain, through which he was commended as righteous, God commending him by accepting his gifts. And through his faith, though he died, he still speaks.<sup>5</sup>By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him. Now before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God.<sup>6</sup>And without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.<sup>7</sup>By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household. By this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.<sup>8</sup>By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going.<sup>9</sup>By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise.<sup>10</sup>For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God.<sup>11</sup>By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age, since she considered him faithful who had promised.<sup>12</sup>Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead, were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as many as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore.<sup>13</sup>These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth.<sup>14</sup>For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland.<sup>15</sup>If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return.<sup>16</sup>But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city.<sup>17</sup>By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son,<sup>18</sup>of whom it was said, “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”<sup>19</sup>He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.<sup>20</sup>By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau.<sup>21</sup>By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, bowing in worship over the head of his staff.<sup>22</sup>By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones.<sup>23</sup>By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict.<sup>24</sup>By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter,<sup>25</sup>choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin.<sup>26</sup>He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking to the reward.<sup>27</sup>By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king, for he endured as seeing him who is invisible.<sup>28</sup>By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood, so that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them.<sup>29</sup>By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land, but the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned.<sup>30</sup>By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days.<sup>31</sup>By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.<sup>32</sup>And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets—<sup>33</sup>who through faith conquered kingdoms, enforced justice, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions,<sup>34</sup>quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight.<sup>35</sup>Women received back their dead by resurrection. Some were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life.<sup>36</sup>Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment.<sup>37</sup>They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword. They went about in skins of sheep and goats, destitute, afflicted, mistreated—<sup>38</sup>of whom the world was not worthy—wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.<sup>39</sup>And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised,<sup>40</sup>since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect.

12.title: Fix Your Eyes on Jesus: The Discipline of the Father
12.overview:
Chapter 11 filled the stadium; chapter 12 says: run. Strip off what slows you, keep going, and look at Jesus, who ran the hardest course and sat down at the finish. Then the writer reads the readers’ hardships for them: not a sign that God has left them, but the training a Father gives his children, painful now and fruitful later.

The chapter ends with two mountains. Sinai was fire, darkness and a voice the people begged to stop. The church has come to Mount Zion: the city of God, angels in festival, the assembly of the firstborn, the righteous dead made perfect, and Jesus, whose blood speaks better than Abel’s. So do not refuse the one speaking, and worship with reverence, because the God of Zion is still a consuming fire.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Run the Race, and Read the Discipline
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Surrounded by so many witnesses to faith, believers should throw off every hindrance and the sin that trips them, and run their race with endurance, keeping their eyes on Jesus, who began and completes our faith. For the joy ahead he endured the cross, scorning its shame, and now reigns at God’s right hand. Considering what he endured from sinners will keep them from losing heart; they have not yet resisted to the point of bloodshed. Their hardships should be understood as a father’s discipline. As Proverbs says, the Lord disciplines those he loves; that is proof that they are his children. Human fathers discipline for a short time as they think best; God disciplines for our good, that we may share his holiness. It is painful at the time, but it produces a peaceful harvest of righteousness in those trained by it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Timescales

Run looking to Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy set before him. The Father's discipline is painful for the moment, but later yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Suffering believers wondered whether God had abandoned them.

Now: Hardship received from God's hand is a mark of sonship, not of rejection. Do not make light of it, and do not faint under it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us,

Meaning first. Hebrews 12 turns the faith of chapter 11 into a call to run. Surrounded by that great cloud of witnesses, believers are to throw off every hindrance and sin and run the race with endurance, fixing their eyes on Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy set before him and now sits enthroned (vv. 1–3). Their hardships are the Father’s loving discipline: the Lord disciplines those he loves, as fathers discipline their sons; it is painful for the moment, but it produces the peaceful fruit of righteousness and a share in his holiness (vv. 4–11). So they must strengthen weak hands and knees, pursue peace with all and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord, and watch that no one falls short of the grace of God, lets bitterness grow, or becomes like Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal and later could not get the blessing back (vv. 12–17). Then a magnificent contrast (vv. 18–24): believers have not come to the terrifying mountain of Sinai, with fire, darkness and a voice that made the people beg to hear no more, but to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, to angels in joyful assembly, to the church of the firstborn, to God the judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to his sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than Abel’s. Then the final warning (vv. 25–29): do not refuse the one who speaks from heaven; God will shake heaven and earth once more, removing what is created so that what cannot be shaken remains; so let us be grateful for an unshakeable kingdom and worship God with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire. It is the chapter of a race, a Father and two mountains.

Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses. “Therefore” (toigaroun, for that very reason), and chapter 11 pays out. Everything that follows depends on the gallery just displayed. “Cloud” (nephos) is a great mass, a crowd, a classical image for a vast multitude. The image is a stadium, and it matters to get it right. These are not spectators watching to see how we do. The word for witness is martys, the same root as martyr, and it is the word used throughout chapter 11 of people being witnessed to by God (11:2, 4, 5, 39). They are witnesses in the sense of having given testimony. The stands are full of people who have already run, and whose lives are evidence that the course can be finished. That is encouragement of a different and better kind than being watched.

Let us also lay aside every weight. Two things to strip off, and the distinction matters. “Lay aside” (apothemenoi) is to put off, strip off, as clothes. A “weight” (onkos) is not a sin. The word is used of bulk, mass, excess, and runners in the ancient games ran stripped, having removed clothing that was perfectly respectable but would slow them down. So there is a category of thing that is not wrong and must still go, for no other reason than that it is heavy: distractions, entanglements, good things that crowd out the best. Each runner has to decide what his own are, and nobody else can decide for him.

And sin which clings so closely. A rare word (euperistatos), possibly meaning easily entangling, readily surrounding: the picture of a long robe wrapping round the legs of a runner and tripping him. Sin is not described here as attractive but as obstructive. It trips you. In context it may be especially the sin of unbelief and turning back (3:12–13), the sin that would bring the whole race to a stop.

And let us run with endurance the race that is set before us. “Run” (trechōmen) is present tense: keep running. The word for race is agōn, the contest, the struggle, from which we get agony. And the discipline required is not speed but endurance (hypomonē), staying under, as in 10:36. The Christian life is not a sprint but a long-distance race, and the letter has never suggested otherwise. And “set before us” (prokeimenon, lying ahead) is a quiet comfort. The course is marked out, and it was marked out by somebody else. A runner does not choose the route; he is not responsible for its length or its gradients, only for staying on it. God has set the course; we must run it.

Where Christians differ: are the departed saints watching us? Some read surrounded by witnesses as teaching that departed believers watch and cheer us from heaven, and some traditions draw from this the practice of praying to the saints. Verdict: the main sense of witnesses is those who testify by their faith, as chapter 11 has just shown (11:2, 4, 5, 39 use the related verb, commended). Whether the departed are aware of events on earth is not clearly taught, and Scripture gives no warrant for praying to them; there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). The departed saints are consciously with the Lord (Philippians 1:23; 12:23), but our eyes are to be fixed on Jesus, not on them (v. 2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we run to earn salvation. We run because we have been saved, toward the prize of final glory. The race is not an entrance examination; it is the life of those who have already been entered.

How do I know what my weights are? Ask what slows you down in following Christ, even if it is not sinful in itself. A useful test: what regularly crowds out prayer, Scripture, worship or love for others? What do you reach for when you should be reaching for God? It might be your phone, a hobby, an ambition, a friendship, a busy diary, or even good church work done at the expense of your family. You do not have to strip off everything at once, and other believers may carry things that you cannot. But if something keeps tripping your heart, lay it down, and see how much lighter the running becomes.

In a sentence. Since, then, we are surrounded by such a vast crowd of witnesses, let us throw off everything that slows us down and the sin that so easily trips us up, and let us run with perseverance the race marked out for us,

On a Tuesday. What weight is slowing you down in the Christian race? Name it, and lay it aside this week: delete the app, cancel the subscription, end the habit, say no to the commitment. And name the sin that most often entangles you. Do not just resolve to try harder; tell a trusted Christian friend, and ask them to ask you about it. Runners who strip for the race do not keep a little of the robe on.

For worship. The stands are full. Abel and Abraham and Moses and Rahab and the martyrs in the caves have run this course before us, and their lives shout that it can be finished, because God carried every one of them to the end. He has marked out the course for us, too, with its hills and its long stretches, and he did not set it so that we would fail. The same God who brought them home is bringing us, and the whole crowd of witnesses is a testimony not to their strength, but to his faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.

Looking to Jesus. The participle (aphorōntes) means looking away from everything else to one thing: a deliberate turning of the eyes. A runner keeps his eyes on the goal, not on the crowd, the other runners, or the obstacles. Which is remarkable given what precedes it. The writer has just filled the stadium with heroes, and now tells his readers to stop looking at them. The cloud of witnesses is an encouragement, not a focus. We look away from the witnesses, away from our circumstances, away from ourselves, to Jesus.

The founder and perfecter of our faith. “Founder” is archēgos, the pioneer word from 2:10: the man at the head of the column who opens the way, the leader, the originator, the champion. “Perfecter” (teleiōtēs) is the completer, the finisher, the one who brings it to its end. He runs first and he finishes; he is at both ends of the course. Note also that the Greek has no our; it is simply the faith. He is not merely the best example of believing, though he is that: the one who trusted God perfectly to the end. He is the one who begins and completes the thing itself, the author and finisher of faith in us (Philippians 1:6).

Who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross. The same phrase as the race set before us in verse 1: he ran a marked course too, and there was something at the end of it that he wanted. “For” (anti) can mean because of, for the sake of the joy ahead, or instead of, in place of the joy he could have had. Most likely the first. Pause on it, because it says something about how he went to the cross. Not grimly, not as a man resigned. There was a joy he was after, and Calvary was the road to it: the joy of completing the Father’s will, of redeeming his people, and of being exalted (Isaiah 53:11; John 17:5; Philippians 2:9). What was the joy? The letter has already said: bringing many sons to glory (2:10). We were the joy set before him. “Endured” (hypemeinen) is persevered under, and the cross was the most painful and shameful death known in the Roman world.

Despising the shame. Not despising the pain: the shame. For a first-century reader that was the worse half. Crucifixion was designed as public humiliation: the victim naked, exposed, mocked, and cursed, for a hanged man is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). “Despising” (kataphronēsas) means thinking little of, disregarding as beneath consideration. He weighed the disgrace against the joy and judged it not worth attention. The readers were facing shame themselves (10:33; 13:13), and Jesus shows them how to bear it.

And is seated at the right hand of the throne of God. “Is seated” (kekathiken) is a perfect tense: he has sat down and remains seated. The letter’s refrain since 1:3 (8:1; 10:12), and here it functions as the finish line. He ran, he endured, he sat down, which is the proof to every runner still on the course that the course ends. Our race too will end in glory with him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus did not feel the shame or the pain. He felt them fully. But he counted them worth bearing for the joy ahead. Nor does it mean his only motive was his own joy; his joy was bound up with his love for the Father and for us.

How do I actually look to Jesus? By deliberately turning your attention to him as he is shown in Scripture: what he did, what he endured, where he is now, and what he has promised. In practice it means reading the Gospels, so that his face becomes familiar; meditating on the cross when you are tempted or ashamed; praying to him as someone present; and, when trouble fills your horizon, asking what it looks like in the light of his throne. Looking to Jesus is not a feeling you wait for. It is a habit of the mind, and it grows stronger the more it is used.

In a sentence. keeping our eyes fixed on Jesus, the pioneer who leads us in faith and brings it to completion, who because of the joy that lay ahead of him endured the cross, thinking nothing of its shame, and has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne of God.

On a Tuesday. Notice where your eyes go when life is hard: to the problem, to other people, to your own weakness, to the screen. Today, at the moment you feel most pressed, look away to Jesus for one minute. Remember that he endured the cross, despising its shame, for joy. Then go back to the task with his throne in view. And if you are bearing shame for him, a mocking colleague, a family who thinks you foolish, count it as he counted his: small against the joy.

For worship. He ran the course before us, and it ran through Gethsemane and Golgotha. He was stripped and mocked and hung up naked before the world, and he thought nothing of the shame, because he was looking past it to a joy, and the joy was us. He did not merely show us how to believe. He began our faith and he will finish it. And now he is seated at the right hand of the throne of God, the finish line in person, and every runner who looks to him will cross it, because the one who started the race in us is the one who is waiting at the end of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted. In your struggle against sin you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted. In your struggle against sin you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.

Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself. The verb (analogisasthe) is an accounting word: reckon it up, compare, work out the proportion. The writer is asking for a calculation, not a sentiment. Compare your sufferings with his. “Hostility” (antilogia) is contradiction, opposition, hostile speech. He endured mockery, slander, betrayal, rejection, beatings and crucifixion from sinners, the very people he came to save. Some manuscripts read against themselves, meaning that sinners who opposed him were really harming themselves, but against himself is better supported.

So that you may not grow weary or fainthearted. Two words for exhaustion. The first (kamēte) means to be worn out, tired; the second (eklyomenoi) to have the soul give way, to lose heart, to collapse like a runner whose strength fails. And the remedy offered is not rest or a change of circumstances, but a comparison. That is the method of the whole letter, and it appears here in miniature. Faced with people running out of strength, the writer does not lower the demand. He points at somebody and says: measure yourself against that. Remembering Jesus restores strength.

In your struggle against sin. “Struggle” (antagōnizomenoi) is contending against, fighting an opponent. And note that he calls it a struggle against sin. He is reinterpreting their persecution. They thought they were enduring hostility from neighbours; he tells them they are in a fight with sin itself: both the sin of those who persecuted them, and the temptation to sin by giving up. It is the same contest Jesus was in.

You have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood. Then he does the measuring for them, and it is the bluntest sentence in the chapter. “Resisted” (antikatestēte) is stood firm against, and shedding your blood means martyrdom. It should be read for what it is: a hard word, and a fair one. These people had genuinely suffered: public humiliation, imprisonment, the plundering of their houses (10:32–34). The writer knows it and has just praised them for it. And he says: nobody has died yet. Set against verse 2 the comparison is complete. He resisted to the point of blood; you have not. And chapter 11 has already listed people who were sawn in two.

Restoring the scale. There is real pastoral wisdom in it, though it is not gentle. Exhaustion distorts perspective, and a suffering person’s own trouble fills the whole horizon, which is a normal feature of being tired rather than a moral failure. What the writer does is restore the scale. He does not tell them their pain is not real. He tells them it is not the biggest thing in the room.

What it does not mean. It does not minimise their suffering. It puts it in perspective. Nor does it mean they will certainly be martyred; it means they should not give up when things are less severe than what Jesus endured.

Is it wrong to feel that my suffering is too much? No. Feelings of being overwhelmed are part of being human, and the Psalms are full of them. Jesus himself said his soul was very sorrowful, even to death (Matthew 26:38). This verse is not a rebuke to your feelings but a help for them: when your pain fills the whole horizon, look at his, and let it give you perspective and company. He knows what hostility from sinners is. Tell him honestly how hard it is, and ask him for strength for the next step. You are not being asked to pretend; you are being invited to consider him.

In a sentence. Think about him who endured such opposition from sinners, so that you will not grow tired and lose heart; in your struggle against sin you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding blood.

On a Tuesday. When you are weary in the Christian life, stop and consider Jesus: what he endured, and why. Read one of the passion narratives slowly this week, perhaps Mark 14–15, and notice each kind of hostility he faced. Then look at your own hardest situation in that light. It will not make your trouble disappear, but it may make it the right size, and remind you that you are not alone in it.

For worship. The Son of God came to his own, and his own did not receive him. He was contradicted, slandered, spat on, beaten and nailed up, by the sinners he had come to save, and he endured it all without once giving up. He resisted sin to the point of blood, his own blood, and he did it so that ours would not have to be shed for our guilt. When we grow weary, he does not shame us; he shows us his wounds and gives us strength. The one who endured is the one who holds us up.

verseByVerse.quote: And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? “My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? “My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives.”

And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? The question is gentle and slightly reproachful. “Forgotten” (eklelēsthe) is completely forgotten. And note what it assumes: Scripture is currently speaking to them. Not spoke, but addresses (dialegetai, speaks with you, reasons with you), the same present tense as 3:7 and 10:15. A passage from Proverbs is treated as a word arriving in the room this morning. And the writer introduces it as an exhortation (paraklēsis), the encouragement word. He regards what follows as comfort, which tells you a good deal about the argument he is making. “As sons” (hōs huiois): the words of Proverbs are God’s fatherly words to his children.

My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord. The quotation is Proverbs 3:11–12, and “my son” is the first thing said, and it governs everything after it. Whatever is coming is said inside a family. “Discipline” (paideia) is training, education, correction, child-rearing: not merely punishment, but the whole process of training a child to maturity, of which correction is only one part. Then two failures to avoid, and they are opposite errors. The first: “regard lightly” (oligōrei), think little of, make light of. Do not shrug it off, brazen it out, or treat a hard providence as meaningless weather.

Nor be weary when reproved by him. The second error: “be weary” (eklyou), lose heart, faint, as in verse 3. “Reproved” (elenchomenos) is rebuked, corrected, convicted. Do not collapse under it either. Most people are prone to one or the other. Some harden and refuse to ask what God might be doing; others are flattened and conclude he has turned against them. The verse forbids both, and leaves a narrow path between.

For the Lord disciplines the one he loves. And there is the sentence the whole passage turns on, with the two things joined that we most naturally separate. “Loves” (agapa): discipline is evidence of love, not rejection. God disciplines because he loves: those whom I love, I reprove and discipline (Revelation 3:19; Deuteronomy 8:5).

And chastises every son whom he receives. The word (mastigoi) is stronger: it means to scourge, to whip, a strong word for severe correction. The writer does not soften it, and the “every” leaves no exemptions. “Receives” (paradechetai) is accepts, welcomes as his own. Every true son experiences it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every affliction is punishment for a particular sin. The letter has just spent a chapter on people who suffered because they were faithful. Discipline here includes training through suffering, including persecution. The readers’ suffering came from faithfulness, not from sin, yet God used it to train them. What the verse claims is that God is at work in the hardship of his children, forming them, not that he is settling accounts. Nor does it mean God is harsh; his discipline flows from love.

How can I tell whether a hardship is God’s correction for a sin? Sometimes it is plain: you sinned, and the consequences followed, and your conscience tells you so. Then repent, and receive the correction as a Father’s love. But often it is not plain, and you should not invent a sin to explain every trouble, as Job’s friends did. Ask God honestly whether there is anything he wants to show you, and listen to Scripture and wise friends. If nothing comes to light, then treat the hardship as training rather than punishment: God is using it to make you more like Christ. The question is not mainly why, but how do I respond as his child.

In a sentence. And have you completely forgotten this word of encouragement that speaks to you as children: My son, do not make light of the Lord’s discipline, and do not lose heart when he corrects you, because the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and he corrects everyone he accepts as his child?

On a Tuesday. Look at the hardest thing in your life right now and ask which error you are more prone to: shrugging it off as meaningless, or being crushed by it as if God had turned against you. Then say aloud the first two words of this proverb, my son, or my daughter, and hear them as God’s words to you. Ask him one question about it today: what are you forming in me through this?

For worship. The God who holds the universe speaks to us in the language of a father: my son. He does not leave his children to grow up wild, and he does not stand at a distance while they suffer. He takes the hardest things in their lives and puts them to work, for their good. And he does it because he loves them, and because he has received them as his own in his Son, the only Son who never needed correction, and who was scourged for us so that the Father’s discipline of his adopted children would always be love and never wrath.

verseByVerse.quote: It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.

It is for discipline that you have to endure. The writer applies the proverb directly to their situation, and the application is startling. “For discipline” (eis paideian): the purpose of their suffering is training. “Endure” (hypomenete). The hostility, the confiscations, the public shaming: he calls all of it God’s training programme. Their hardships were not random or meaningless. Notice what that does not say. It does not say the persecutors were doing God’s will, or that the injustice was not injustice. It says God is using it, and that a Christian may read his hardest circumstances as a Father’s work without excusing the people causing them.

God is treating you as sons. “Treating” (prospheretai) is dealing with, bringing himself to you. Which reverses the natural inference entirely. Their suffering had raised the question of whether God had abandoned them; the writer says it is the evidence that he has not. Discipline is a mark of sonship.

For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? An appeal to ordinary experience, and in that world it needed no argument (Proverbs 13:24; 19:18). A father who took no trouble over a boy’s formation was not indulgent but negligent. A father who loved his son trained him.

If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated. “All have participated” (metochoi gegonasi pantes) means all have become sharers. Every true child of God experiences it, including Jesus himself, who learned obedience through what he suffered (5:8). Not because he needed correcting, but because he was a true Son walking the road of sons.

Then you are illegitimate children and not sons. And there is the sharpest form of the argument. The logic is uncomfortable and inescapable. “Illegitimate” (nothoi) is born out of wedlock. A man does not train somebody else’s children. In that society an illegitimate son might be housed and fed and would not be raised; he would not inherit, and nobody was investing in what he would become, because nothing depended on it. So the absence of discipline is the frightening thing, not its presence. A life in which God never interferes, never corrects, never makes anything difficult, is not evidence of his favour. If God never disciplined you, it would show you were not truly his.

This is what having a Father looks like. That is the exact inversion of what the readers were feeling, and it is the pastoral point of the paragraph. They looked at their troubles and wondered whether they were still his. The writer looks at the same troubles and says: this is what having a Father looks like.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the more we suffer, the more God loves us, or that those who suffer less are less loved. It means that every true believer will experience God’s training, in various forms, and that hardship is not a sign of God’s absence.

Should I worry if my life is fairly easy at the moment? No. God gives seasons of rest and blessing, and they are to be received with thanks, not suspicion. Discipline does not always mean dramatic suffering; it includes the daily correction of conscience by Scripture, the frustration of plans, the small humblings that keep us dependent. If God is at work in you through his word, convicting you of sin and drawing you to holiness, you are being trained. What would be alarming is a life in which sin never troubles you and God never seems to interfere. Use the easy season to grow, to give, and to prepare for harder days.

In a sentence. Endure hardship as discipline; God is treating you as his children, for what child is not disciplined by their father? If you are not disciplined, as every child is, then you are not true sons and daughters at all.

On a Tuesday. If life is hard right now, receive it as from your Father’s hand. That does not mean calling evil good, or not seeking relief; it means trusting that he is at work in it. Write down one way you can see God using a past hardship to shape you, and thank him for it. Then bring your present hardship to him with the same trust. And if you are a parent, let this passage shape how you discipline: with love, for your child’s good, with the aim of forming character, never in anger for your own relief.

For worship. God does not raise strangers. When he disciplines us, he is treating us as what we are, his own children, heirs of everything he has. And he made us sons at the cost of his only Son, who walked the road of suffering before us and learned obedience in it. Every correction we receive is a sign that our adoption is real. We are not illegitimate, tolerated in the house but not loved. We are sons and daughters of God, and he is taking the trouble to raise us.

parallels.desc: as a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you

verseByVerse.quote: Besides this, we have had earthly fathers who disciplined us and we respected them. Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live? For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness. For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Besides this, we have had earthly fathers who disciplined us and we respected them. Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live? For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness. For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.

Besides this, we have had earthly fathers who disciplined us and we respected them. The argument runs from lesser to greater again, and the observation is a shrewd one. Children generally end up respecting the parent who took the trouble, and thinking little of the one who did not. “Earthly fathers” is literally fathers of our flesh (tēs sarkos hēmōn pateras). “Respected” (enetrepometha) is showed reverence. We submitted to imperfect human fathers.

Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live? The title distinguishes him from fathers of the flesh: God, the creator of our spirits, the God of the spirits of all flesh (Numbers 16:22; 27:16; Zechariah 12:1). And the promise attached is not comfort but life. Submission to God’s discipline leads to life; rebellion against it leads to death (Deuteronomy 21:18–21).

For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them. Then the comparison is made explicit, and it is entirely honest about human fathers. “For a short time” (pros oligas hēmeras) is a few days: a few years of childhood, and then the influence ends. “As it seemed best to them” (kata to dokoun autois) is the concession. Human discipline is a matter of judgment, and the judgment is often wrong. Fathers correct in anger, or inconsistently, or for the wrong things, or out of their own frustration. The writer does not pretend otherwise.

But he disciplines us for our good. “For our good” (epi to sympheron), for what is profitable. No guesswork and no mixed motives. God’s discipline is never mistaken, never excessive, never selfish (Romans 8:28).

That we may share his holiness. And the aim named is startlingly high. “Share” (metalabein) is partake of; “his holiness” (tēs hagiotētos autou). Not that we should behave better, but that we should share his holiness, have a portion in what God himself is. The goal is that we become like God, holy as he is holy (1 Peter 1:15–16). Suffering refines character as fire refines gold (1 Peter 1:6–7).

For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant. One of the most humane sentences in Scripture, and it should be quoted to anyone being told to enjoy their trials. “Painful” (lypē) is grievous, sorrowful. It is not supposed to feel good. The writer concedes it flatly, and “all” leaves no heroic exceptions. God does not ask us to pretend otherwise.

But later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness. “Later” (hysteron, afterwards) is the hinge. Two timescales are in the verse, and almost everything depends on which one a person is standing in. At the moment: pain. Later: fruit. The “peaceful fruit of righteousness” is a harvest of righteous character and of peace with God (James 3:18). The pain is temporary; the fruit lasts.

To those who have been trained by it. And the last clause is the qualification. The fruit is not automatic; it comes to those who have been trained (gegymnasmenois), the gymnasium word from 5:14, exercised as an athlete is. The same trouble can leave one person bitter and another gentle, and the difference lies in whether it was received as training or merely endured, submitted to and learned from, or resisted and resented.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all human fathers are good models. Some are abusive, and God’s discipline is never abuse. The comparison is from lesser to greater: if even imperfect human discipline is respected, how much more God’s perfect discipline.

How can I think of God as a Father if my own father was harsh or absent? Slowly, honestly and with help. This passage itself admits that earthly fathers fail; God is not a larger version of your father, but the true Father of whom every good human father is a faint copy. Look at how the Father is revealed in Jesus: the Father who runs to the prodigal (Luke 15:20), who knows what you need before you ask, who gave his Son for you. Let Scripture redefine the word for you, and if the wounds are deep, talk with a pastor or a trusted counsellor. If your father abused you, that was wrong, and God hates it; it was never his discipline.

In a sentence. Moreover, we all had human fathers who disciplined us, and we respected them for it; how much more should we submit to the Father of our spirits and live! They disciplined us for a little while as they thought best, but God disciplines us for our good, so that we may share in his holiness; no discipline seems pleasant at the time, but painful; later, though, it produces a harvest of righteousness and peace for those who have been trained by it.

On a Tuesday. In your current hardship, ask God: what are you teaching me? How do you want me to grow in holiness through this? Then look for one sign of the peaceful fruit already: more patience, less pride, more compassion for others who suffer, a deeper prayer life. And notice any bitterness creeping in. Bitterness is the sign that the trouble is being endured but not received; confess it, and ask God to turn the pain into training.
