For worship. Our Father is never wrong. He disciplines for our good, never in a temper, never too much, never for his own relief, and his aim is nothing less than that we should share his own holiness. He is making us like himself. And he is patient with the process, for the harvest comes later. The pain is for a moment; the fruit is for ever. Every tear his children shed under his hand is being turned into something that will shine in glory, and the Father of spirits will not stop until the work is done.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So they should strengthen weak hands and shaky knees and make straight paths, so that the lame are healed rather than disabled. They must pursue peace with everyone and the holiness without which no one will see the Lord, making sure no one falls short of God’s grace, that no bitter root springs up to poison many, and that no one is immoral or careless of holy things like Esau, who sold his birthright for a meal and later found no way back. The writer contrasts two mountains. They have not come to Sinai, with its fire, darkness, storm and a voice so terrifying even Moses trembled. They have come to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, to countless angels, the assembly of the firstborn, God the judge of all, the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and Jesus, mediator of the new covenant, whose blood speaks better than Abel’s. So they must not refuse the one who speaks from heaven. God will shake earth and heaven once more, and only what cannot be shaken will remain. Receiving an unshakable kingdom, they should be thankful and worship God with reverence and awe, for he is a consuming fire.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Mountains

Believers have not come to the terrors of Sinai but to Mount Zion, to Jesus and his sprinkled blood. And our God is still a consuming fire: what has changed is our access, not his nature.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Esau sold his birthright for a single meal.

Now: Watch for anyone falling short of grace, and ask what you could not bear to lose — that shows what your life rests on.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed.

Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees. “Therefore”: since hardship is God’s loving training. The words are Isaiah’s (Isaiah 35:3), a promise of restoration spoken to exhausted exiles, and they are a picture of exhaustion rather than rebellion. “Drooping” (pareimenas) is hanging down, slack; “weak” (paralelymena) is enfeebled, paralysed. Hands that hang down and knees that will not hold are what a person looks like at the end of endurance: a runner whose arms drop and knees buckle near the end of the race. Notice that this is the writer’s picture of his readers: not wicked, not rebellious. Tired. And the instruction is issued to them: lift your hands, strengthen your knees. There is something a weary person must do, and being told to do it is itself part of the help. Get up and keep going.

And make straight paths for your feet. From Proverbs 4:26 in the Greek. The image shifts from the runner to the road. “Straight” (orthos) is level, upright. A straight path is not a moral metaphor here so much as a practical one: smooth the way, remove what would turn an ankle. Live in a straightforward, obedient way, without crooked compromises.

So that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed. Here is the reason for the road-mending, and it is corporate. “Lame” (chōlos) is limping, crippled; “put out of joint” (ektrapē) is dislocated, turned aside. The writer is not thinking about the strong runner’s convenience. He is thinking about somebody in the group who is already limping. A rough path is manageable for a sound man and dangerous for an injured one. The same stretch of ground that a healthy Christian crosses without noticing can put a struggling one out of joint entirely, or turn him off the road altogether. The instruction is to consider the limping member when deciding how the church walks. That is a striking piece of pastoral thinking, and it is the practical form of 10:24. The question is not merely what I can manage. It is what the weakest person in the room can manage, and whether my path-making is helping or wrecking him.

But rather be healed. And the note to end on is hope. The lame are not written off as casualties. The expectation is that they recover, and that the straightening of the path is part of how. Our faithfulness helps others.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can make ourselves strong by willpower. The strength comes from God: he gives power to the faint, and those who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength (Isaiah 40:29–31). But we are called to respond actively.

What does making straight paths look like in a church? It means arranging our common life so that the weakest can keep walking. Practically: not flaunting a freedom that will stumble a weaker brother (Romans 14:13–21); being honest and consistent, so that young believers are not confused by the gap between what we say and do; welcoming those who struggle instead of making them feel they must pretend to be strong; preaching and teaching clearly; and helping in concrete ways, a meal, a lift to church, a listening ear. It also means removing obstacles that we ourselves put there: gossip, cliques, harshness. A straight path is one a limping person can walk.

In a sentence. So lift up your tired arms and strengthen your weak knees, and make level paths for your feet, so that those who are lame will not be disabled further, but healed.

On a Tuesday. Who in your church is limping spiritually: a new believer, someone recently bereaved, someone struggling with doubt or sin, someone on the edge who has stopped coming? How could your example or practical help make the path straighter for them? Do one thing this week. And if you are the one limping, do the one small thing this verse asks: lift your hands, in prayer, and take the next step.

For worship. The Lord does not give up on the lame. He is the God who promised through Isaiah that the eyes of the blind would be opened and the lame would leap like a deer, and in Christ he kept that promise. He bends over drooping hands and weak knees and lifts them. And he has made his church a road for the weak: a people who carry one another, so that no limping child of his is left on the way. The healing he began in his Son, walking among the sick and lifting them up, he continues in his body.

verseByVerse.quote: Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.

Strive for peace with everyone. Two pursuits in one verse, and they are held together deliberately, because each without the other goes wrong. “Strive” (diōkete) is the pursuing word: chase it down, run after it. Peace does not happen by accident; it must be pursued (Psalm 34:14; Romans 14:19). And “peace with everyone” (meta pantōn) is as wide as it sounds: not merely with the congregation, but with the neighbours who had plundered their houses. Paul supplies the necessary qualification elsewhere: if possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18). Peace-making is a duty, and it is not always within a Christian’s power, since it takes two.

And for the holiness. And there is the balance. “Holiness” (hagiasmos) is sanctification, the process of being made holy. It too is to be pursued. Holiness is God’s gift and work in us (v. 10; 10:10, 14), but we must actively seek it. Peace pursued alone becomes appeasement, a willingness to agree with anything for the sake of quiet. Holiness pursued alone becomes a separatism that treats other people as contaminants. The verse chases both, and the tension between them is where most pastoral wisdom lives.

Without which no one will see the Lord. A hard clause, and it needs handling carefully, because read on its own it could terrify a believer into thinking his sight of God depends on his own achieved purity. To see the Lord is to enter his presence and enjoy him for ever: blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matthew 5:8; 1 John 3:2–3; Revelation 22:4). Practical holiness is not optional for believers. It is the evidence of genuine faith and the path to glory. Those who show no desire for holiness show that they do not know God.

Status and pursuit. The whole letter forbids the terrifying reading. It has already said that by a single offering Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (10:14): the status is settled, and Christ settled it. What this verse describes is the holiness that necessarily accompanies that settlement, not a qualification a person earns to obtain it. The two are not in competition, and the letter has already used both tenses in one sentence. Nobody will see the Lord who has not been made holy by Christ; and nobody who has been made holy by Christ will fail to be pursuing holiness. The pursuit is the evidence, exactly as with the conditional clauses of 3:6 and 3:14. And the verb should be kept: pursue, which implies the thing is not yet caught, and that the man doing it is still running.

What it does not mean. It does not mean holiness earns salvation, or that we must make ourselves perfect to enter heaven by our own efforts. We are accepted in Christ’s righteousness alone (Philippians 3:9). But those whom Christ saves, he also sanctifies (1 Corinthians 6:11; Romans 8:29–30). Holiness is the necessary fruit, not the root, of salvation. And at death believers are made perfect in holiness (12:23).

How holy do I have to be to see the Lord? As holy as Christ, and in him you already are. Your right to see God rests entirely on his righteousness counted to you and his blood that cleanses you. But the same Christ who justifies you also sanctifies you, and the proof that you belong to him is not that you have arrived, but that you are pursuing. Ask: do I want to be holy? Do I hate my sin and fight it? Am I, over the years, being changed? If so, you are on the road, however slowly. On the last day God will finish the work, and you will see him and be like him.

Must I make peace with someone who keeps hurting me? You must be willing for peace, and do what is in your power: forgive in your heart, refuse revenge, speak the truth kindly, and seek reconciliation where it is safe and possible (Matthew 5:23–24; Romans 12:17–21). But peace with everyone does not mean pretending wrong is right, or putting yourself or others in danger. Reconciliation needs repentance on both sides, and where someone is abusive or unrepentant, you may and sometimes must keep your distance while still wishing them good and praying for them. Holiness and peace go together; neither requires you to stay under abuse.

In a sentence. Make every effort to live in peace with everyone and to be holy, for without holiness no one will see the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you need to make peace with? Make the first move this week: a message, a call, an apology for your part. Is there a sin you are tolerating? Pursue holiness actively: identify one habit to put off and one to put on, and ask a friend to pray with you. Run after both. Neither will come to the person who waits for it.

For worship. The God we will see is holy, and he is the God of peace. In Christ he has made peace with us by the blood of the cross, and he has made us holy by the same blood. Now he chases us with both, and calls us to chase them too. And the day is coming when the pursuit will end in sight. We shall see him as he is, the holy and peaceful Lord, and we shall be like him. Everything he has started in us is aimed at that face.

verseByVerse.quote: See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no “root of bitterness” springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled;
verseByVerse.commentary:
See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no “root of bitterness” springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled;

See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God. “See to it” (episkopountes) is the verb from which we get episcopate, meaning to oversee, to watch over, to take care; it is the root of overseer and bishop. And it is addressed to the whole congregation, not to its leaders. Everyone is to be watching over one another. “Fails to obtain” (hysterōn) means to fall short of, to come late and miss it, to lag behind, the same idea as 4:1, where the danger was seeming to have failed to reach the rest. Not that God’s grace is insufficient, but that someone might not receive it, falling back before reaching it. Note again the individual concern in a corporate instruction. No one. The letter keeps scanning the room for the single person quietly slipping, and here it makes that scanning everybody’s job.

That no root of bitterness springs up and causes trouble. The phrase is from Deuteronomy 29:18, and its original sense matters, because it is sharper than the usual application. Moses warns against anyone whose heart turns away from the LORD to serve other gods, lest there be among you a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit. The root is a person: someone in the congregation whose heart has turned. So this is not primarily about an individual’s private resentment, though the application is fair enough. It is about what one turned-away heart does to a community. Here it means a person, or an attitude, that begins small and hidden underground, then sprouts and spreads poison. “Causes trouble” (enochlē) means to crowd in, to disturb, to harass.

And by it many become defiled. “Defiled” (mianthōsin) is stained, polluted. And the three verbs trace the progress exactly. It springs up: a root is invisible until it surfaces, and by then it is established. It causes trouble. And many become defiled: the damage is never contained to the person. Anyone who has watched a bitter person work through a congregation knows the sequence. It begins underground, surfaces as a grievance that seems reasonable, gathers sympathisers, and leaves a trail of people who have caught something they did not go looking for. Apostasy and bitterness are contagious. Which is why the instruction is to watch early. Roots are dealt with far more easily before they surface, and the whole congregation is told to look.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every negative feeling is a root of bitterness. It refers to a settled turning from God that grows and spreads. Nor does it mean the church should be suspicious and harsh; it should watch over each other in love.

How do I know if bitterness is taking root in me? Watch for the signs: you replay the hurt over and over; you rehearse speeches you will never give; you find yourself telling others about it to gather sympathy; you cannot hear the person’s name without a tightening inside; you begin to resent God for allowing it. Those are roots surfacing. The remedy is to bring the hurt to God honestly, to forgive as you have been forgiven (Ephesians 4:31–32), which means releasing the debt to God even when feelings lag behind, and, where possible, to speak to the person directly rather than about them. Bitterness grows in the dark; take it into the light.

How should I watch over others without becoming a busybody? By caring, not policing. Watching over one another in Scripture looks like noticing who is missing, asking how someone really is, praying for people by name, and speaking gently when you see someone drifting or bitter (Galatians 6:1). It does not look like gossip, suspicion or checking up on people’s private lives. If you are concerned about someone, go to them, not to others about them. And let others watch over you: the person who receives loving correction gratefully is the one best placed to give it.

In a sentence. Watch over one another, so that no one falls short of the grace of God, and so that no bitter root grows up to cause trouble and poison many.

On a Tuesday. Think of one person in your church who seems to be slipping: absent lately, cooler than they were, or nursing a grievance. Reach out to them this week, not to correct them but to care for them. And examine your own heart for any root of bitterness: a person you have not forgiven, a disappointment with God you have not brought to him. Pull it up while it is small.

For worship. The grace of God is not scarce. It is enough for every sinner in every congregation, and it is offered freely to all who come. God does not want one of his people to fall short of it, and so he has set them to watch over one another, a whole church of overseers, each one caring for the rest. And for the bitterness that poisons, he has a remedy: the forgiveness of the cross, poured out on us so that we can pour it out on others. The God who forgave us everything is the God who can pull up every root.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one is sexually immoral or unholy like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal. For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that no one is sexually immoral or unholy like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal. For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears.

That no one is sexually immoral. “Sexually immoral” (pornos) is one who commits sexual sin. Esau is the letter’s final warning, but was he sexually immoral? Genesis does not say so, though his marriages to two Hittite women grieved his parents (Genesis 26:34–35). Some later Jewish writings did describe him that way, and the writer may have that tradition in mind. But the more likely reading is that only unholy describes Esau: the writer warns against two dangers, sexual immorality and the godlessness of a man like Esau.

Or unholy like Esau. Esau is a well-chosen warning, because he is not a monster. He is a man who was hungry. The word for “unholy” (bebēlos) means profane, godless: literally what is outside the temple, common, unconsecrated, treating sacred things as common. It describes a person for whom nothing is sacred, not because he is wicked, but because he cannot see why it would be. Esau’s sin was contempt for spiritual things.

Who sold his birthright for a single meal. The “birthright” (prōtotokia) was the rights of the firstborn: a double inheritance, family leadership, and above all the covenant promise of Abraham (Genesis 25:29–34). Esau traded it for a bowl of stew. That is the horror of the story, and the writer presses it. Genesis records the exchange in a few words: he ate and drank and rose and went his way. Thus Esau despised his birthright (Genesis 25:34). No agonising, no calculation. He was hungry now, and the birthright was a thing you could not eat. He chose immediate gratification over eternal blessing.

Drift with a price tag on it. That is exactly the danger these readers were in. Nobody was asking them to renounce Christ in a formal ceremony. They were being offered relief, property restored, neighbours placated, an end to the shame, in exchange for something that could not be seen or eaten. Tempted to give up their heavenly inheritance to escape present suffering, they were in danger of doing what Esau did. Esau’s trade is drift with a price tag on it.

For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. Later, when Isaac blessed Jacob instead, Esau wanted the blessing back but could not have it (Genesis 27:30–40). “Rejected” (apedokimasthē) is disqualified, failed the test.

For he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears. This is a distressing sentence, and it should be read exactly. “No chance to repent” is literally he found no place for repentance (metanoias topon ouch heuren), and it is debated. Two main readings: first, that Esau could not change his father Isaac’s mind, because the blessing, once given, was irrevocable (Genesis 27:33); second, that Esau himself could not find genuine repentance, because his tears were for the lost blessing, not for his sin. The “it” (autēn) most naturally refers to the blessing, which he sought with tears (Genesis 27:34, 38). It does not say Esau repented and was refused forgiveness, which would contradict everything Scripture says about God. Genesis is plain about it: he cried out for the inheritance he had thrown away, and there is no record of his ever regretting the contempt that threw it. No change of mind, whether Isaac’s or his own, could undo what was done. Some decisions cannot be unmade, and grief afterwards, however real, does not restore what was sold. Esau regretted the loss, but his heart did not change toward God. That is the warning, and it is a mercy that it comes while there is still time to hear it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God refuses those who truly repent. Anyone who genuinely turns to God in Christ will be received: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). Esau’s tears were tears of regret over lost advantage, not repentance toward God. Nor does it mean that every believer who sins has lost their inheritance.

Is it too late for me, as it was for Esau, if I have made choices I deeply regret? If you are grieving over your sin and turning to Christ, no. The very fact that you are sorry for the sin itself, and not only for its consequences, shows that you are not where Esau was. Some consequences of past choices may remain: a marriage ended, health damaged, years lost. But God’s forgiveness is never closed to the one who comes to him through Christ, and he is skilled at bringing good out of ruined things (Joel 2:25). Do not let Esau’s story frighten you away from God. Let it send you to him now, while it is called today.

Why does Scripture put sexual sin next to Esau’s godlessness? Because both trade something holy for a momentary appetite. Sexual immorality takes a gift God made sacred, the union of a husband and wife, and treats it as common, something to be grabbed for immediate pleasure. It is the same contempt for holy things that Esau showed. And it is often how drift happens: not by argument, but by appetite. If you are struggling here, do not hide it. Confess it to God, tell a trusted believer, put practical barriers in place, and remember that Christ’s blood cleanses sexual sin as fully as any other (1 Corinthians 6:9–11).

In a sentence. See that no one is sexually immoral, or godless like Esau, who for a single meal sold his rights as the eldest son; afterwards, as you know, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he could find no way to reverse what he had done, even though he sought the blessing with tears.

On a Tuesday. What single meal tempts you to trade away spiritual blessing: a pleasure, a comfort, someone’s approval, an evening when you are too tired to pray, a relationship you know is wrong? Name it. Then refuse the trade, today, and do it concretely: close the tab, make the phone call, go to the meeting. And remind yourself what your birthright is: an inheritance kept in heaven, and the right to be called a child of God.

For worship. Esau sold his birthright for a bowl of stew. Christ, the true Firstborn, gave up everything he had, not for himself, but to give his birthright away to people like Esau. He was hungry in the wilderness and refused to turn stones into bread; he would not trade his calling for a meal. And because he held on, every believer is now a firstborn, enrolled in heaven, an heir of God. What Esau despised, Christ purchased for us at the cost of his life. Let us never sell cheaply what he bought so dearly.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have not come to what may be touched, a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest and the sound of a trumpet and a voice whose words made the hearers beg that no further messages be spoken to them. For they could not endure the order that was given, “If even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.” Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, “I tremble with fear.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you have not come to what may be touched, a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest and the sound of a trumpet and a voice whose words made the hearers beg that no further messages be spoken to them. For they could not endure the order that was given, “If even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.” Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, “I tremble with fear.”

For you have not come to what may be touched. The letter’s final great contrast begins, and it is between two mountains. “Come” (proselēlythate) is a perfect tense: you have come and are there. It is the same verb the letter uses for drawing near to God (4:16; 7:25; 10:22). “What may be touched” (psēlaphōmenon) is a physical, tangible mountain: Mount Sinai. The old covenant was earthly and physical. And the writer’s first word about the mountain is the one thing nobody was allowed to do: touch it. The boundary was set, and the penalty was death.

A blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest. Describing Sinai when God gave the law (Exodus 19:16–19; 20:18–21; Deuteronomy 4:11–12; 5:22–26). Seven terrifying features are listed: fire, darkness, gloom, storm, trumpet, voice, and the command not to touch. The first four come in a row, and the combination is deliberately disorienting: fire that gives no light, darkness with a storm in it. Exodus 19 describes the mountain wrapped in smoke, quaking greatly, while the people stood at a distance.

And the sound of a trumpet and a voice whose words made the hearers beg that no further messages be spoken to them. That is the detail to sit with. God spoke, and the people begged him to stop. They said to Moses: you speak to us, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die (Exodus 20:19; Deuteronomy 5:25–27). It is one of the saddest requests in Scripture. Offered the direct voice of God, a nation asked for a mediator, and they asked out of terror rather than reverence.

For they could not endure the order that was given, If even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned. From Exodus 19:12–13. The severity extended to animals, which is the point: an ox that wandered across a line it could not understand was killed. The mountain was so holy that even an animal touching it had to die. Holiness is not negotiable, and it does not make allowances for ignorance. God’s holiness at Sinai kept sinners at a distance.

Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, I tremble with fear. The final touch, and it is devastating. Moses’ words recall Deuteronomy 9:19, where he feared God’s anger after the golden calf. Moses, who spoke with God face to face, who went up the mountain when nobody else could, was shaking. If the mediator was frightened, what was it like at the bottom? All of which the writer sets up for one purpose. He is about to say that his readers have come somewhere else entirely.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the God of Sinai is different from the God of the gospel. He is the same holy God (v. 29). The difference is the covenant: at Sinai sinful people met God’s holiness without a perfect mediator; in Christ they meet the same God through the blood that brings peace.

Why did God make Sinai so terrifying? To show what his holiness means for sinners who approach him without a perfect mediator. The fire, the darkness and the boundary were not cruelty; they were truth. Sin cannot stand in the presence of a holy God, and Israel needed to learn it before they could understand why a sacrifice and a priest were needed. The terror of Sinai is the background against which the welcome of Zion becomes good news. Without it we would think God easy to approach; with it we see what Christ has done in bringing us near.

In a sentence. You have not come to a mountain that can be touched, burning with fire, to darkness, gloom and storm, to a trumpet blast and a voice that made those who heard it beg that no more words be spoken to them, for they could not bear the command, If even an animal touches the mountain, it must be stoned to death; the sight was so terrifying that Moses said, I am trembling with fear.

On a Tuesday. Read Exodus 19 this week, slowly, and let yourself feel the fear of it: the boundary, the smoke, the trembling mountain, the command not to touch. Then, when you pray, notice that you are not standing at the bottom of that mountain. Do not take your welcome for granted. Begin your prayer by thanking God that you may come near, and why.

For worship. The God of Sinai has not changed. He is still the consuming fire whose holiness made the mountain quake and Moses tremble. But he has not left us at the foot of the mountain, begging him to stop speaking. He has spoken to us in his Son, and the voice that once terrified now invites. The boundary that no beast could cross, Christ crossed for us. He went into the fire and the darkness of the cross, and came out to bring us into the presence of the same holy God, not as terrified sinners, but as welcomed children.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.

But you have come to Mount Zion. And the tense is the astonishing thing: “you have come” (proselēlythate), a perfect tense: arrived, and standing there. Not one day you will come; already, now, by faith. These people were sitting in an ordinary room in a hostile city, and the writer tells them where they actually are. Not only in the future but in present reality, believers have been brought into this heavenly assembly, especially in worship. Zion was the hill of Jerusalem where God dwelt in the temple, the symbol of his presence and kingship (Psalm 2:6; 48:1–2). Seven things are listed, and it repays going slowly, because it is the fullest picture of the church in the New Testament.

And to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. The city with foundations that Abraham was looking for (11:10, 16), the Jerusalem above, which is free, and she is our mother (Galatians 4:26; Revelation 21:2). He never reached it. They have.

And to innumerable angels in festal gathering. “Innumerable” (myrias) is myriads, tens of thousands. “Festal gathering” (panēgyris) means a festival assembly, a crowd gathered for celebration (Revelation 5:11–12). At Sinai the angelic presence was terrifying (Deuteronomy 33:2); here it is a party.

And to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven. The “assembly” (ekklēsia) is the church. And note that every member is a firstborn (prōtotokoi, plural). Not one heir and a crowd of others; everyone has the birthright, sharing the privileges of the firstborn Son as heirs (Romans 8:29). That lands with some force a few verses after Esau, who sold his. “Enrolled” (apogegrammenoi) is registered, written down: their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 21:27). This is the whole church, on earth and in heaven.

And to God, the judge of all. And the title is not softened. He is still the judge, even in the festal gathering. We come to God himself. But we come to him through Jesus (v. 24), and that changes everything about how the judge receives us.

And to the spirits of the righteous made perfect. The believing dead, and the whole of chapter 11 among them. “Spirits” (pneumasi) are believers who have died, existing consciously in God’s presence before the resurrection of their bodies. “Made perfect” (teteleiōmenōn): completed at last, as 11:40 promised, and not apart from us. Their salvation is complete in that they are free from sin and in God’s presence, though they await the resurrection. This verse is strong evidence for the conscious intermediate state.

And to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant. The sixth, and the reason for all the rest. The climax: Jesus himself. “New” here (neos) is young, fresh. He is the one who makes our access possible. At Sinai the people begged for a mediator and got a frightened one; at Zion they have a mediator who is not afraid of God, because he is God’s Son, and who is not distant from them, because he is their brother.

And to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel. The “sprinkled blood” is Christ’s blood, which cleanses (9:13–14, 19–22; 10:22). Abel’s blood cried from the ground for justice (Genesis 4:10; 11:4). This blood speaks too, and it says something better: not vengeance but pardon and peace. Abel’s blood called for vengeance against the murderer; Christ’s blood pleads mercy even for those who shed it.

Two mountains side by side. Set the two mountains side by side, and the contrast is complete. There: fire, darkness, a boundary, and a voice people begged to stop. Here: a city, a festival, a family of firstborn sons, and blood that speaks in your favour. And the readers were considering going back to the first one.

Where Christians differ: do the dead sleep until the resurrection? Some teach that the soul sleeps, or ceases to exist, between death and resurrection. Verdict: this verse speaks of the spirits of the righteous made perfect as already present in the heavenly assembly. Jesus promised the thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43), and Paul longed to depart and be with Christ (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). Believers who die go immediately and consciously into Christ’s presence, made perfect in holiness, awaiting the resurrection of their bodies.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we are already in heaven physically, or that we should pray to the departed saints. It means we already belong to that heavenly assembly, and in worship we join with it.

Why does Sunday worship feel so ordinary if this is where we are? Because we see with our eyes, and this verse describes what is true by faith. The building may be plain, the singing thin, the sermon unremarkable, and still, every time God’s people gather in Christ’s name, they are joined to the worship of angels and of the saints in glory, before the Judge of all, through Jesus. The readers of this letter met in a house in a hostile city, and this was their reality. Come to worship expecting to meet God, not to be entertained, and ask the Spirit to open your eyes to where you really are.

In a sentence. But you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem; to thousands upon thousands of angels in joyful assembly; to the church of the firstborn, whose names are written in heaven; to God, the Judge of all; to the spirits of the righteous made perfect; to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant; and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better message than the blood of Abel.

On a Tuesday. Next time you gather for worship, remember where you really are: in Zion, with angels and saints, before God, through Jesus. Before the service begins, read this passage quietly. And when you think of believing loved ones who have died, remember that they are in the same assembly you join every Sunday. You worship with them, though you cannot see them. Grieve, but grieve as one who belongs to the same gathering.

For worship. We have come to Mount Zion. Not one day: now. The city Abraham waited for, the festival of angels, the church of the firstborn with every name written in heaven, the spirits of the faithful made perfect, God the Judge of all, and in the middle of it all Jesus, with his sprinkled blood speaking for us. Abel’s blood cried out against his brother. Christ’s blood cries out for his brothers, and its word is mercy, mercy, mercy, and the Judge of all hears it and is satisfied. There is no better place in the universe to be, and in Christ we are already there.
verseByVerse.note: Abel’s blood cried out for justice; Jesus’ blood speaks of pardon.

verseByVerse.quote: See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven. At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven. At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.”

See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. The fifth and final warning of the letter. “Him who is speaking” (ton lalounta) is a present participle, and that is the thing to notice. Not him who spoke, but who is speaking: God, who speaks now through his Son (1:1–2) and through the sprinkled blood of the previous verse. It is the same insistence as 3:7 and 12:5, and the letter’s whole doctrine of Scripture is in that tense. And the verb “refuse” (paraitēsēsthe) means to beg off, to decline, to ask to be excused. It is the word used in verse 19 of the people at Sinai begging that no further message be spoken. So the warning is: do not do what they did. Israel begged not to hear; do not refuse to hear.

Declining without disputing. That is a subtle and searching form of the danger. Nobody at Sinai denied that God was speaking. They simply asked him to stop, because hearing him was unbearable, and the writer says the same thing is available to his readers in a more comfortable form. You can decline a word without disputing it. You can own a Bible, agree with every line of it, and quietly arrange your life so that it never actually speaks to you.

For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth. At Sinai God warned them on earth, through Moses, and those who rejected him perished in the wilderness (3:16–19).

Much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven. “Reject” (apostrephomenoi) is turn away from. The letter’s standing argument from lesser to greater, as at 2:2–3 and 10:28–29. God now speaks from heaven, through his exalted Son, and the responsibility is greater, because the speaker is greater and the word is clearer.

At that time his voice shook the earth. Sinai quaked, and the whole mountain trembled greatly (Exodus 19:18; Judges 5:4–5; Psalm 68:8).

But now he has promised, Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens. The quotation is Haggai 2:6, spoken to men rebuilding a modest temple after the exile and grieving over how small it was compared with Solomon’s. In Haggai God promised to shake the nations and fill his house with glory. The writer sees its final fulfilment in the last great shaking at Christ’s return, when the whole created order will be transformed (2 Peter 3:10–13; Revelation 6:12–14). The contrast between the two shakings is one of scale, and it is total. The first rattled a mountain; the second takes in the heavens. And note that it is called a promise rather than a threat, which tells you which side of it the writer expects his readers to be standing on. For God’s people it is a promise.

When is this final shaking? At Christ’s return, when the present heavens and earth give way to new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13). Some apply it to the end of the old covenant order in AD 70, when the temple was destroyed, and that event was a foretaste; but a shaking of heaven as well as earth looks to the end. Meanwhile the kingdom that cannot be shaken is already ours (v. 28).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God speaks new revelation from heaven today. He speaks through his Son, whose word is recorded in Scripture. To refuse Scripture is to refuse him.

How might I be refusing God without realising it? By hearing without heeding. Common forms are: always applying sermons to other people; reading the Bible for information but never asking what it requires of me; skipping the passages that make me uncomfortable; filling every quiet moment so that there is no room to listen; agreeing with a command but postponing obedience indefinitely. None of these is open rebellion. All of them are ways of begging God to stop speaking. The remedy is simple, and hard: when God’s word touches something in your life, respond to it that day, in some concrete way.

In a sentence. See to it that you do not refuse the one who speaks, for if those who refused him when he warned them on earth did not escape, how much less will we escape if we turn away from him who warns us from heaven? At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, Once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.

On a Tuesday. When you read Scripture this week, listen as to God speaking from heaven, in the present tense. Before you read, ask him to speak; as you read, ask what he is saying to you; after you read, write down one thing to do or believe because of it, and do it. And notice any passage you have been avoiding. That may be exactly where he is speaking.

For worship. The God who shook Sinai with his voice has spoken again, and this time from heaven, in his Son. He has not stopped speaking to us. He did not grant Israel’s request to fall silent; instead, he sent a mediator who was himself the Word, so that we could hear God without dying. And the same voice that warns us has promised to shake heaven and earth one last time, and to leave standing everything that belongs to him. His warnings are mercies, and his promises are certain, and the one who speaks from heaven is the one who loved us and gave himself for us.

verseByVerse.quote: This phrase, “Yet once more,” indicates the removal of things that are shaken—that is, things that have been made—in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This phrase, “Yet once more,” indicates the removal of things that are shaken—that is, things that have been made—in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.

This phrase, Yet once more. The writer draws an inference from two words, as he did from new in 8:13. “Once more” (eti hapax) is literally yet once for all, and hapax is the word used of Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice (9:26–28). Once more implies a last time, and a last shaking implies that whatever survives it is permanent. It points to a final, decisive shaking.

Indicates the removal of things that are shaken. “Removal” (metathesis) is change, transformation, transfer, the same word used of the change of priesthood (7:12). The present created order will be removed or transformed.

That is, things that have been made. That is the definition of what goes: created things, the present heavens and earth, which will perish and wear out like a garment (1:10–12). Everything temporary, everything belonging to this passing age. It is a large category, and it includes the temple these readers were being drawn back to, along with everything else visible.

In order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain. Note the purpose clause, because it changes the character of the whole event. “Cannot be shaken” (ta mē saleuomena); “remain” (meinē), abide, last. The shaking is not destruction for its own sake. It happens in order that the unshakable may remain. It is a sifting, and its object is to leave standing what was always going to stand: God himself, Christ, his people, his word, which stands for ever (Isaiah 40:8; 1 Peter 1:23–25), and the new creation.

A mercy inside a frightening image. That is a considerable comfort inside a frightening image. A shaking removes only what was going to fall anyway. Nothing worth keeping is lost in it, and the tremor is a mercy to anyone whose house is built on the right ground. And it reframes what these readers had already been through. Their property had been shaken out of their hands (10:34), and they had discovered at the time that they still had a better possession and an abiding one. That was a small rehearsal of this. They had already learned, under pressure, which of their possessions were made things.

A question worth asking now. The verse also supplies a practical question worth asking deliberately. If everything that can be shaken will be, then it is possible to find out in advance what a life is built on, by noticing what a person cannot bear to lose.

What it does not mean. It does not necessarily mean creation will be annihilated and replaced from nothing. Scripture speaks of renewal and transformation: the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption (Romans 8:19–21). What is shaken and removed is the old order of sin, decay and death; what remains is renewed creation.

Will the things I love on earth be lost? Everything that belongs to the old order of sin and decay will go. But the new creation is this creation renewed, not abandoned, and God is not a wasteful builder. Whatever is good and done in Christ is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58), believers who have died will be raised in bodies, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into the city (Revelation 21:24). We do not know every detail, and should not pretend to. But what you love rightly, in God, you will not finally lose; you will find it again, purified, in him.

In a sentence. The words once more show that what can be shaken, that is, created things, will be removed, so that what cannot be shaken may remain.

On a Tuesday. Make a quiet list of the things you would find it hardest to lose: health, money, reputation, a person, a plan. These are made things, and they can be shaken. Hold each of them before God and thank him for it, and then tell him that it is his, and that your life is built on him and not on it. Then ask what would change in how you spend your time and money this week if you really believed it.

For worship. Everything that can be shaken will be, and God will do it. He will shake the heavens and the earth and every proud thing in them, and he will do it in order that what is his may remain. And what is his cannot be moved. His throne, his Son, his word and his people stand when everything else falls. The God who shakes is also the God who holds, and those who are built on Christ, the rock that cannot be shaken, will be left standing when the dust clears, in a new creation where nothing ever falls again.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.

Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken. The response commanded is gratitude, which is not the obvious one after a passage about consuming fire. And the phrase (echōmen charin) can also mean let us have grace. Both senses fit: grace received produces thanks, and thanks is how grace is held. “Receiving” (paralambanontes) is present tense and passive in feel: we are receiving. Nobody in this letter builds a kingdom or earns one. It is handed over, and it is the one thing in the universe that will still be there when the shaking stops. “A kingdom that cannot be shaken” (basileia asaleutos) is God’s eternal kingdom, promised in Daniel, where the saints of the Most High receive a kingdom that will never be destroyed (Daniel 7:14, 18, 27). We are already receiving it now, by faith, though it will be fully revealed at Christ’s return. Christ reigns now, and his kingdom grows through the gospel, until it is revealed in fullness at his single, visible return.

And thus let us offer to God acceptable worship. The word for worship (latreuōmen) is the term for priestly service, and by now the reader knows that the whole congregation is doing what priests once did. “Acceptable” (euarestōs) is well-pleasing. Gratitude leads to worship. The right response to grace is a whole life of worship (Romans 12:1), expressed especially in praise and good works (13:15–16).

With reverence and awe. “Reverence” (eulabeia) is godly fear, devout respect, as of Jesus in 5:7. “Awe” (deos) is fear, dread. This is the note the letter refuses to drop. It has spent twelve chapters removing the barriers, opening the curtain, and telling frightened people to come boldly, and it will not let that boldness slide into familiarity. Grace does not make worship casual. We come with confidence (4:16) but also with awe.

For our God is a consuming fire. Then the last sentence of the chapter, and it is a quotation from Deuteronomy 4:24. It is a startling place to end. The chapter began by contrasting Sinai’s blazing fire with the festal gathering of Zion, and it closes by saying that the God of Zion is the same God, and still a fire. That is the balance the whole letter has been holding, and it must not be broken in either direction. The mountain has changed, and God has not. What has altered is not his nature but our access, the blood, the curtain, the priest, and a person who concludes from the open way that God has become manageable has misunderstood the achievement. For those outside Christ he is a consuming fire of judgment (10:27). For those in Christ his fire purifies (1 Corinthians 3:13–15; Malachi 3:2–3), and his holiness draws out worship. Grace and holiness are not opposites.

Our God. Note the pronoun the writer chooses: our God. He does not say God is a consuming fire, in the abstract, to be feared from a distance. He says the fire is ours, which is either the most frightening sentence in the letter or the most comforting, depending entirely on which mountain you have come to.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should live in terror of God. We have peace with him through Christ (Romans 5:1). But we must never treat him lightly. Reverent awe and childlike confidence belong together.

What does reverence look like in worship today? It is mainly a matter of the heart, not of style. It shows itself in coming prepared rather than distracted; in singing words you mean; in listening to God’s word as God’s word; in confessing sin honestly; in taking the Lord’s Supper soberly; and in a sense that the God you meet is holy and great. Reverence can be joyful and loud, as the Psalms are, or quiet; it can be in a cathedral or a front room. What it is never is casual, as if God were a friend we could take or leave, or a performance we have come to judge. Come gladly, and come awed.

How can God be both a consuming fire and my loving Father? Because in Christ the fire has already fallen. The holiness of God is unchanged, and it is a fire against sin. But for those in Christ, the judgment that sin deserves was borne by him at the cross; the fire burned there, on him. What remains for believers is the same holy God, now our Father, whose fire refines rather than destroys, burning away what is unworthy in us so that we may share his holiness (12:10). The same sun that would scorch a man without shelter warms one who lives in its light. Fear him rightly, and you will find there is nothing to fear in him.

In a sentence. Since we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us be thankful, and so worship God in a way that pleases him, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.

On a Tuesday. Come to worship this Sunday with both gratitude and awe: you are receiving an unshakeable kingdom from a holy God. Before you go, spend five minutes thanking him for three specific gifts of grace, and then five minutes remembering who he is: holy, holy, holy. And let gratitude shape the week too. When you are tempted to grumble, say what you are receiving instead. A grateful person is hard to shake.

For worship. Everything else will be shaken, but the kingdom we are receiving will not. It is God’s kingdom, promised to the saints of the Most High, purchased by the blood of his Son, and given to us as a gift. We did not build it and we cannot lose it. And the King of it is a consuming fire, holy beyond our thought, whose fire fell on his own Son so that it could warm and purify his children instead of destroying them. Let us be grateful, and let us worship him with reverence and awe, for he is our God, and there is no other like him.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us,<sup>2</sup>looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.<sup>3</sup>Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted.<sup>4</sup>In your struggle against sin you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.<sup>5</sup>And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? “My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him.<sup>6</sup>For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives.”<sup>7</sup>It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline?<sup>8</sup>If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.<sup>9</sup>Besides this, we have had earthly fathers who disciplined us and we respected them. Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live?<sup>10</sup>For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness.<sup>11</sup>For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.<sup>12</sup>Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees,<sup>13</sup>and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed.<sup>14</sup>Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.<sup>15</sup>See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no “root of bitterness” springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled;<sup>16</sup>that no one is sexually immoral or unholy like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal.<sup>17</sup>For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears.<sup>18</sup>For you have not come to what may be touched, a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest<sup>19</sup>and the sound of a trumpet and a voice whose words made the hearers beg that no further messages be spoken to them.<sup>20</sup>For they could not endure the order that was given, “If even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.”<sup>21</sup>Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, “I tremble with fear.”<sup>22</sup>But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering,<sup>23</sup>and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect,<sup>24</sup>and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.<sup>25</sup>See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven.<sup>26</sup>At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.”<sup>27</sup>This phrase, “Yet once more,” indicates the removal of things that are shaken—that is, things that have been made—in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.<sup>28</sup>Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe,<sup>29</sup>for our God is a consuming fire.

13.title: Outside the Camp: The Unchanging Christ
13.overview:
The sermon lands in ordinary life: keep loving each other, welcome strangers, visit prisoners, honour marriage, be content with what you have. This is not a change of subject. People who have come to Mount Zion live this way in their own streets.

At the centre stands verse 8: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” The founding leaders have died; Christ has not changed, so there is nothing newer to chase. Then the letter’s last appeal: Jesus suffered outside the gate, so go out to him, bearing his disgrace, for here we have no lasting city. The Christian’s sacrifices now are praise and practical kindness. The letter closes with a great benediction: the God who raised the great Shepherd works in us what pleases him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter turns to practical life. Brotherly love must continue. Believers should show hospitality to strangers, for some have entertained angels without knowing it, and remember prisoners and the mistreated as if sharing their suffering. Marriage is to be honoured by all and the marriage bed kept pure, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers. Their lives should be free from the love of money, content with what they have, because God has promised never to leave or forsake them, so they can say with confidence that the Lord is their helper and they need not fear what people can do.
verseByVerse.theology:
Where the Argument Lands

The letter's theology ends in hospitality, prison visiting, marriage and money. Contentment rests on a promise: “I will never leave you nor forsake you.”
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Visiting prisoners marked a believer out publicly, and these readers had done it before.

Now: Keep loving, keep welcoming, keep remembering those in prison as though in prison with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Let brotherly love continue. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let brotherly love continue. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.

Meaning first. Hebrews 13 shows what life in the unshakeable kingdom looks like day to day, and closes the letter. It begins with practical love (vv. 1–6): keep loving one another as family, welcome strangers, remember prisoners and the mistreated, honour marriage and keep it pure, stay free from the love of money and be content, because God has promised never to leave or forsake his people. Then it turns to leaders and teaching (vv. 7–19): remember your former leaders and imitate their faith, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and for ever; do not be carried away by strange teachings about foods, for the heart is strengthened by grace. We have an altar, Christ’s sacrifice, from which those who cling to the old system have no right to eat; as the sin offering was burned outside the camp, Jesus suffered outside the city gate to make his people holy by his blood. So let us go to him outside the camp, bearing his disgrace, because here we have no lasting city but seek the one to come; let us offer the sacrifice of praise and of doing good and sharing; obey and submit to your present leaders, who watch over your souls; and pray for the author. The letter closes with a magnificent benediction (vv. 20–21): may the God of peace, who brought again from the dead the great Shepherd of the sheep by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you to do his will. Then a final appeal and greetings (vv. 22–25). After twelve chapters inside the sanctuary, the letter walks out into the street, and shows that the worship of the heavenly Zion looks like a spare bed, a prison visit, a faithful marriage and a contented heart.

Let brotherly love continue. After twelve chapters of priesthood and covenant, the letter’s practical section opens with the plainest instruction in it. The word is philadelphia, love of brothers and sisters, the affection between members of a family. The church is a family (2:11), and Christ is not ashamed to call us brothers. And note the verb: continue (menetō, remain, abide). It is already there. The writer is not telling a cold congregation to start loving one another; he is telling a tired one not to let go of something they have. Which fits everything else we know about them. They had served the saints and visited prisoners and shared each other’s losses (6:10; 10:33–34). What was failing was not their love but their stamina, and the danger is that love quietly lapses along with everything else, especially under pressure, when relationships fray.

Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers. The Greek is a single word, philoxenia, love of strangers, deliberately set beside philadelphia in the previous sentence. Family affection is to widen into welcome for people you do not know. In a world without reliable inns, which were often dangerous, dirty and immoral, and for a persecuted movement whose travelling teachers, missionaries and refugees depended entirely on believers’ homes (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9; 3 John 5–8), this was not a social grace. It was infrastructure. And it carried risk: opening your house to an unknown Christian in a city that was confiscating Christian property was a decision with consequences.

For thereby some have entertained angels unawares. The reference is Abraham at Mamre, running out to meet three travellers in the heat of the day and hurrying to feed them (Genesis 18:1–8), and Lot at Sodom (Genesis 19:1–3), Gideon (Judges 6:11–24) and Manoah (Judges 13:15–21). In each case the guests were more than they appeared, and the host did not know it at the time. “Unawares” (elathon, without knowing it) is the point. Abraham was not being tested; he was being ordinarily hospitable, and the significance was invisible while it was happening. We never know whom we are serving. Jesus said that whoever welcomes the least of his brothers welcomes him: I was a stranger and you welcomed me (Matthew 25:35, 40).

Something larger than you knew. Which is the encouragement for anyone doing something small and unremarkable for a person they will not see again. The writer does not promise angels. He says that people who have opened their doors have sometimes found they were doing something far larger than they knew, and that the discovery came later.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should show hospitality hoping to meet angels, or that angels regularly come to our doors in disguise, or that we should treat every stranger as one. It means that ordinary acts of welcome can have extraordinary significance in God’s eyes. Nor does it require naivety; wisdom in protecting one’s household, especially children, is still needed. The first readers would have opened their homes chiefly to travelling Christians and believers in need.

How can I show hospitality if I am not a good host and my home is small? Hospitality is not entertaining; it is welcome. It does not need a large house, good cooking or a tidy kitchen. It needs an open door and a willing heart: soup at the kitchen table, a cup of tea, a sofa for a night, an invitation to Sunday lunch for the person sitting alone at church. If your home is not suitable, take someone out for coffee, or host with a friend. Start small and ordinary. The point is that strangers become guests and guests become family, and Christ is welcomed in them.

In a sentence. Keep on loving one another as brothers and sisters, and do not forget to welcome strangers into your homes, because by doing so some people have shown hospitality to angels without realising it.

On a Tuesday. Invite someone into your home this month: a newcomer to church, a lonely neighbour, an international student, a widow, a visiting missionary. Put a date in the diary now. And think of one brother or sister in your church with whom love has cooled, through a disagreement, a slight or simple neglect. Let brotherly love continue: send them a message today.

For worship. The God of heaven is the great host. He welcomed us when we were strangers and enemies, and he did not wait for us to become presentable. He sent his Son to stand at the door and knock, and he spread a table for us at the cost of that Son’s body and blood. Christ himself came to his world as a stranger, and was given no room. Now he is the one who will welcome us home, to a house with many rooms. Every act of hospitality his people offer is a small echo of that welcome, and when we take in the stranger, we find that it is he who has been our guest.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham, Lot and others welcomed angels without first knowing who they were.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated, since you also are in the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated, since you also are in the body.

Remember those who are in prison. “Remember” (mimnēskesthe) is keep in mind, care for: not just think about, but act on behalf of. Roman prisons did not feed inmates. A prisoner without visitors bringing food and clothing simply deteriorated, and the practical content of remember was a basket of bread carried through a door that everyone in the street could see you entering. That is why this instruction cost something. Visiting a prisoner identified you publicly with his offence, and these readers had done it before (10:34), at a time when it was dangerous. Many Christians were imprisoned for their faith. The writer is asking them to keep doing it.

As though in prison with them. The phrase (hōs syndedemenoi, as fellow prisoners, bound together with them) lifts the whole instruction. Not remember them charitably, from a safe distance, but as if you were in the cell. The imagination is being commanded to do something specific: place yourself there, and feel their chains.

And those who are mistreated. “Mistreated” (kakouchoumenoi) is ill-treated, tortured, the same word as 11:25 and 11:37, of Moses and the prophets. The persecuted of the present are put in the same company as the heroes of chapter 11.

Since you also are in the body. The last clause has been read two ways, and both are true and worth having. It may mean: you are in the body of Christ, and therefore what happens to one member happens to you (1 Corinthians 12:26). Or it may mean: you are still in a physical body yourself, and therefore capable of exactly the same treatment. Probably the second. It has a bracing realism about it. Sympathy is easier for people who have not forgotten that they are made of the same material, and a Christian who imagines himself exempt from what has happened to another is not merely unkind but mistaken. You too are vulnerable, so feel for them as you would want them to feel for you.

Refusing the natural instinct. What the verse is really doing is refusing the natural instinct of a frightened community, which is to distance itself from the members who have been arrested. That is the sensible thing to do, and it is what most groups under pressure do. The letter forbids it, and asks for the opposite: identification so close that it is as though you were chained too.

What it does not mean. It does not limit care to Christian prisoners only, though they are the focus. Compassion for all who suffer, including those imprisoned for real crimes, reflects Christ’s heart: I was in prison and you came to me (Matthew 25:36).

How can I remember prisoners when I do not know any? Start by finding out. Several organisations publish the names and stories of Christians imprisoned for their faith around the world, with addresses for letters and guidance on how to pray; choose one person and pray for them by name each week. Many prisoners say that letters from strangers made all the difference. Nearer home, prison chaplaincies and prison fellowship ministries welcome volunteers, letter-writers and supporters, and the families of prisoners often need practical help. Remembering begins with knowing one name.

In a sentence. Remember those in prison as if you were in prison with them, and those who are ill-treated as if you yourselves were suffering, because you too live in a body.

On a Tuesday. Learn the name of one Christian imprisoned for their faith today. Pray for them, and write to them or support an organisation that helps them. And think of anyone in your own church who is mistreated or suffering in a way that isolates them: a member caring for a disabled child, someone with a long illness, a believer whose family has cut them off. Remember them as though you were in it with them, and do one concrete thing.

For worship. The Son of God did not remember us from a distance. He came into our prison and took on our body, so that he could be bound with us and for us. He was arrested, mistreated, mocked and beaten, and he knows exactly what the persecuted feel. He is not ashamed of the prisoner who is faithful to him; he is in the cell with him. And on the last day he will say to those who visited his brothers in prison, you did it to me. The Lord of glory identifies so completely with his suffering people that their chains are his.

verseByVerse.quote: Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterous.

Let marriage be held in honor among all. “Honor” (timios) is precious, valued, held in high esteem. And “among all” (en pasin) means by everybody, not merely by the married, or possibly in every respect. Single people are included in the instruction, and so is the whole congregation’s attitude to the marriages around it. Honouring marriage is a corporate duty. Marriage is God’s good gift from creation (Genesis 2:18–25), and the command had two contemporary edges. Some in the ancient world despised marriage as a spiritual encumbrance, and the ascetic strand that Paul had to correct, forbidding marriage, was already about (1 Timothy 4:3). Others, influenced by pagan culture, treated it as no obstacle to anything they wanted. Both are wrong, and the verse faces both directions at once, honouring the institution and guarding it.

And let the marriage bed be undefiled. The plainness should be noticed. “Marriage bed” (koitē) is a euphemism for sexual union, and “undefiled” (amiantos) is pure, unstained, the word used of Christ himself in 7:26. Scripture does not treat the physical side of marriage as embarrassing or as a concession to weakness; it says it is undefiled: clean, honourable, and not to be spoiled. Sexual union within marriage is good and pure. Outside marriage it is defiled.

What does undefiled require? Faithfulness. Sex belongs to one man and one woman within marriage and nowhere else: not in adultery, not in pornography, not in the lustful look that Jesus called adultery of the heart (Matthew 5:28). Within marriage Scripture is glad and generous (Proverbs 5:18–19; the Song of Songs), and it calls husband and wife to give themselves to each other freely and not to withhold themselves (1 Corinthians 7:3–5). Scripture gives no list of acts. It gives the principles: faithfulness, mutual consent, love and care, and nothing that degrades or harms.

For God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterous. Two words, the first general, the second specific to the breaking of a marriage. The “sexually immoral” (pornoi) are those who engage in sexual relations outside marriage; the “adulterous” (moichoi) are those who violate their own or another’s marriage. And the reason given is the striking part. Not that adultery damages people, though it does; not that it is socially destructive, though it is. God will judge (1 Corinthians 6:9–10; Galatians 5:19–21; Revelation 21:8). The matter is between the person and God before it is between the person and anybody else, and the verse assumes a court that meets whether or not the injured party ever knows. Sexual sin is not a private matter; God sees and will judge.

Pressure does not exempt. This lands in a particular way in a chapter about a suffering church. Sexual sin is not usually what a persecuted congregation is warned about, and the writer includes it without comment among prison visits and hospitality. Pressure does not exempt anybody from ordinary temptations, and it frequently increases them: people who are frightened and exhausted reach for comfort. Note also the placing, immediately after two verses about self-giving. The chapter’s movement is consistent: love that goes out to strangers and prisoners, and a private life kept clean. The same person is being addressed in both.

Where Christians differ: what counts as marriage, and how should the church respond to sexual sin? Some Christians today accept sexual relationships outside of marriage between a man and a woman. Verdict: Scripture consistently teaches that sexual union is reserved for the lifelong covenant of marriage between one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6). All sexual activity outside it is sin. This is held with compassion: many struggle in this area, and the gospel offers full forgiveness and cleansing to all who repent (1 Corinthians 6:11). The church must uphold the standard and extend grace together.

What it does not mean. It does not mean single people are less honourable. Singleness is also a good gift (1 Corinthians 7:7–8), and the Lord Jesus himself was single. Nor does it mean that past sexual sin cannot be forgiven; judgment falls on those who persist unrepentant, and such were some of you, Paul says, but you were washed (1 Corinthians 6:11). Nor does honouring marriage mean that anyone must stay in a home where they are being abused; abuse dishonours marriage, and the victim should be protected and helped.

Can I still honour marriage if I have fallen sexually in the past? Yes, and you must not let shame tell you otherwise. If you have confessed your sin and turned to Christ, you are washed, sanctified and justified in his name (1 Corinthians 6:11), and God does not hold it against you. Honouring marriage now means guarding your present purity, speaking well of marriage, and if you marry, giving yourself wholly to your spouse. There may be consequences to deal with, trust to rebuild, or things to tell a future spouse honestly. Get wise help from a pastor if you need it. But your past is not the final word about you; Christ’s blood is.

In a sentence. Marriage should be honoured by everyone, and the marriage bed kept pure, for God will judge those who commit sexual sin and adultery.

On a Tuesday. If married, do one thing this week to honour your spouse and your marriage: a word of thanks, an evening protected for each other, a confession of something you have hidden, a filter put on a device. If single, honour marriage in how you speak about it and how you guard your own purity, and honour the marriages of others in your church by praying for them and never undermining them. And if you are struggling with sexual sin, tell one trusted Christian this week. Secrecy is where it grows.

For worship. Marriage was God’s idea from the beginning, and he made it to be a picture of something greater: Christ and his church. The Bridegroom loved his bride and gave himself up for her, to make her holy and present her to himself without spot or wrinkle. He has never been unfaithful to her, and he never will be. Every faithful marriage is a small sermon about that love, and every honoured marriage bed is a sign of a covenant kept. And the judge of the immoral is also the Saviour of sinners, who washes those who come to him and makes them clean.

verseByVerse.quote: Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you.” So we can confidently say, “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me?”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you.” So we can confidently say, “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me?”

Keep your life free from love of money. The word (aphilargyros) is literally not silver-loving, the same quality required of elders (1 Timothy 3:3). Money is not evil, but the love of it is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:10). And there is a particular sting in saying this to these people. They had watched their property carried out of their houses (10:34), and they had accepted it joyfully at the time. Now, years later, the sting of the loss had presumably settled in, and they might be tempted to cling to what they had left, or to compromise to regain it. Going back to the old ways would very likely have meant getting some of it returned.

And be content with what you have. The pairing with contentment is exact. “Content” (arkoumenoi) is satisfied, having enough, as in Philippians 4:11 and 1 Timothy 6:8. The cure for wanting more is not having more, but being satisfied with what is already in the house.

For he has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you. Then the ground, and it is not an argument about the futility of wealth. It is a quotation. “He” is God himself (autos, emphatic). The words are God’s to Joshua at the border of the land (Joshua 1:5), and behind that to Israel and Joshua through Moses (Deuteronomy 31:6, 8), and to Solomon through David (1 Chronicles 28:20). The Greek piles up negatives, five of them, in a way English cannot reproduce: never, not ever, by no means will I let you go; never, no never, will I forsake you. Notice what the promise offers. Not provision, though God provides. Not the restoration of the property. Himself.
