The remedy for the love of money in this verse is not a better financial position but a person who has undertaken never to leave. If we have him, we have everything.

So we can confidently say. “Confidently” (tharrountas) is being of good courage. God has spoken; the congregation answers with Scripture of its own.

The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me? From Psalm 118:6. “Helper” (boēthos) is one who runs to help at a cry, as in 2:18. It is a defiant question rather than a naive one. Man can do a great deal: these people knew it, and had the empty houses to prove it. The psalm does not deny the capability. It asks what any of it finally amounts to, when the one who has promised never to leave is standing beside you. If God is for us, who can be against us (Romans 8:31; Matthew 10:28)?

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should never work to provide or save. Diligence and provision are biblical; anyone who does not provide for his household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). It means our security and contentment rest in God, not in money.

How do I know if I love money? Notice what you think about when your mind is free, what makes you anxious, and what makes you envious. Love of money shows itself in worry about having enough even when you have plenty; in reluctance to give; in decisions made mainly for financial gain; in measuring yourself and others by what they own; and in a sense that more would finally make you secure. It can afflict the poor as much as the rich. The test is not your bank balance but your heart: could you lose it and still be content, because you have God?

What if I genuinely do not have enough? Contentment does not mean pretending that need is not real, or refusing help, or not seeking work or better provision. Paul knew hunger and need, and learned contentment in it (Philippians 4:11–13). It means trusting that God, who has promised never to leave you, will give you what you truly need (Matthew 6:31–33), and that your worth does not depend on what you have. Pray honestly, take the practical steps you can, and let the church know; it is part of the church’s calling to share with those in need (v. 16). Being content and asking for help are not opposites.

In a sentence. Do not let love of money rule your lives; be satisfied with what you have, because God himself has said, I will never leave you; I will never abandon you; so we can say with confidence, The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid; what can mere people do to me?

On a Tuesday. Repeat God’s promise to yourself today: I will never leave you nor forsake you. Let it cure your anxiety about money. Then do something that loosens money’s grip: give away a sum that you will notice, cancel a purchase you were planning only to feel better, or write down three things you already have and thank God for them. And when a financial worry wakes you in the night, answer it with the psalm: the Lord is my helper.

For worship. God has made us a promise with five negatives in it, so that no fear can find a gap: never, not ever, will he leave us or forsake us. He gave the promise to Joshua on the edge of the land, and he has given it to every believer through his Son, who was forsaken on the cross so that we would never be. Money will leave us, health will leave us, and in the end everything we have will leave us. He will not. The Lord is our helper, who runs at our cry, and in him we have everything and lack nothing that matters.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They should remember the leaders who taught them God’s word, consider the outcome of their lives and imitate their faith, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever. They must not be carried away by strange teachings, especially about ritual foods; the heart is strengthened by grace. Christians have an altar from which the old priesthood has no right to eat. Just as the bodies of sacrificial animals were burned outside the camp, Jesus suffered outside the city gate to make his people holy by his blood. So believers should go out to him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace he bore, because here they have no lasting city but seek the one to come. Through him they are to offer God a continual sacrifice of praise and not neglect to do good and share, which pleases God. They should obey and submit to their leaders, who keep watch over their souls and must give account, so that their work is a joy and not a burden. And they should pray for the writer, who has a clear conscience and hopes to be restored to them soon.
verseByVerse.theology:
Outside the Camp

Jesus suffered outside the gate, as the sin offering was burned outside the camp. Go to him there, bearing his reproach, and offer the sacrifices that please God: praise, doing good and sharing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: For these readers the camp was home — temple, synagogue, festivals and family table.

Now: Leaving what is not lasting is not homelessness; it is going to where he is.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God. Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God. Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.

Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God. The tense suggests men who had finished: the founding generation of that church, perhaps including apostles, who first preached the gospel to them (2:3), and quite possibly some who had died for it. “Leaders” (hēgoumenoi) are those who lead, guide. And note how they are identified: those who spoke to you the word of God. Not by office or by title, but by what came out of their mouths. That is the whole of their credential. Their authority was the word they preached.

Consider the outcome of their way of life. “Consider” (anatheōrountes) is look carefully at, observe closely. The word for “outcome” (ekbasis) means the exit, the end, the way out: how it ended. The congregation is told to look at the finish of these men’s lives and draw a conclusion. Perhaps some died as martyrs, others in faith. They finished well. That is a searching instruction, and it is the practical form of chapter 11. Doctrine is tested over a lifetime, and the end of a life is where the verdict shows. Anybody can hold a position at forty; what a man is at the close is the evidence.

And imitate their faith. “Imitate” (mimeisthe), as in 6:12. Not their manner, not their gifts, not their personalities or methods, not their circumstances. Their faith: the one transferable thing.

Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. Then verse 8, and it arrives here rather than anywhere else for a reason. “The same” (ho autos) echoes 1:12: you are the same, and your years will have no end. It is the most quoted sentence in the letter, and it is usually detached from its setting. Read where it stands, it is the answer to a specific grief. The leaders who spoke the word to them are gone. The founders die, the teachers die, and a congregation that has buried the men who brought it the gospel feels the ground move. The writer says: the men had an outcome, and he does not. Yesterday: in his earthly life and ministry, and when they first heard the gospel from their leaders. Today: in the difficulty they are in now, interceding for them (7:25). For ever: past every succession of leaders they will ever have, unchanging in his person, his promises and his power. The same Christ who sustained their former leaders will sustain them.

Nothing later to be had. And it sets up the next verse, because a Christ who does not change is the reason strange new teachings are not worth chasing. There is nothing later to be had.

Does this verse mean the miracles of the apostles continue today? This verse is often quoted to argue that if Jesus healed and worked miracles then, he must do the same through his people now. But the context is about who Christ is. The leaders have died, strange teachings are blowing about (v. 9), and Christ remains the same: his character, his saving work and his word do not change. That does not mean every gift he gave in every age continues. The signs that confirmed the apostles’ message belonged to that first generation (2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). Continuationists reply that an unchanging Christ will act as he acted; but by that argument he would still be walking in Galilee. What stays the same is Jesus Christ himself, and that is enough. God still answers prayer and heals as he wills; this app holds, charitably, that the sign gifts of the apostolic age have ceased.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ is static or inactive. He acts in every generation, building his church. It means his character, his promises and his saving work do not change.

How do I imitate someone’s faith without copying their personality? Look at what they trusted and how it shaped their choices, not at their style. Ask: what did they believe about God that made them live and die as they did? How did they handle suffering, money, temptation and death? What did they do when they failed? Then ask God for the same trust, expressed in your own temperament and circumstances. A quiet person need not become loud to imitate a bold preacher’s faith; he needs to trust the same Christ as fully, in the place God has put him.

In a sentence. Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you; think about how their lives turned out, and imitate their faith, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and for ever.

On a Tuesday. Name one person who first taught you the gospel or helped you grow: a parent, a pastor, a Sunday school teacher, a friend. If they are alive, write and thank them this week. If they have died, thank God for them, and think about the outcome of their life. What one thing about their faith could you imitate? And when you feel the ground moving under you, a pastor leaving, a friend falling away, a church changing, say this verse to yourself: Jesus Christ is the same.

For worship. Leaders come and go. Pastors retire and die; the faithful men and women who first told us of Christ are carried one by one to the grave. But Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and for ever. He was faithful to Abraham, to Moses, to the apostles, to the martyrs, to our grandparents, and he will be faithful to us and to our children. He is not a new teaching or a passing movement. He is the eternal Son, who never changes, and the whole weight of history and eternity can rest on him.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those devoted to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those devoted to them.

Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings. “Led away” (parapheresthe) is carried aside, swept off course, like a ship drifting (2:1). The adjectives are chosen with care. “Diverse” (poikilais) is various, many-coloured, and the plural itself is an argument, since truth does not come in a range. “Strange” (xenais) is foreign, alien to the gospel, from outside. Set against verse 8 the contrast is complete. Christ is the same; teachings are diverse. The very variety that makes new ideas attractive is the evidence against them. Since Christ does not change, new teachings that depart from him should be rejected.

For it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace. “Strengthened” (bebaiousthai) is made firm, established. “By grace” (chariti): by God’s free favour in Christ. The heart is established by grace, received through the gospel, not by rituals.

Not by foods. And here the actual issue surfaces, as it has throughout the letter. Whatever these teachings were, ceremonial meals, food laws, sacrificial meals at which worshippers ate part of the offering, some development of the temple system, they were about eating. The old covenant sacrificial meals may be in view, given verse 10.

Two ways of steadying a heart. The contrast the writer draws is between two ways of stabilising a heart. One is grace: something received, from outside, on the basis of what somebody else has done. The other is food: something managed, on the basis of what you take in and abstain from. The second is enormously attractive, and it is worth understanding why. Rules about eating are measurable. You know whether you have kept them, they can be performed today, and they produce a sense of progress that grace never does. A man who has kept the food laws this week has something to show for it.

Which have not benefited those devoted to them. “Devoted to them” is literally those who walk in them (hoi peripatountes), who live by them. The verdict is empirical rather than theoretical. Look at the people who have given their lives to this, the writer says, and ask whether it has done them any good. Such practices never truly strengthened anyone spiritually (9:9–10; Colossians 2:16–23). That is a fair question to put to any system of religious observance, and it is the same test as 10:2. If the practice worked, the practitioners would show it. What Hebrews claims is that they do not, and that hearts are steadied only by what is given, never by what is achieved.

Are Christians bound by the Old Testament food laws today? No. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), Peter was told, what God has made clean, do not call common (Acts 10:15), and Paul says that everything created by God is good (1 Timothy 4:4). Those who still keep such rules out of conscience are not to be despised (Romans 14:1–3). The danger the writer warns against is trusting rules about food to strengthen the heart. Only grace can do that.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be indifferent to what they eat for health. It means food rules do not make us right with God or spiritually strong: the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking (Romans 14:17; 1 Corinthians 8:8).

How can I tell a strange teaching from a true one? Test it against Scripture, and above all against the Christ of Scripture (Acts 17:11; 1 John 4:1–3). Warning signs include: teaching that adds something to Christ as necessary for salvation or spiritual strength; teaching that promises secret knowledge or a higher level of Christian life through special practices; teaching that cannot be found in the plain words of the Bible; teaching that flatters the hearer or centres on the teacher; and teaching that leaves you anxious about rules rather than resting in grace. Ask what it does with the cross. True teaching always makes Christ larger and grace sweeter.

In a sentence. Do not be carried off course by all kinds of strange teachings, for it is good for our hearts to be strengthened by grace, not by rules about food, which are of no value to those who observe them.

On a Tuesday. Be wary of teachings that offer spiritual strength through rules and rituals rather than through grace: a diet that will make you holy, a routine that will guarantee God’s favour, a technique of prayer that will unlock blessing. Feed your heart on the gospel instead. This week, when you feel weak or unsettled, do not reach first for a new method. Read a passage about the grace of God in Christ, such as Romans 5 or Ephesians 2, and let it strengthen you.

For worship. The heart that God strengthens is strengthened by grace, and grace is not a technique but a gift. It is the free favour of God, purchased by the blood of his Son, given to the undeserving and kept for them by his power. No diet, ritual or secret teaching has ever made a heart steady before God. Only the cross has. And the Christ who is the same yesterday, today and for ever does not need supplementing. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and the grace that saved us is the grace that will hold us to the end.

verseByVerse.quote: We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood.

We have an altar. The sentence is startling, because Hebrews has spent twelve chapters dismantling the apparatus of altars, and now claims one. “Altar” (thysiastērion) is the place of sacrifice. The claim is not to a piece of furniture. It is to the cross, to Christ’s sacrifice itself, and to the meal that cannot be had without it. We eat from it by faith, feeding spiritually on Christ crucified: whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life (John 6:53–58).

From which those who serve the tent have no right to eat. And the exclusion is pointed. “Those who serve the tent” are those who cling to the old tabernacle worship, the readers being drawn back to the old system. “No right” (ouk echousin exousian) is no authority. Under the old covenant the priests ate portions of many sacrifices, but never of the Day of Atonement sin offering, which was wholly burned (Leviticus 6:30; 16:27). Christ is the true sin offering, and those who stay with the old system cannot share in him. You cannot hold both. That is the sharpest thing the letter has yet said to people considering a quiet return. Those who serve the tent have no right to eat because they still cling to the shadow and refuse the substance.

For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. Then the argument from the ritual itself, and it is beautifully exact. On the Day of Atonement the blood of the bull and the goat was carried into the Most Holy Place, and the bodies of those animals were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27). Of all the sacrifices, that was the one no priest ate. The holiest offering ended on a rubbish fire beyond the boundary.

So Jesus also suffered outside the gate. Golgotha was outside the walls of Jerusalem (John 19:17, 20; Matthew 27:32), and the writer has noticed that this is not an accident of Roman administration, but the pattern of the ritual, kept to the letter. Like the sin offering, he was put outside, rejected, treated as unclean. Outside the camp was the place of the unclean, the leper, the outcast, the blasphemer taken out to be stoned (Leviticus 13:46; Numbers 15:35–36). Weigh what that means. The place of ultimate rejection, outside, where the refuse went, where the unclean were sent, is where the sanctifying happened. Jesus was not merely executed; he was put out. Excluded, on the far side of the boundary that defined the people of God.

In order to sanctify the people through his own blood. “Sanctify” (hagiasē) is make holy, as in 10:10 and 10:14. “The people” (ton laon) are his people. And he was put out in order to sanctify them. The one thrown outside is the one who makes those inside holy. Through his rejection and death, he made his people holy. Every reader who has ever felt themselves to be on the wrong side of a boundary should sit with that sentence for a while.

Where Christians differ: is the Lord’s Table an altar? Roman Catholic and some Anglo-Catholic traditions identify this altar with the communion table, on which the sacrifice of the Mass is offered. Others take it as the Lord’s Supper understood as a meal. Verdict: the New Testament never calls the Lord’s Table an altar. The altar here is Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice on the cross (7:27; 10:10–14). This letter has said again and again that Christ’s sacrifice was offered once for all and is never repeated (7:27; 9:25–28; 10:12–14), so the verse gives no support to a sacrifice in the Mass. We eat from the altar by faith in his finished work, especially as we receive the Lord’s Supper, where Christ is spiritually present and we feed on him by faith; but there is no new sacrifice offered.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should despise Jewish people. The point is that the old covenant system cannot give access to Christ’s benefits; only faith in him can. The gospel is for the Jew first, and many of the first readers of this letter were Jews who had found their Messiah.

What does it mean to eat from this altar? It means to receive by faith the benefits of Christ’s death: forgiveness, cleansing, peace with God, and life. You feed on him when you trust him, when you meditate on his cross, when you hear the gospel preached and believe it, and in a special way at the Lord’s Supper, where the bread and the cup are given as signs and seals of his body and blood, and faith receives him spiritually. It is not a matter of physical eating, but neither is it merely remembering; it is real communion with the living Christ who died for you.

In a sentence. We have an altar from which those who minister at the tabernacle have no right to eat; the high priest carries the blood of animals into the Most Holy Place as a sin offering, but their bodies are burned outside the camp; in the same way Jesus suffered outside the city gate to make the people holy through his own blood.

On a Tuesday. If you feel yourself to be an outsider, in your family, at work, or even in your church, remember where Jesus suffered: outside. He knows that place, and he made it the place of holiness. And at the next Lord’s Supper, come as one eating from the altar: not offering anything, but receiving everything, by faith, from the one who was put outside for you.

For worship. The holiest offering of the old covenant ended on a fire outside the camp, and no priest ever tasted it. Then the Son of God was led out of the city, carrying his cross, and was burned up in the fire of God’s judgment against sin, outside the gate, with the outcasts and the unclean. And from that altar we are invited to eat. The one who was thrown out has made us holy, and the sacrifice that no priest could share is now the food of every believer. He went outside so that we could come in.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured. For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured. For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come.

Therefore let us go to him outside the camp. This is the letter’s whole appeal in a single line, and everything has been building to it. Thirteen chapters of argument about a better priest, a better covenant, a better sacrifice, and here is what it asks: come out. “Go” (exerchōmetha) is go out, keep going out. Understand what was being requested. These were Jewish Christians. The camp was not paganism. It was the temple, the synagogue, the festivals, the family table, everything that had made them who they were. Going out meant being cut off from their own people, and it meant losing the legal shelter that Judaism enjoyed under Roman law. The pull backwards was not toward sin. It was toward home.

Not into nothing. But notice where the invitation points. Not out into nothing: let us go to him. He is not inside the camp any more. If you want him, you have to go where he is, and where he is happens to be outside. That is the argument, and it is not primarily about courage. It is about location. Following Jesus means going where he went.

And bear the reproach he endured. And the writer does not pretend the cost is small. “Reproach” (oneidismos) is disgrace, insult, as of Moses in 11:26: the shame he told them in 12:2 that Jesus despised. He is asking them to carry the same thing, not something milder. Identifying with Christ brings shame from those who reject him. The readers were tempted to avoid it by returning to Judaism. They must embrace it.

For here we have no lasting city. Then verse 14 removes the objection before it forms. Somebody was thinking: if we go out, we lose everything we have. The answer is that what you have was never permanent. “Lasting” (menousan) is abiding, permanent. Jerusalem itself, the holy city, was not permanent; it would be rubble in AD 70, within a few years of this letter. No earthly city, nation or institution is our permanent home.

But we seek the city that is to come. “Seek” (epizētoumen) is search for, long for. The city is the heavenly Jerusalem (11:10, 16; 12:22). It is the same logic as chapter 11, where Abraham lived in tents while looking for the city with foundations. You are not being asked to trade a permanent home for homelessness. You are being asked to stop pretending a temporary one is permanent, and to go and find the man who is standing outside it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should withdraw from society or not care about their earthly cities. We are to seek the welfare of the city where we live (Jeremiah 29:7). But we do not put our ultimate hope there.

What does outside the camp look like for me? For the first readers it meant leaving the security and respectability of the temple system. For you it means wherever loyalty to Christ costs you belonging. It may be the family that thinks your faith is an embarrassment, the workplace where honesty marks you out, the friends who drift away when you stop joining in, the culture that calls biblical convictions hateful. You go out not by being needlessly odd or harsh, but by refusing to deny Christ to keep your place. And remember: outside the camp is where he is. You never go out alone.

In a sentence. So let us go out to him outside the camp, carrying the disgrace he bore, for here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is coming.

On a Tuesday. Where does following Jesus mean going outside the camp for you: risking reputation, comfort or acceptance? Name one place, and take one step toward him there this week: speak up gently for what is true, refuse a compromise, stand with a believer who is being mocked. And look at where you have put your roots. Anything you would deny Christ to keep is a camp, and he is not in it.

For worship. He went out first. The Son of God left the glory of heaven and then the shelter of Jerusalem, and carried his cross outside the gate, bearing the reproach of the whole world. He did not ask us to go anywhere he had not gone before us. And he is not a fugitive waiting in the wilderness; he is the King of the city that is to come, whose foundations cannot be shaken. When we go out to him, we lose a camp that was always going to fall, and we find a Saviour who will bring us home.

verseByVerse.quote: Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name. Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name. Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.

Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God. If Christians have an altar (v. 10), what do they put on it? The writer answers in two verses, and both offerings are things anybody can bring. The first is praise, and note the qualifier that governs it: “through him” (di’ autou), through Christ, our High Priest. Even praise is not offered directly. It goes up through the priest, like everything else in this letter (1 Peter 2:5), which means the worship of a struggling Christian is acceptable for the same reason his forgiveness is. And “continually” (dia pantos) is a deliberate word in a letter that has insisted the sacrifice for sin was made once for all. That one is finished and never repeated; this one never stops. The old priests offered continually (9:6), and the daily round they kept has not been abolished so much as transferred, and the new offering is words. “Sacrifice of praise” (thysia aineseōs) is the Old Testament thank offering (Leviticus 7:12; Psalm 50:14, 23; 116:17). No more sacrifices for sin are needed (10:18), but thank offerings continue.

That is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name. The phrase is from Hosea 14:2 in the Greek. “Acknowledge” (homologountōn) is confess, profess. Praising God and confessing Christ openly: the very thing the readers were tempted to stop doing. Praise is not only singing in church; it is saying his name aloud in a world that would prefer you kept quiet.

Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have. Then the second offering, and it is the surprise. “Do good” (eupoiia) is doing good, kindness; “share” (koinōnia) is fellowship, generosity, sharing possessions. Practical kindness is put on the altar beside worship, and the same word is used for both.

For such sacrifices are pleasing to God. “Pleasing” (euaresteitai), as in 11:5–6, of Enoch, who pleased God. Two kinds of Christian sacrifice: praise, Godward, and good works, manward, and both are worship (Romans 12:1; Philippians 4:18). A meal cooked for someone, money given, a spare room offered: these are called sacrifices, and God is said to be pleased with them in the same breath as he is pleased with praise. That is a striking answer to anyone who suspects that the ordinary help they give is the lesser part of their Christianity, the bit that does not really count as spiritual. Hebrews has spent chapters on blood, sanctuaries and mediation, and when it finally names what we offer, one of the two items is sharing what you have.

What it does not mean. It does not mean these sacrifices atone for sin. They are responses of gratitude to Christ’s completed atonement.

How can I praise God continually when life is hard? By remembering that praise is a sacrifice: it costs something, and it is often offered through tears. The psalmists praised God in caves and exile, and Paul and Silas sang in prison at midnight (Acts 16:25). Praise does not require you to feel happy; it requires you to say what is true about God, even when your circumstances say otherwise. Start small: thank him for one thing each hour, sing one line of a hymn you know, read a psalm aloud. Praise offered through Christ is always acceptable, and it often lifts the heart that offers it.

In a sentence. Through Jesus, therefore, let us keep offering God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that openly confess his name, and do not forget to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.

On a Tuesday. Offer God two sacrifices today: praise from your lips and a generous act for someone in need. Make the praise specific: name three things God is and has done. Make the generosity specific too: a gift to a struggling family, a meal for a new mother, time given to someone lonely. And if you are tempted to think your practical kindness is less spiritual than prayer, read verse 16 again. God is pleased.

For worship. The altar of the old covenant smoked with blood day and night. Our altar smokes with praise, and with the quiet sacrifices of kindness, and both rise to God through his Son. He has made the one great sacrifice for sin, and he has made us priests, so that the whole of our lives can be offering. Our words of praise are acceptable, though they are stammering, because they go up through Christ. Our small acts of sharing are pleasing to him, because he has received us. And the God who receives them is worthy of every one.

verseByVerse.quote: Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account. Let them do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no advantage to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account. Let them do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no advantage to you.

Obey your leaders and submit to them. The letter mentions leaders three times: those who first spoke the word (v. 7), these, and those to be greeted (v. 24). Here is the instruction about the living ones, their present leaders, in contrast with the former. “Obey” (peithesthe) is be persuaded by, follow; “submit” (hypeikete) is yield, defer. In a time of temptation and false teaching, the church must follow its faithful leaders, the elders who teach God’s word. The command is real and should not be softened, but its ground is worth noticing, because it is not office or authority as such.

For they are keeping watch over your souls. “Keeping watch” (agrypnousin) is literally staying awake, losing sleep, being vigilant: the sentry image, the shepherd on the hillside at night keeping watch over his flock (Luke 2:8). Faithful elders lose sleep over their people.

As those who will have to give an account. “Give an account” (logon apodōsontes) is the accounting word: these men will stand before God and be asked about the people entrusted to them (James 3:1; Ezekiel 34; 1 Peter 5:1–4). That is the reason submission is owed. Not because they are senior, but because they are answerable. Which cuts in both directions, and the passage means it to. It tells a congregation to be led. And it tells anyone who leads that the job is night-watch and audit, not position, a fact that should make a man think twice before wanting it.

Let them do this with joy and not with groaning. The word for groaning (stenazontes) means sighing, grieving: the sound a man makes when the weight is more than the encouragement. Leaders can serve joyfully or with grief, depending partly on how the people respond.

For that would be of no advantage to you. “Of no advantage” (alysitelēs) is unprofitable, harmful. And the reason given is entirely practical. Not you would be hurting them, though you would. A congregation that exhausts its leaders damages itself, because a discouraged man watches less well. There is no version of this where the church wins and the leaders lose. Ask, plainly, which sound your own church makes in the ear of the people who serve it. Most of us have no idea, and the people concerned are unlikely to tell us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean blind obedience to leaders who teach error or command sin (Acts 5:29; Galatians 1:8–9). It means willing, respectful following of leaders who faithfully teach God’s word and care for the flock. Nor does it support a single ruling bishop; leaders is plural, consistent with a plurality of elders. Christians differ over how churches should be governed, and this verse does not settle every question, but it does show leadership shared among several, and accountable.

How far must I obey? The leaders in view are those who speak the word of God (v. 7), and they are to be followed as they lead by it. Their authority is real but not unlimited. Where they command what Scripture forbids, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29); the Bereans were commended for checking even an apostle’s teaching against the Scriptures (Acts 17:11); and elders are not to be domineering over those in their charge (1 Peter 5:3). A leader who uses this verse to control, silence or exploit people has left the ground it stands on. He should be confronted, and if he will not listen, brought before the other elders (1 Timothy 5:19–20); a believer harmed by him may seek help and, if need be, leave. Where abuse is a crime, it should be reported to the authorities.

What if I disagree with my elders on something? Most disagreements are not about sin, but about judgment: a decision, a style, a priority. Then the godly course is to speak to them directly and respectfully, give your reasons, listen to theirs, and if they still decide otherwise, defer gladly unless conscience is at stake. Do not gather a faction or complain to others; that is exactly how leaders come to groan. If the disagreement concerns the gospel itself or a clear command of Scripture, it is more serious, and you should press it humbly, and if necessary seek help from outside. Trust that God holds them accountable, and pray for them.

In a sentence. Have confidence in your leaders and follow their guidance, because they keep watch over you as people who must give an account; let them do this with joy, not with sighs of grief, for that would do you no good.

On a Tuesday. How can you make your elders’ work a joy this week? Encourage them by telling them specifically how God has used their teaching or care; pray for them by name; follow their faithful guidance without grumbling; and come to them with problems rather than talking about them to others. And if you are a leader, remember the night-watch and the audit. Ask God to make you the kind of shepherd who will give your account with joy.

For worship. Over every under-shepherd stands the great Shepherd, who never sleeps and never groans over his sheep, though he has every reason to. He kept watch over our souls on the cross, and he gave his account to the Father for every one of us: of all whom you have given me, I have lost none. He gives his church shepherds who watch for our souls, and he will call them to account. And he will be the judge of all who lead, and the joy of all who follow, and the keeper of the flock that the Father gave him.

verseByVerse.quote: Pray for us, for we are sure that we have a clear conscience, desiring to act honorably in all things. I urge you the more earnestly to do this in order that I may be restored to you the sooner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pray for us, for we are sure that we have a clear conscience, desiring to act honorably in all things. I urge you the more earnestly to do this in order that I may be restored to you the sooner.

Pray for us. “Pray” (proseuchesthe) is keep praying, and “us” is the author and his companions. The writer has spent thirteen chapters instructing this congregation with complete authority, and now asks them for something. That is a small thing and not nothing: the traffic in a healthy church runs both ways, and a teacher who can only give is not in fellowship with anybody. Every leader needs the prayers of God’s people.

For we are sure that we have a clear conscience. “Sure” (peithometha) is are persuaded; “clear conscience” (kalē syneidēsis) is good conscience. The claim is interesting, and slightly defensive. It suggests somebody had said otherwise: that his motives had been questioned, perhaps by people who resented the letter’s pressure. He does not argue the point. He states it and moves on, which is usually the right handling of an accusation you cannot disprove.

Desiring to act honorably in all things. “Honorably” (kalōs) is well, rightly, nobly. His goal is integrity in everything.

I urge you the more earnestly to do this in order that I may be restored to you the sooner. “Restored” (apokatastathō) is given back. He knows them, they know him, he has been separated from them by something he does not explain, illness, imprisonment, distance, and he wants to come back. He believes their prayers will make a real difference. And notice what he asks prayer for. Not for his ministry in the abstract, but to be given back to these particular people. He misses them.

A name nobody recorded. Here the anonymity of Hebrews becomes almost painful. We do not know who he is. The most learned writer in the New Testament, who could handle the Greek Old Testament like a master and construct an argument of this scale, is a man whose name nobody recorded. There is something fitting in that for a letter which has just told its readers to go outside the camp and seek a city that is to come. The author practises his own doctrine: the work outlasts him, and his name was never the point.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the author claimed sinlessness. A clear conscience means not knowingly living in hypocrisy or unconfessed sin.

Does my prayer really make a difference to whether God acts? Yes. God has ordained to work through the prayers of his people, and he does not merely tolerate them; he answers them (James 5:16–18). The writer expected that their prayers would hasten his return. God’s sovereignty does not make prayer pointless; it makes it effective, because we are asking the one who rules everything. You may not see how your prayer fitted into his purposes, and he may answer differently from what you asked. But no prayer offered in Christ’s name is wasted, and the prayers of ordinary believers have upheld missionaries, pastors and persecuted churches across the centuries.

In a sentence. Pray for us; we are sure that our conscience is clear, and we want to live honourably in every way; and I especially urge you to pray so that I may be returned to you soon.

On a Tuesday. Pray today, by name, for your pastor and for a missionary you know. Ask what they would like you to pray for, and then do it. Your prayers matter. And examine your own conscience as this writer did: is there anything you are knowingly hiding, any dishonesty you are living with? Put it right, so that you too can say you desire to act honourably in all things.

For worship. The God who could do all things without us has chosen to do many things through the prayers of his people. He hears the stammering petitions of a small church for a teacher far away, and he answers. He has given us a High Priest who always lives to intercede for us, so that our prayers rise to the Father on the strength of his. And he has kept the name of this writer hidden, so that the glory of the letter would go where the writer wanted it to go: to Christ, who is better than all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter closes with a prayer of blessing. The writer asks that the God of peace, who raised our Lord Jesus from the dead, the great shepherd of his flock, through the blood that seals the everlasting covenant, will supply them with every good thing they need to do his will, and will himself produce in them what pleases him, through Jesus Christ, to whom glory belongs for ever. He asks them to take his short message of encouragement patiently, tells them Timothy has been set free and may travel with him, sends greetings to their leaders and to all God’s people, including from believers from Italy, and ends with grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The God Who Works in Us

The God of peace, who brought again from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, equips his people and works in them what pleases him. What he requires, he supplies.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The writer calls his letter a “word of exhortation”, a sermon sent to people he knows and misses.

Now: After its hardest warnings, the letter ends with grace for all.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the God of peace who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now may the God of peace who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

Now may the God of peace. One of the greatest benedictions in Scripture, and every phrase in it gathers up something the letter has argued. “The God of peace” (ho theos tēs eirēnēs) is the title Paul reaches for when relationships are in view (Romans 15:33; 16:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:23): the God who has made peace with sinners through Christ’s blood, and who gives peace. It is apt here, since this congregation is under strain, tempted toward division, and its leaders are groaning.

Who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus. Stop there, because it is remarkable. “Brought again” (anagagōn) is led up, brought back. This is the only explicit mention of Jesus’ resurrection in the whole letter. Hebrews has concentrated on the ascension and the session, the priest who passed through the heavens and sat down, and only at the very end does it name the rising itself. It has been assumed on every page; a seated priest is necessarily a living one, and his priesthood rests on the power of an indestructible life (7:16).

The great shepherd of the sheep. The one pastoral image in a letter full of priests and sanctuaries, and it comes from Isaiah 63:11, where God brought up Moses, the shepherd of his flock, out of the sea. A new exodus, a greater shepherd, brought up not out of water but out of death. Jesus is the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, the shepherd and overseer of our souls, the chief shepherd who will appear (John 10:11, 14; 1 Peter 2:25; 5:4).

By the blood of the eternal covenant. The instrument of the resurrection is the blood of the cross: not merely its cause but its ground. God raised him by that blood, because his sacrifice was accepted, and the covenant it sealed could not have a dead mediator. The resurrection is the Father’s seal on the covenant. And “eternal” (aiōnios) is the letter’s answer to everything the readers were tempted back toward. The old covenant was becoming obsolete and growing old, ready to vanish away (8:13); this one does not, and will never be replaced (Isaiah 55:3; Jeremiah 32:40; Ezekiel 37:26).

Equip you with everything good that you may do his will. Then the petition. The verb (katartisai) means to put right, to make complete, to fit out, to mend: it is used of setting a broken bone, and of the fishermen mending their nets. God is asked to repair them into working order. “Do his will”: as Christ came to do God’s will (10:7, 9), so his people do it by his equipping.

Working in us that which is pleasing in his sight. And the sentence turns on a hinge that ought to be underlined. Not merely equipping them to work, but working in them (poiōn, doing, producing). It is the principle of Philippians 2:13, it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure, and it is the only reason the whole letter’s demand, go outside the camp, bear the reproach, is not crushing. What he requires, he supplies. Our obedience is real, but it is God’s work in us.

Through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. “To whom” is probably Christ, though possibly God the Father; either way, glory is given to God through Christ. The letter that has exalted Christ above angels, above Moses and above Aaron ends by giving him eternal glory.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we are passive. God equips us so that we do his will. Divine work and human obedience go together, and the one is the cause of the other.

If God works in me what pleases him, why do I struggle so much? Because his work in you is real but not yet finished, and it works through your struggle, not around it. Sanctification is God mending a broken net, and mending takes time and sometimes hurts. The struggle itself, your hatred of sin, your desire to please him, your getting up after falling, is evidence that he is at work. Do not wait to feel equipped before you obey. Obey, trusting that he is working in you as you do, and when you fail, return to the great Shepherd who was brought back from the dead for you.

In a sentence. Now may the God of peace, who through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep, equip you with everything good for doing his will, and may he work in us what is pleasing to him, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

On a Tuesday. Pray this benediction over yourself and your church today, slowly, phrase by phrase. Then pray it by name over one person who is struggling: may the God of peace equip them with everything good. And when you face a task this week that feels beyond you, a hard conversation, a temptation, a duty you dread, remember the hinge: he is working in you what is pleasing in his sight. Ask him to, and then step into it.

For worship. The God of peace has done everything. He made peace by the blood of his Son. He brought that Son back from the dead, the great Shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep and took it up again. He sealed an eternal covenant that will never grow old. And now he bends to mend his broken people, fitting them out for his will and working in them what pleases him, so that even our obedience is his gift. Every good thing in us is from him, through Jesus Christ, and to him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, bear with my word of exhortation, for I have written to you briefly. You should know that our brother Timothy has been released, with whom I shall see you if he comes soon. Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those who come from Italy send you greetings. Grace be with all of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I appeal to you, brothers, bear with my word of exhortation, for I have written to you briefly. You should know that our brother Timothy has been released, with whom I shall see you if he comes soon. Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those who come from Italy send you greetings. Grace be with all of you.

I appeal to you, brothers, bear with my word of exhortation. “Bear with” (anechesthe) is put up with, listen patiently. The warnings have been severe, and the author asks them to receive them in good spirit. And “word of exhortation” (tou logou tēs paraklēseōs) is the technical phrase for a synagogue sermon: it is what Paul was invited to give at Antioch, if you have any word of encouragement for the people (Acts 13:15). So Hebrews is not really a letter. It is a sermon that was sent, which accounts for its missing greeting, its oral rhythms, and the fact that it argues by quotation the way a preacher does.

For I have written to you briefly. “Briefly” (dia bracheōn) is either dry humour after thirteen chapters or, more likely, an honest estimate. Hebrews takes under an hour to read aloud, and given the vastness of its subject it is brief: a man who could see how much more there was to say knew he had been economical (9:5; 11:32).

You should know that our brother Timothy has been released. The one name in the letter, and it is a tantalising one. “Released” (apolelymenon) is set free; Timothy had evidently been in prison. This is the only mention of Timothy’s imprisonment in the New Testament, perhaps after Paul’s death in Rome. If the writer travels with Timothy, he stood somewhere near Paul. It is the strongest hint we have about the circle this came from, and it settles nothing.

With whom I shall see you if he comes soon. The author planned to travel with Timothy to visit the readers. The sermon would be followed by the preacher.

Greet all your leaders and all the saints. “All your leaders”: plural, the elders (v. 17). “All the saints”: every believer, holy in Christ. All, twice. This has been a hard letter, with warnings in it that have frightened readers for two thousand years. It ends by including everybody.

Those who come from Italy send you greetings. “Those who come from Italy” (hoi apo tēs Italias) can be read two ways: Italians living abroad, sending greetings home to Rome, or people in Italy sending greetings elsewhere. Scholars have argued both for centuries. The first reading suggests the letter was sent to Rome, which fits other evidence: the earliest known use of Hebrews was by Clement of Rome, around AD 95. It is a fair reminder that a document can be entirely authoritative and still leave its circumstances obscure.

Grace be with all of you. The last word of the letter: grace. Five words in English, and they are the right last ones. The letter has argued from Genesis to Jeremiah that the old apparatus could not finish the job, that a better priest has sat down, and that the only way forward is outside the camp with him. It has warned, exhorted and taught, but all rests on grace (4:16; 12:15; 13:9). And it closes not with a demand but with the thing that makes the demand possible.

Who wrote the letter? Some early Christians thought Paul did, and the mention of Timothy points to Paul’s circle. But the style differs from Paul’s letters, and the writer says he received the gospel from those who heard the Lord (2:3), which Paul insisted he did not (Galatians 1:12). Apollos, Barnabas, Luke and Priscilla have all been suggested, and none can be proved. The more likely conclusion is that the author was a gifted teacher in the apostolic circle whose name God has not preserved. The letter’s authority does not rest on its author but on the God who speaks in it, and the church received it as Scripture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the letter’s warnings were overstated. The author asks them to bear with his exhortation precisely because it was serious, and loving.

How should I respond to a hard word from Scripture or a preacher? Bear with it, as this writer asked. Do not dismiss it because it stings, and do not be crushed by it as if it were God’s rejection. Ask whether it is true to Scripture; if it is, receive it as the loving word of a Father who disciplines his children. Take it home, pray over it, and act on what it shows you. The warnings of Hebrews were written by a man who loved his readers and wanted them to arrive. Hard words in Scripture are always spoken inside grace, and they end, as this letter does, with grace.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, I urge you to listen patiently to my message of encouragement, for I have written to you only briefly; I want you to know that our brother Timothy has been released, and if he arrives soon I will come with him to see you; greet all your leaders and all God’s people; those from Italy send you their greetings; grace be with you all.

On a Tuesday. Think back over this whole letter. Which warning do you most need to bear with, and which promise do you most need to hold? Write them both down. Then greet someone this week in the spirit of this ending: a leader you have not thanked, a saint you have overlooked. And let your last word to people, in a letter, a message or a conversation, be grace.

For worship. The letter to the Hebrews began with God speaking by his Son, the radiance of his glory, who made purification for sins and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. It ends with grace. Everything between has been the unfolding of that grace: a better priest, a better covenant, a better sacrifice, a better hope, a city that cannot be shaken. Christ is better than angels, better than Moses, better than Aaron, better than every shadow, and he is ours. The writer’s name is lost, but his Saviour’s name is above every name. Grace be with all of you, and glory to the one who gives it, for ever and ever.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy had evidently been in prison. “Those who come from Italy” may be Italians abroad sending greetings home, or believers in Italy itself.
